text:
I started the recycling programme in Year 11 because I had counted the bins. There were nine bins in our school and every one of them was general waste. I wrote a proposal, got sixty-two signatures, and by October we had blue bins in the science block, the library, and the sixth form common room, with a rota of volunteers who emptied them on Fridays into the big container behind the kitchens.

In February the head of site services cancelled it. I got a two-line email. Contamination rates were too high, the contractor had begun charging us as if the blue container were general waste, and the arrangement was costing the school money it did not have.

I was furious for about three weeks. I told anyone who would listen that this was exactly the problem - that adults said they cared and then folded the moment it cost forty pounds. I drafted a letter to the governors. I had a paragraph in it about moral seriousness that I thought was very good.

Then I actually went and looked in the bins.

That is the moment. It was a Tuesday, before first period, and I lifted the lid of the blue bin in the library expecting to build my case, and what was in it was a half-eaten pasta pot, three crisp packets, and a can with about an inch of energy drink still in it, sitting on top of the paper. I checked the science block one. Same. I had been emptying these for four months on Fridays and I had never once looked at what I was tipping in. I had been carrying contamination to the container with my own hands and then blaming a man in the site office for noticing.

I had designed the whole thing around access. Put a bin near people and they will use it. I had never designed anything around what happens after, which is the only part that costs money, and I had never checked, because checking would have made the number of bins I could report go down.

I asked for a meeting and I did not bring the letter. I asked what the contractor's threshold actually was. It is five percent. I asked what a single-stream paper-only bin would cost and it turns out nothing, because paper alone has a buyer. So we came back in September with four bins instead of nine, paper only, a slot instead of an open lid so a pasta pot physically does not fit, and a photograph taped to the wall above each one showing what it is for.

It is smaller than what I started. It has run for a year. I check them on Fridays now, before I empty them, and I write down what I find.

text:
My aunt Rosalind taught me chess when I was eight, on a set with a missing white bishop that we replaced with a thimble, and she is the person I have been arguing with about it ever since.

The argument started properly two years ago, when I told her I was going to start a chess club at my school. She asked how many people at my school played chess. I said, honestly, none that I knew of. She said then what you are starting is not a chess club, and I said that was precisely the point, and we have not got past that exchange in twenty-two months.

Her belief - and it is a belief, held seriously, by a woman who was county under-18 champion in 1989 and still plays league on Thursdays - is that chess is not a hobby you distribute. It is a thing you fall into. Nobody talked her into it; she found a book at eleven and disappeared for a decade. She thinks clubs founded by enthusiasts for the benefit of non-enthusiasts produce a soft, social, tepid version of the game, where nobody studies, nobody loses badly enough to learn anything, and the whole thing dissolves when the founder leaves. She has watched it happen at three schools. "You will teach forty people to move the pieces," she said, "and none of them will ever play chess."

I thought she was wrong for a reason I could not articulate at the time and can now. Her account of how people find things assumes the book is on the shelf. She found chess at eleven because there was a chess book in a house where a chess book could plausibly be. There is no chess book in most of the houses I know. Our school library has one, published in 1978, on obscure endgame studies, which is roughly like introducing someone to music via a treatise on the fugue. The absence of chess players at my school was not evidence that nobody there would love chess. It was evidence that nobody there had been given the chance to find out.

So I started it, and I did it in a way that I knew she would disapprove of. No ladder, no ratings, no clock for the first term. I bought fourteen sets from a wholesaler with money from the student fund and left them out at lunch in the humanities corridor with a sign saying you do not need to know how. I taught the moves individually, badly, twelve or fifteen times over. We played a lot of games that were not chess: four-player nonsense, a variant where captured pieces come back, one afternoon that was mostly building towers out of rooks.

By the second term we had thirty-one people on a list and about twelve who came every week.

Here is what I have to concede to her. Of those twelve, I would say two actually play chess in the sense she means it. One is a Year 9 called Devan who is now better than I am and who studies openings on his phone on the bus, and one is a girl in my year who took up correspondence chess and will not tell anyone her rating. The other ten come for the room. They play a game and a half in an hour and talk the whole time and one of them still hangs his queen most weeks. Rosalind, if she saw it, would say: exactly.

But I have stopped thinking that the number two is a failure. Before the club there was a zero. Devan did not exist as a chess player in 2023 and would not have existed in 2033 either, because there was no shelf and no book. Two out of thirty-one is a terrible conversion rate and an infinite improvement.

What I actually changed my mind about, in the middle of all this, was subtler and it is the thing I would want to argue with her about now if she would let me. I began believing that the ten who chat and hang their queens were the cost of finding the two. I have come round to thinking they might be the point, or at least a point of equal size. I do not think chess is doing anything mystical for them. But there is a room, at lunch, on a Wednesday, where the entry requirement is nothing and the activity gives your hands something to do while you talk, and about a third of the people who come to it are people who were previously eating lunch alone.

Rosalind still says I am running a youth club with boards in it. She may be right about what it is. We disagree about whether that is an insult.

She sent me a chess book for my seventeenth birthday. It was for Devan. She had written his name in it.

text:
There were twenty-two dead laptops in a store room behind the physics lab, stacked like bricks, and for two years I walked past them almost every day. Most were the same model the government gave out in 2019. In eleventh I asked our vice-principal if I could try to fix some, and after three weeks and a letter from my father he said I could take eight, on the condition that I did not touch anything with a school sticker still on it. They all had stickers. He meant it as a joke, I think.

The first three were easy and made me stupid. One needed a RAM stick reseated. One had a dead CMOS battery. One had a charging port that had come off its pads, and I paid a man in the market forty rupees to re-solder it while I watched. Three working laptops went back to the school in a month, and I was, briefly, the boy who fixed the computers. I let people say it.

The other five did not go like that. Two would not post at all, and I decided the problem was the BIOS, because that is what a forum said about that model, and I flashed a chip using a programmer I had borrowed and a file I had not verified. I did it to both boards in the same evening, which is the single dumbest thing in this essay. If I had done one, waited, and seen it fail, I would have had one left. Instead I had two boards that were now genuinely dead instead of maybe dead, and a third that I cracked around the hinge trying to open it the wrong way.

I did not tell anyone for eleven days. When the vice-principal asked, I said the parts were not available, which was not a lie and was not the truth either. The project was stopped in December, politely, with the remaining laptops put back in the store room. I have to say that nobody was angry with me. That made it worse in a way I still cannot explain properly.

My father and I have not agreed about this for a year and a half. He repairs air conditioners and washing machines and he has done it since he was nineteen, so he has an opinion, and his opinion is that the mistake was doing the work for free. He says a man who is not paid is not allowed to say no, and cannot ask for time, and cannot say I do not know this one, bring it back Thursday. He is not wrong about the pressure. I did rush because I wanted to show three more before the term ended. But I think he is defending the wrong thing. I did not brick those boards because nobody paid me. I bricked them because I could not admit, out loud, in front of a teacher, that I had reached the end of what I knew. He says that is the same thing. I say it is not, and we go around like this, usually at the dinner table, usually with my mother telling us to eat.

What I did next was smaller than the story deserves. I bought a cheap logic probe and a multimeter and spent last summer at my father's workbench, not on laptops, on things he was already fixing, mostly holding the torch. I learned to write down the symptom before touching anything, and to change one variable, and to keep the old part in a bag with the date on it. In July I asked the school for four laptops again and this time I gave them a page saying what I could do, what I could not, and what I would do if I damaged one. Two are working. One is a screen I cannot afford. One I have not opened, and I am not going to until I know what is wrong with it.

My father still thinks I should charge. I still think that is not the lesson. He was the one who drove me to the school in July with the four laptops in the back of the scooter, so I know what he actually believes, whatever he says at dinner.

text:
For most of last year I wanted the cows gone. I want to be honest about that first, because the story only works if you know I was on the wrong side of it and pleased with myself for being there.

We have two. Sona is older and has a torn ear from a dog when she was a calf. Lali kicks. Between them, on a good week, eleven litres a day, which the collection centre at the crossing takes at forty-two rupees. I know the number because I was the one who started writing it down.

That was the whole trouble. Ninth standard, I had learned to make a table in a notebook, and I made one. Fodder, the green stuff and the dry, the vet twice a year, the man who comes for artificial insemination, the medicine after Lali's fever, the four hours a day my mother spends that nobody costs at anything. Against it, milk. The bottom line came out to something like eighty rupees a day, and I remember thinking eighty rupees, that is one plate of chowmein at the bus stand.

I argued it at dinner for about seven months. Sell them, put the money in the bank, sleep past five in the morning like a normal person. My father mostly said nothing, which I took as winning. My mother said things I dismissed, about dung for the field and for the fuel cakes, about how you cannot buy milk for a house where a child has to have milk, about Sona being there before I was. Sentiment, I thought. I had a table.

In February a man from Bakewar came with a tempo and an offer for both. Papa walked him around the shed and then walked him to the road, and came back and sat on the charpai and said the number out loud, and then he said what it was for. Coaching in Kanpur. Physics, chemistry, maths. Two years. For me. He did not say it like a big speech. He said it the way you say the price of diesel.

I had done a whole table and left myself out of it. That is the part I keep going back to. Every rupee I had counted as a loss was a rupee holding up a house that was about to spend everything it had on one person, and that person had been sitting there for seven months explaining efficiency. I said no. Out loud, straight away, before I had a reason ready. It surprised everybody including me.

We kept them. The argument did not end that night, it just changed sides, and my mother is the one who now says maybe we should sell Lali, who is genuinely a menace. I do the five o'clock feed four days a week now. I am not good at it and Lali still kicks and I have not become a person who loves cows. Sona's ear still has the tear in it. I check it without meaning to.

What changed is smaller and harder to say. I had thought being right was a matter of getting the arithmetic correct. Now I think the difficult part is knowing what belongs in the table. Four hours of my mother's morning was in mine as a cost, but four hours of hers was never in it as a gift, and I was not in it at all. Somebody who is very sure of his numbers should probably check who wrote the categories.

I still have the notebook. The last page has the eighty rupees on it, underlined twice, which I am leaving there.

text:
My uncle taught me to drive in a 1994 Ford F-150 with a manual transmission and a passenger door that only opened from the outside. We did it in the hay field behind his house in Cass County, where there was nothing to hit except one walnut tree and, in theory, the irrigation pump. He gave me exactly one rule that first afternoon: if you don't know what's about to happen, put in the clutch. Everything else, he said, we would figure out.

I was fourteen. I got good fast, or I thought I did. Within three weeks I could start on the hill by the culvert without rolling back, and I could downshift into second without the truck bucking, and I had started to enjoy the specific arrogance of a kid who can do something adults find difficult. By July I was driving the truck alongside the baler while my cousin Wes stacked bales in the bed, which meant holding a steady four miles an hour across uneven ground with a person standing up behind me.

The thing I got wrong happened on a Tuesday. Wes yelled something I could not hear over the tractor. I turned around to look at him. I did not put in the clutch, and I did not stop, and while I was turned around the truck drifted maybe six feet to the left, and the right rear tire dropped into a shallow washout. The truck lurched. Wes went down onto the bales and then off the side of the bed and landed on his back in the stubble.

He was fine. That is the part I have to say early, because it changes what kind of story this is. He got up, swore at me with real creativity, and had a bruise across his shoulder blades for two weeks. Nothing was broken. My uncle came over, looked at the washout, looked at me, and said, "You looked away," and then he had me get back in and finish the row, which at the time felt like cruelty and which I now understand was the whole lesson.

What I still think about is not the drift. Trucks drift. What I think about is why I turned around. Wes was yelling and I wanted to know what he was saying, and underneath that, I wanted him to see that I was the kind of driver who could hold a conversation while working. I had gotten good enough at the mechanics that I had started spending my attention on how I appeared instead of on what I was doing. The competence made me careless in a way that pure incompetence never had. When I was terrible at it, I stared at the field like it might attack me.

I have found that pattern in myself since, and I do not think I have solved it. It showed up in chemistry when I stopped writing out the intermediate steps because I could do them in my head, and then could not find my own error on the semester exam. It showed up in debate when I started improvising rebuttals because improvising looked better than reading from a flow sheet, and lost a round I should have won on the extended argument I forgot to extend. Both times the tell was the same: I was performing the task instead of doing it.

I do not have a clean method for catching it. What I have is Wes on his back in the stubble, and my uncle's flat sentence, and a physical memory of my own hands on a wheel I was not looking through. When I notice I am enjoying being observed, I try to put in the clutch. Sometimes I remember in time.

text:
In the summer after tenth I spent eight thousand rupees on phone cases, and there are still thirty-one of them in a carton under my bed. The money was mine, from two years of birthday envelopes and a set of tuitions I took for a boy in seventh, but my mother had to co-sign the order because the website wanted an adult's name. That detail matters later.

The idea was simple and I thought it was clever. A supplier in Delhi sold blank cases at forty rupees and printed whatever design you uploaded for another thirty. I made eleven designs on my laptop, mostly line drawings of things from our town, the clock tower, the bridge, a chai glass, and I priced them at two hundred and fifty. The margin looked beautiful written down. I ordered a hundred and ten pieces because the per-unit rate dropped at a hundred. Ninety of them were for the iPhone 11 and the iPhone 12.

I sold nine. Two to my cousin, one to a teacher who I think felt sorry for me, and six at a stall I set up outside school on a Saturday, which the guard shut down at noon anyway. Almost nobody in my class has an iPhone. They have Redmis and Realmes and one boy has a Vivo he has dropped so many times it is held together with tape, and none of them were going to pay two hundred and fifty rupees for a drawing of a clock tower they see every day.

For about six months I told the story with the supplier as the villain. The print on the first batch was slightly off-centre, and the edges of a few cases were rough, and that was true, and it let me say the word quality in a tone that made it sound like the failure had happened to me. I said it to my mother, to my friends, to an uncle who asked at a wedding.

The thing I actually got wrong is smaller and worse. I never asked anybody. Not one person. I had a hundred and forty classmates and a phone full of their numbers, and it would have cost me an afternoon to walk around asking what phone they had and what they would pay, and I did not do it, because I did not want an answer that would stop me. I wanted the ordering part. I wanted the box arriving. That is the part I still think about, because it is not a business mistake, it is a thing about me that shows up elsewhere.

What I did next was unglamorous. I dropped the price to eighty, below cost, and sold about forty more over two months, mostly through my cousin's college group. I gave a dozen away at Diwali, which felt like cheating until my mother pointed out that a gift is not a loss if you were never going to sell it. I went back to tutoring, two students instead of one, and put the money in the same envelope until it was more than eight thousand, which took until March. Nobody had asked me to do that.

Last month a friend told me about an idea for selling custom cricket-team jerseys and asked if I wanted in. The first thing out of my mouth was a question about who had already said they would buy one, and he did not have an answer, and I heard myself being annoying in exactly the way somebody should have been annoying with me. I still have the carton. I keep one case on my desk, the clock tower one, on a phone model I do not own and never did. It is a good drawing. That was never the problem.

text:
My dad and I still don't agree about this and I don't think we're going to.

Three years. Freshman year, sophomore year, junior year. Same gym, same list taped to the same door outside the athletics office, same feeling in my stomach at 3:40 on a Thursday. Basketball. I'm five foot ten, which is nothing, and I have hands that are honestly kind of small, and I can shoot from the corner if nobody is standing near me. That last part turned out to matter a lot.

The first year I cried in the car. My dad didn't say much, he just drove, and then when we got to the light on Chester he said, "next year." That was the whole conversation. Next year.

The second year he had a plan. Six a.m. at the rec center before school, three days a week, and he came with me every single time, which is the part I want to be clear about, because he was working a double most weeks and he still got up. He'd rebound for me. He'd count out loud. Two hundred shots and then we'd go home and he'd shower and go to work. In March I got cut again, and this time he was angry, not at me, at Coach Delgado, and he wanted to go talk to him, and I begged him not to, and he didn't, and I think he's still a little bit sorry that he listened to me.

The third year is the one we fight about.

Because by then I knew. I'd played summer league and I could see it, plainly, the way you can see the weather. Devon and Marcus and the sophomore kid whose name I never learned were just better than me. Not by attitude. Not by hours. Their bodies did things mine wasn't going to do, and I had spent two years of six a.m.s buying about four inches of vertical and a decent left hand, and it wasn't enough and it wasn't going to be enough. So I went to tryouts anyway, because I said I would, and I got cut, and I came home and I told my dad I was done and I was going to do something else.

He said I was quitting.

He didn't say it meanly. He said it like it was a fact about the world he was informing me of. And I said no, I'm not quitting, I'm reading the situation correctly, and he said that's what quitting sounds like from the inside, and that landed on me hard enough that I've thought about it probably once a week since.

Here's where I ended up. I started keeping stats for the team instead. Which sounds pathetic when I write it down, the kid who couldn't make it hanging around with a clipboard, and yeah, it felt like that in November. But I got interested. I built a spreadsheet that tracked where every shot came from, and by January I could tell Coach Delgado that our second-quarter offense was generating almost nothing from the left wing, and he actually changed something because of it. We went 16-6. I'm not saying that was me. I'm saying I was in the room.

My dad came to games. He's proud of me, he says so. But there's a thing he does where he'll mention someone from his old job whose son walked on somewhere, and it's not pointed, he's just talking, and I hear it anyway.

What I think now is that we're arguing about two different questions and calling it one. He thinks the question is whether you keep going. I think the question is whether you're honest about what you're good at. Both of those are real. Neither of us has convinced the other.

He'd want me to add that I could still try out senior year.

I'm not going to. But I love him for the six a.m.s, and I'd like him to know that the thing he was actually teaching me stuck, just not in the shape he wanted.

text:
I got into sewing costumes for the Marlow Players the way most people get into anything at fifteen, which is that my mother volunteered me. Their wardrobe mistress had broken her wrist three weeks before a production of Blithe Spirit, and my mother, who had once heard me say I could use a sewing machine, offered my Saturdays without consulting me.

I could use a sewing machine in the sense that I had made a drawstring bag in Year 8.

For about eighteen months after that I thought of the whole thing as a chore I was too polite to get out of. I was good at it fairly quickly - I have decent hands and I can read a pattern - and I did not enjoy it. It was a church hall with a strip light that hummed, and a rail of donated clothing that smelled of other people's houses, and a group of adults between forty and seventy who had opinions about hemlines. I did what I was asked. I altered things. I turned a 1980s bridesmaid dress into something that could pass for 1927 if the audience was more than four rows back. I let out trousers for a man called Gordon three times in one season and did not ask why.

I told people I did it for the UCAS form. I think I believed that.

The thing that changed my mind happened during a production of A View from the Bridge, which is a play I did not know and had not read. I was making a work shirt for Eddie, the longshoreman, from a pattern I had drafted myself because we could not find anything that was right. The man playing him was called Ray, mid-fifties, a plumber, not a good actor in any technical sense - he had two volumes and a habit of looking at the floor on his own lines.

At the third fitting I had put the shirt on him and was pinning the shoulder, and I asked him to lift his arm so I could check the range, and he lifted it, and something happened to how he was standing. I do not know how to describe it better than that. He stopped being a plumber in a church hall wearing a shirt with pins in it. His weight went into his heels. His hands hung differently. He said, to nobody, "this is what he'd wear," and then he did about four lines of a scene we were nowhere near rehearsing, quietly, into the middle distance, and they were the first lines I had heard him say that sounded like a person.

He apologised afterwards. He said he'd got carried away.

I went home and thought about the shoulder seam. I had put it about two centimetres wider than his actual shoulder, deliberately, because a workman's shirt from 1955 is cut for movement and not for fit, and the effect of a wider shoulder seam is that the sleeve hangs from further out, and the arm swings from a different place, and you cannot hold yourself the way a man in a modern shirt holds himself. I had made a decision about a seam allowance and it had walked into the room ahead of him.

That was the turn. Before that I thought costume was decoration - the thing you put on top of the acting so the audience knows what year it is. After that I understood it as the opposite: a set of physical constraints and permissions applied to a body, which the body then has to answer. A corset does not make you look like a Victorian woman. It makes you breathe like one, and everything else follows from the breathing. A cassock does not signify a priest. It makes you take shorter steps.

I have done nine productions now. I have made a hooped skirt out of curtain wire and a great deal of swearing. I have learned to ask actors how they intend to move before I cut anything, which nobody taught me and which most amateur wardrobe departments do not do. I have started keeping a notebook of what I call solved problems: how to make a fat suit that does not slide, how to age a jacket with sandpaper and cold tea, how to build a quick change into a garment that also has to look like it has buttons.

I would like to study this properly, and I am aware that "I sew" sounds like a hobby. It is not a hobby. It is the study of how clothing writes instructions to a body, and I found it in a church hall under a humming light, and I did not notice what I had found for a year and a half because I was too busy resenting my mother for signing me up.

Gordon still needs his trousers let out. I still do not ask.

text:
My grandmother kept a single wooden spoon on a nail by the stove, worn so smooth on one edge that it had gone the color of caramel. She didn't call it anything, because she didn't call most things by name in English, not to me - the only English she had was "hot," "sit," "wait," and a fast "no, no, no" when I reached for something before it was ready. I was twelve when she came to live with us, and that spoon became, without either of us planning it, the only language we actually shared.

For the first few weeks I stood in the kitchen and failed constantly. I chopped onions too thick. I let garlic burn while I checked my phone under the counter. She would take the spoon out of my hand, not unkindly, just fast, like she couldn't stand to watch a mistake finish happening, fix what I had done, and hand it back. I wanted her to explain, in words, what I was doing wrong, and she couldn't, and one afternoon I got so tired of not understanding that I put the spoon down on the counter and walked out of the kitchen.

She didn't come after me. When I came back an hour later, ready to apologize for something I couldn't even name, she was rolling out dough at the counter, and she just handed me the spoon again, like nothing had happened. That was the moment I actually started paying attention - not to her mouth, but to her hands. The way she tilted the pan a half second before the oil began to smoke. The way she pressed two fingers into rising dough and waited for it to spring back a particular way. None of that was translatable. I had to learn it the way you learn to catch a ball, by getting hit in the face a few times first.

By spring I could tell, just from the smell coming off the pan, whether the mustard seeds were about to pop or whether I had already lost them to burning. I still didn't know most of the words for what we were doing together. But I knew the weight of the spoon in my hand, and I knew what her silence meant when I had gotten something right - she would take a spoonful, taste it without looking at me, and set the spoon back down on the counter instead of taking it out of my hand. That was the whole compliment. It took me months to learn to hear it.

What I actually failed at that year wasn't cooking. It was my assumption that understanding required language, that if we couldn't talk to each other we couldn't really know each other. I was wrong about that in a way that still embarrasses me a little. She taught me an entire craft, and something about patience I don't think I could have learned any other way, using maybe forty words of English and one wooden spoon, and I came out the other side able to make her dal exactly the way she made it, and able to sit in a room with someone and not feel the need to fill every silence with talking.

She died the winter before I started writing this application, and the spoon is in a drawer in our kitchen now. I still use it sometimes, not because I need to, but because my hand remembers what to do with it before I do, and that, it turns out, was the whole point.

text:
"You didn't even read the rubric," Priya said, not looking up from her laptop, and I said something back I don't fully remember except that it ended with her snapping the laptop shut harder than she needed to.

That was ninth grade, the invasive species project, and it was the end of something that had actually started three years earlier over a much smaller argument - whether pineapple belonged on pizza. We decided, with great seriousness, at her eleventh birthday party, that it did. From then on, every Friday, one of us texted the other a single word. Pineapple. No context, no greeting, nothing before or after it. If I forgot, she sent it twice the next week, doubled, like a fine I owed her.

It sounds like nothing, and for a long time I thought it was nothing, just a dumb inside joke neither of us had the heart to retire. But it went on for three years without a single missed Friday, through her parents' divorce, through the year I didn't talk to anyone at lunch, through two different schools for her and one very bad summer for me. It was never a conversation. It was just proof, delivered weekly, that the other person was still there and still thinking of you, even when everything else you might have said felt too big to say.

The project came in April of ninth grade. We were assigned to the same group along with two people neither of us knew well, and somewhere in the second week I stopped doing my share and let her carry it, telling myself I was busy, telling myself she was better at this kind of thing anyway, which was true and also not an excuse. She noticed. She said something about it in front of the group, not cruelly, just tired, and I got defensive in the specific way people get defensive when they know they're wrong, and it turned into the kind of fight that isn't really about the thing it's about.

We finished the project. We got a decent grade. We did not speak for the rest of that year, not really, not beyond what the hallway required.

The Fridays didn't stop right away, which is the part I still think about. For three more weeks, I texted her pineapple, and she texted it back, one word passing between two people who otherwise had nothing left to say to each other. I don't know if she kept sending it out of habit or because some smaller, stubborn part of her wasn't ready to let the whole thing go either. Eventually one of us stopped - I genuinely don't remember which - and neither of us restarted it, and that was that.

We're civil now, in the way people are civil about things that used to matter more. She's dating someone I don't know. I run track with someone who used to be her best friend. Sometimes I still think, on a Friday, unprompted, of a single word, and I don't send it, and I couldn't tell you exactly why I don't, except that some habits only mean something as long as both people are still choosing them, on purpose, every single week, without being asked.

text:
Mr. Halvorsen's rule was you didn't touch the MIG gun until he'd watched you dry-run the joint three times. I hated that rule. I was fifteen, I'd wanted to weld since I was about nine years old and watched my uncle patch a trailer hitch in our driveway, sparks going everywhere, and here was this guy making me practice moving a fake torch over a piece of scrap steel like some kind of ritual. Felt like a waste of a class period. I wanted to burn metal, not pretend to.

So the first time he actually let me strike an arc, I rushed it. Didn't hold the angle he'd shown me - dragged the gun instead of pushing it, which he'd explained maybe four times, and which I'd nodded along to without really absorbing. The bead came out ugly. Humped in the middle, undercut on one side, the kind of weld that looks like a scab. He picked it up, turned it over once, didn't say anything for a second, then handed it back and said, "Grind it off and do it again." Not mean about it. Just flat.

I did that probably nine times that semester. Not exaggerating much. Same mistake, roughly - I'd get impatient two seconds into the bead and speed up, and the whole thing would go wrong right where I sped up, like the metal was keeping score. Somewhere around attempt six I started getting mad about it, at him a little, mostly at myself, because I could see exactly what I was doing wrong while I was doing it and I still couldn't make my hand slow down.

What finally worked wasn't advice, honestly, or not new advice anyway. He'd said the same three things to me the whole time. What worked was he stopped fixing it for me. He'd walk by, glance at a bad weld, and just keep walking. No comment. And somehow that was worse than the grinding-it-off speech, because now I had to decide for myself whether it was good enough, and I couldn't lie to myself the way I could sort of half-convince a teacher.

By December I could lay a bead that didn't look like it belonged in a horror movie. Nothing fancy - a flat fillet weld, nothing structural, nothing anyone would trust to hold up a bridge. But consistent. And I still think about the gap between knowing what I was doing wrong and actually being able to stop doing it, because those turned out to be completely different skills, and nobody had told me that going in. I'd assumed if you could name the mistake you were basically done fixing it. You're not. Not even close.

I think about it more than I probably should for something that's just a welding class. I catch myself doing the same thing in other places now - rushing the part where I already know I should slow down, math homework, an essay draft, whatever - and some part of my brain goes back to that ugly humped bead and Mr. Halvorsen not saying anything, just walking past. It's a weirdly specific memory to keep returning to, a guy in safety glasses not commenting on a piece of scrap steel, but it's the one that actually stuck, more than any speech anyone gave me about effort or grit or whatever word gets used for this stuff. I still have the bad one, the sixth attempt, sitting in a drawer in the garage. I don't know why I kept it instead of the good ones. Maybe because it's the one that's honest about how long it actually took.

text:
Mrs. Okafor's phone had a cracked screen protector shaped almost exactly like a spiderweb, radiating out from a point near the top left corner where she'd dropped it on her kitchen tile the week her son bought it for her. She never replaced the protector. By the time I met her, eight months later, the crack pattern had become, in a strange way, the thing I used to navigate the phone with her - I'd say "tap just above the crack" or "swipe from the corner where the web starts," because those landmarks meant more to her than any menu name I could offer.

I started coming over on Tuesdays because my mother asked me to, initially, in the vague way parents ask you to be nice to a neighbor, and I expected one visit, maybe two. Mrs. Okafor was eighty-one and had moved from Lagos to our street eleven years earlier to be near her son, and her son had, with good intentions, bought her a smartphone and then moved to Seattle for work eight months later, leaving her with a device she said made her feel, in her words, "stupid in my own hand."

The first Tuesday, we spent forty minutes just learning to unlock it. Not because she couldn't understand the concept - she ran a shop for thirty years, she understands systems fine - but because nobody had ever explained it to her the way you'd explain something to a person, rather than a problem. The people at the phone store had shown her once, fast, using words like "swipe up" and "long-press," and she'd nodded because that's what you do, and then gone home and been unable to reproduce any of it alone.

I stopped using their words. I used the crack instead. "See where the web starts, near the top? Put your finger there and drag it down toward you, slow." She liked that I was patient about repeating things, and she told me so more than once, which embarrassed me a little because I didn't think I was being especially patient - I was just going at the speed that actually worked, which happened to be much slower than I was used to going for anything.

By the fourth Tuesday she could video call her son without help. I remember standing in her kitchen doorway, trying to give them privacy, and hearing her laugh at something he said, and hearing in her voice the specific brightness of someone talking to a person they miss and can suddenly, finally, actually see. I hadn't done anything sophisticated. I hadn't taught her calculus or fixed anything broken in a technical sense. I had just kept showing up on Tuesdays and using a cracked screen as a map instead of assuming she should already speak the language everyone else spoke.

We kept meeting on Tuesdays for almost two years, past the point where she needed the lessons, because by then it wasn't really about the phone. She told me stories about Lagos, about a market stall her mother ran, about a boat trip she took as a young woman that she'd never told her own son about because he "asks a hundred questions and I only want to tell it once." I got the whole story, slowly, over many Tuesdays, partly, I think, because I'd earned it by being someone who didn't rush her.

I think about what I'd bring to a campus in terms of that cracked screen protector, honestly. Not because I'm particularly good with technology - I'm not, not especially. It's that I learned, sitting in that kitchen, that the gap between someone feeling stupid and someone feeling capable is usually not a gap in intelligence. It's a gap in how patiently someone is willing to meet you where you actually are, landmarks and all, instead of where they assume you should already be. I'd bring that same patience into a lab, a dorm, a group project with someone struggling to keep up - the willingness to find the spiderweb crack instead of insisting on the menu name.

text:
I entered the Hargrove Essay Prize under the name "M. Reyes" for three years running, starting in ninth grade, and I never told anyone, not even my best friend, until this year.

Here's the dumb origin of it. Freshman year I wrote something for the contest - an essay about my dad's job loss, pretty raw, more honest than anything I'd turned in for a grade before - and I chickened out at the submission form. There's a box where you type your name and it shows up on the printed program if you place, read out loud at the little ceremony they do in the library. I typed M. Reyes instead of my actual name, hit submit before I could think about it more, and then more or less forgot about it until the results went up and M. Reyes had gotten an honorable mention.

Nobody knew who M. Reyes was. A few people guessed, wrongly, at lunch. I sat there and said nothing, which felt strange and also kind of great, like getting away with something, except the thing I was getting away with was just being seen without being known.

So I did it again the next year. And the year after. Same fake name, three different essays, none of them about anything I would've felt okay putting my real name next to - the year my parents almost split up, a specific bad week with an eating thing I still don't fully talk about, a friendship that ended badly and mostly my fault. I placed all three years. Second, then first, then second again. The librarian who ran the contest, Ms. Ferris, pinned the print-outs to a corkboard by the front desk every spring, "M. Reyes" typed at the top, and I used to walk past it on purpose, most days, just to look at it for a second.

It wasn't really about winning. I think if I'm honest it was closer to the opposite - I wanted to say true things and not have anyone attach them to me walking down the hallway. M. Reyes could write about the eating thing and nobody looked at me differently at lunch the next day. That mattered more to me than the ribbon did.

This year I finally told Ms. Ferris, mostly by accident, mentioning something in passing that only M. Reyes could've known, and she went quiet for a second and then said she'd wondered for three years and had a running guess with another teacher, both wrong. She asked if I wanted my name on the board this time, for the essay I'd write senior year, and I said yes before I'd really decided anything, surprising myself.

I wrote about the eating thing again, for real this time, my actual name typed into the box, and I stood at that little library ceremony and read four minutes of my own handwriting out loud to about thirty people I see every day. My hands were shaking. It was worse than any test I've ever taken and also, somehow, the first time in four years I felt like the thing I'd written and the person standing there were actually the same person.

I still don't fully know what to make of the fact that it took a fake name, repeated three separate springs in a row, before I could get to that. But I think that's the part I'd actually bring somewhere new - not confidence, exactly, more like the long, slow habit of practicing honesty in private until you're ready to do it in front of people, one submission box at a time.

text:
My dad thinks the pallet furniture thing is a phase, and I've stopped trying to convince him otherwise, mostly because I don't think I'll win, and partly because some stubborn part of me likes that we still haven't settled it.

It started two summers ago behind the hardware store where I worked weekends, where a stack of broken shipping pallets sat waiting for the scrap truck. I asked the manager if I could take a few. He shrugged and said sure, they were trash anyway, and I dragged three of them home on a hand truck and had no real plan beyond the vague sense that I could turn them into something.

The first thing I built was a coffee table, and it was bad - uneven, one leg shorter than the others, splinters everywhere because I hadn't sanded properly. My dad looked at it in the garage and said, not unkindly but not encouragingly either, that I could buy a table at the store for less than what the sandpaper and stain had cost me. He wasn't wrong about the money. He's an accountant; he's rarely wrong about the money. But that wasn't really what the table was for, and I couldn't explain that to him in a way that landed, then or really since.

I kept building anyway. A bench for the porch. A shelf unit that actually turned out decent, that my mom uses for her plants now. A headboard I gave my sister for her birthday, which she still has, three years later, in her dorm room a thousand miles from home. Each one got a little better, a little less crooked, and I got faster at seeing which broken slats were still usable and which ones needed to go straight to the scrap pile. My dad watched all of this from a distance, mostly approving of the results and mostly still unconvinced of the premise. He still says, every few months, some version of "you know you could just buy furniture," and I still say some version of "that's not the point," and neither of us has ever really finished that argument. We just set it down and pick it back up later, like a bookmark neither of us wants to lose.

I think what he doesn't fully get, and what I've never managed to say right, is that I'm not building furniture because I need furniture. I'm building it because there's a specific, quiet satisfaction in taking something the world has already decided is garbage and proving, with my own hands, that it wasn't finished being useful. A pallet gets thrown away because it did one job - carrying boxes across a warehouse floor - and everyone assumes the job was the whole point of it existing. I don't think that's true of pallets, and if I'm honest, some of why I keep doing this is that I don't think it's true of a lot of things people write off too fast, including, some days, myself.

I haven't said that to my dad in exactly those words. Maybe I will eventually. For now the garage still smells like sawdust most Saturdays, and he still stops by to look at whatever's half-finished on the workbench, and shakes his head a little, and doesn't leave. That's its own kind of answer, even if neither of us has said the thing out loud yet.

text:
My uncle Ray gave me his old Zenith radio the year it stopped working, which tells you something about the gift already. Big wooden cabinet, cracked dial glass, a knob missing off the front so you had to turn the tuning shaft with pliers. He said, "It's yours if you want it, it's junk otherwise," and I said yes before really thinking it through, because I liked the idea of fixing something more than I understood what fixing it would actually take.

It took about a year, on and off. I learned to solder that spring, badly at first, burned myself twice, replaced capacitors that had gone bad decades before I was born, chased a hum through the circuit for six weeks that turned out to be one bad ground wire the whole time. Ray helped some of it, especially early on, showing me how to read the tube layout, but mostly he just let me struggle through it, coming by every couple weeks to ask how the "old girl" was doing, like she was a horse and not a radio.

Here's the part we still argue about. When it finally worked - actually pulled in a station, static clearing into an AM broadcast one night in my garage, loud enough that I yelled for my mom to come hear it - Ray wanted me to sell it. Said a working Zenith from that era was worth real money to a collector, more than I'd guess, and that I should let it go and put the money toward something useful, a car, college, whatever. I said no. I'm still saying no. He brings it up maybe twice a year, usually at Thanksgiving, half-joking but not entirely, and I give him the same answer every time, and neither of us has budged an inch in three years of this.

I don't think he's wrong that the money would help. I think about that sometimes, actually, more than I let on to him. But I didn't spend a year chasing a bad ground wire because I wanted a radio-shaped investment. I spent it because there was something about bringing a dead thing back to a state where it could do the one job it was built for - pull a signal out of the air and turn it into a voice in a room - that felt more important than what the wood and the tubes were worth to a stranger. Ray, who has sold off half his own collection over the years, genuinely doesn't understand this distinction, or maybe he understands it and just disagrees with where I've landed on it, which might be worse, in a way, because it means we're not confused, we're just different.

The radio sits in my room now, and it still works, mostly - the volume knob sticks a little in humid weather, and I still haven't found a replacement for the missing tuning knob, so the pliers live on the shelf next to it, part of the whole apparatus at this point. Ray still asks about her at Thanksgiving. I still say she's not for sale. We've never resolved it and I don't think we're going to, and there's something almost comforting in that now, the two of us circling the same argument every November, both of us right about our own reasons, neither one giving ground, the radio playing quietly in the next room the whole time we talk about it.

text:
Every Sunday for the past two years, I've read out loud to strangers for an hour, and for a long time I thought I was the one doing the giving.

I started at Hollis House, the hospice near my grandmother's old apartment, because a volunteer coordinator visited our school looking for readers and I signed up mostly to get out of a Sunday-morning family obligation I didn't want to explain to anyone. I expected it to be sad in a way I could brace for once and then get through. It was sad, some days. It was also, most days, much stranger and more ordinary than I'd braced for.

The first patient I read to regularly was a man named Walt who wanted nothing but westerns, the pulpy kind with a gunslinger on the cover, and who fell asleep about fifteen minutes into most sessions, and who I kept reading to anyway because the nurse told me his breathing changed when the room went quiet, so the sound mattered more than whether he was following the plot. I read him probably nine or ten of these books over four months. I have never once discussed a Louis L'Amour novel with anyone in my actual life, and I could now, with some confidence, hold a conversation about frontier justice tropes that nobody in my world wants to have.

The challenge, if I'm being honest about what the challenge actually was, wasn't the sadness. It was showing up on the Sundays I didn't want to. There were mornings I sat in the car in the parking lot for five minutes before going in, mornings after a bad week at school where the last thing I wanted to do was walk into a building full of people near the end of their lives and perform cheerfulness I didn't feel. I almost quit twice. Once in the fall of sophomore year, when a patient I'd been reading to for three months died on a Tuesday and nobody told me until I showed up the following Sunday expecting her, book in hand, and found her room already occupied by someone else. I sat in the parking lot that day for closer to twenty minutes.

I went back the next week anyway. I don't have a clean explanation for why, except that the habit itself had become load-bearing in some way I couldn't fully explain to my parents when they asked if I wanted to stop. It wasn't that I'd gotten used to loss. I don't think you get used to it. It was that showing up had turned into the thing I did regardless of whether I felt like it, the same way you show up to practice on a day you're tired, and somewhere in there the habit started teaching me something the individual Sundays couldn't have taught me on their own - that consistency isn't the same as enthusiasm, and you can build the first without waiting around for the second.

I still read on Sundays. Different patients now, mostly, since two years is a long time in that building. I still don't love every visit. Some weeks I still sit in the parking lot a minute longer than I need to before going in. But I go in. That's the entire lesson, as far as I can tell, distilled down to something almost embarrassingly simple after two years of showing up: the value was never really in any single Sunday. It was in not letting a bad week decide whether the next one happened.

text:
I've kept the scorebook for my dad's weekend cricket league since I was eleven, which means I have opinions about his batting that he does not want to hear, and I tell him them anyway, and we have never once agreed on the actual answer to the argument we keep having.

The scorebook is a real thing, a physical ledger with a cloth cover that the league has used for something like fifteen years, passed from scorer to scorer, and I inherited the job when the previous scorer's kid went off to college and nobody else wanted to sit on the sideline for four hours doing arithmetic. I took to it fast. There's something I like about the precision of it - every run accounted for, every dismissal recorded in a little code, byes and wides and no-balls all separated out so that at the end of the season you can point to a page and say, with total confidence, exactly what happened on a specific Saturday two months ago.

What I like less is that the scorebook makes my dad's decline as a batsman completely undeniable, in a way conversation lets him avoid. He's forty-nine. He still thinks of himself as the guy who used to open the batting for his college team, and some Saturdays he still is, more or less. But the numbers over the past three seasons tell a clearer story than he wants told - his average down almost eight runs, his strike rate slower, more dismissals to spin bowling that he used to handle easily. I know this because I wrote every single one of those numbers down myself, in my own handwriting, and I've shown him the book more than once when he's insisted a particular bad outing was a fluke.

He doesn't like it. We argue about it, actually argue, not the fake kind of arguing families do to pass time - real disagreement, him insisting the numbers don't capture "match situation" or the state of the pitch that day, me insisting that's exactly what averaging over a whole season is supposed to correct for. Neither of us has ever backed down. He still bats. I still write down what actually happens when he does, honestly, without softening it, even though I know some Saturdays he'd rather I didn't.

I've thought about whether I should just fudge it a little for him, once or twice, and I haven't, and I think that refusal is close to the actual center of what I'd bring somewhere new - not the specific skill of scorekeeping, which is not a skill anyone is desperate for, but the stubborn insistence on an honest record even when the person the record is about is someone I love and would rather protect. It would be easier, most Saturdays, to round a number in his favor. I don't do it. He knows I don't do it. It's part of why, underneath the arguing, I think he still hands me the book every single week instead of asking someone else to keep it - because an honest scorer, even an infuriating one, is worth more to him than a comfortable one, even if he'll never quite say so out loud.

We'll probably have the same argument next Saturday. I'll probably still be right, according to the book. He'll probably still disagree, according to himself. Neither of us is going to change on this, and at this point I think we've both stopped expecting to.

text:
"You're guessing," my mother said, watching me squint up at the sky, one hand shading my eyes, trying to decide between two shutter speeds I was choosing basically at random. "Yes," I said, "that's the whole camera."

The camera was a Pentax K1000 that had belonged to my grandfather, no battery, no light meter, nothing but a mechanical body and a lens and whatever judgment I could bring to it, which in the beginning was none at all. I'd asked for it after finding it in a closet, mostly because it looked cool sitting on my desk, and I had no real plan to use it seriously until I loaded a roll of film out of stubbornness one Saturday and went out to shoot the empty lot behind our house, wanting to prove to myself I could figure it out without an app or a meter telling me what to do.

The first roll came back from the lab almost entirely ruined. Half the frames were black, overexposed into nothing, or so underexposed you could barely make out a shape. I remember standing at the counter of the drugstore, going through the prints one by one, feeling genuinely stupid, like I'd wasted eleven dollars and an afternoon proving I had no eye for this at all. I almost put the camera back in the closet that same week. It felt less like a hobby and more like a machine specifically built to embarrass me.

I didn't put it back, though I couldn't tell you exactly why, except that something in me wanted to understand what I'd gotten wrong rather than just accept that I had. I started reading about the Sunny 16 rule, about how film speed and aperture and shutter speed relate to each other, doing the math by hand before I even lifted the camera, treating exposure less like an art and more like a puzzle with a right answer I hadn't found yet. My second roll, shot two weeks later, had maybe four usable frames out of thirty-six. My third had closer to twenty.

The real shift happened on the fourth roll, on a gray, flat, overcast afternoon that gave me no obvious cues at all - no hard shadows to read, no strong sun to work off - the exact kind of light I would have guessed wrong on a month earlier. I stood in the backyard for a long moment, ran the calculation in my head, adjusted for the cloud cover, and took a photo of my little sister on the swing set that came back sharp, correctly exposed, genuinely good, the kind of photo where you can see individual strands of her hair against the gray sky. I remember standing at the drugstore counter with that print in my hand and feeling something click into place that hadn't clicked before - not just relief that I'd finally gotten one right, but the specific, quiet thrill of having reasoned my way to a correct answer with nothing but a lens and a bit of math and my own two eyes.

After that I stopped thinking of the missing light meter as a limitation and started thinking of it as the entire reason I liked the camera. Every other device I owned told me the answer before I'd had to think about the question. This one made me actually look at the sky, estimate, commit, and live with the result thirty-six frames at a time, with no undo button and no do-over until the next roll. I've shot maybe forty rolls since that gray afternoon in the backyard, and I still do the calculation by eye every time, even now that I could just buy a meter, because doing it by eye is the part I actually love.

meta.topic: learning photography with a camera that had no light meter
