text:
I have a spreadsheet on my laptop with fourteen tabs. Cost of goods sold, labor as a percentage of revenue, rent-to-sales ratios for restaurants in three different zip codes, a whole tab just for how delivery apps take their cut before the money ever reaches the register. Nobody made me build this. I built it at midnight, most nights, for almost a year, and I could not tell you exactly why except that it feels like the only way I know how to keep asking a question that doesn't have a good answer anymore.

The restaurant was called Marchetti's. My great-uncle opened it, my grandfather ran it after him, and my dad took it over when I was seven. Twenty-two years, one location, a kitchen that still had my grandfather's handwriting taped above the stove telling whoever was cooking not to rush the sauce. It closed in March. I was in the dining room the last night, folding chairs, and I did not cry, which surprised me, because I'd been crying about smaller things for weeks before that.

Here is the part I keep circling back to on the spreadsheet at midnight. Two years before it closed, my dad wanted to sign up with the delivery apps. Everyone else on our street already had. I told him not to. I was fifteen and I had strong opinions about things I did not fully understand, and I remember standing in the kitchen telling him that the apps take almost a third of every order, that it would make us look like everyone else, that people came to Marchetti's because it felt like it belonged to somebody, not like it belonged to an algorithm. He listened to me. He usually did, which I understand now was its own kind of mistake on his part.

We held out for another year while three other places on the block signed up and started showing up in searches I didn't know people were doing. By the time my dad finally did add us, the accounts you need to build up, the reviews, the ranking inside the app itself, all of it takes months to earn, and we didn't have months left to spend earning it. I don't actually know if the apps would have saved us. That's the thing about the spreadsheet. I have run the numbers eleven different ways and I still don't know, and there is a version of this essay where I tell you I found the answer and it fixed something in me, but that isn't true.

What is true is that I spend hours now reading about unit economics for restaurants that have nothing to do with mine, comparing margins, reading forum posts from line cooks about why their places failed, watching hour-long videos from people who ran diners in Ohio, because somewhere in all of that I think I'm looking for the version of the story where fifteen-year-old me wasn't wrong. Or where being wrong wouldn't have mattered anyway. I lose entire nights to it. My mom will knock on my door at one in the morning and ask what I'm even looking at, and I never have a clean answer.

I don't turn to any one person for this, honestly, which feels like it should embarrass me more than it does. I turn to strangers on the internet who ran small businesses and are willing to talk about exactly how they failed, because nobody in my actual life wants to talk about the specifics of ours. My dad especially doesn't. So I go looking on my own, tab after tab, trying to build something out of numbers that might explain a year I can't undo, and mostly what I've learned is that I'm still not done asking.

text:
My grandmother's pincushion is a red tomato with a little strawberry hanging off it by a thread, and half the pins in it don't match anymore because I've been losing hers one at a time for three years and replacing them with whatever's in the jar. It sits on my sewing table, which is really just the kitchen table with a sheet under it so I don't scratch the wood, and it has been there through four shows now at the Millbrook Community Playhouse, where I'm the seventeen-year-old they somehow trust to run wardrobe for eighty adults who mostly can't sew a button.

I got the job because nobody else wanted it. That's the honest version. I said yes because my grandmother taught me to sew when I was nine, mostly Halloween costumes, and it felt like something I could actually be useful at, unlike, say, the acting, which I have zero talent for and everyone agrees on that, including me.

The failure happened during Beauty and the Beast, last winter. I was in charge of the Beast costume - not just a costume, honestly, more like an engineering project, this huge layered coat with fake fur and shoulder pieces built up on foam to make him look bigger than he is, plus a cape that had to move right under stage lights. I'd never built anything with that much structure before. I measured our Beast, a guy named Trevor who works at the hardware store during the day, back in October, and then built the whole thing over two months mostly working off those first measurements, because I was proud and didn't want to keep bothering him for fittings.

Big mistake. Huge, actually. Trevor lost about fifteen pounds over the fall - some health thing, nothing dramatic, he's fine now - and nobody told me because why would they, it's not the kind of thing you announce, and I never scheduled a second fitting because I was so sure I already had it right. Dress rehearsal, four days before opening. He puts the coat on. The shoulders sit an inch too wide on each side, which sounds small, but on stage, under lights, it read as a man wearing a coat built for someone else. Which, it turns out, he was.

I sat in the greenroom after that rehearsal and did not handle it well. I cried, actually, in the bathroom, which I'm only admitting because this essay is supposed to be honest. Four days. A structural costume that had taken two months. My director, a woman named Diane who has run that theatre for something like thirty years, found me and did not say it would be fine, because it might not have been, and I appreciated that she didn't lie to me about it.

What I did instead was take the coat apart at the shoulder seams - actual surgery on something I'd already finished - and rebuild just that section, working off Trevor himself this time instead of a two-month-old number on an index card. I used my grandmother's pincushion the whole time, the actual physical object, pinning and repinning that seam probably nine times before it hung right, losing two more of her pins to the carpet in the process. I didn't sleep much those four days. The coat was ready by dress on the last night before opening, not before, and it looked right, and nobody in the audience ever knew any of this happened.

Here's what I actually took from it, and it isn't some tidy lesson about perseverance, because I think that undersells what happened. What I learned is that I trust my own first measurement too much, and that trusting it is a kind of laziness dressed up as confidence. I don't build anything now without a second fitting scheduled in, no matter how sure I feel walking out of the first one. The pincushion still sits on my table missing more of its original pins every season, and I like that about it, actually - it isn't the same object it was when she gave it to me, and neither, honestly, am I.

I still have the shoulder piece I cut off that night, in a drawer with extra buttons and thread that doesn't match anything. Every so often I find it and remember exactly what four days with no sleep feels like, and exactly what it's for.

text:
The bell above the door does this thing where it doesn't ring so much as clatter, like it's annoyed at being disturbed, and I have heard that clatter probably four thousand times and I could still draw you the exact pitch of it from memory. I used to hate that sound. It meant someone needed something, and needing something at our store almost always meant me putting down whatever I was doing and going to find it, because my dad believed customers should never have to ask twice.

I started working the register the summer I turned thirteen, which is younger than you're supposed to legally be doing much of anything, but our store is small enough that nobody was checking. My parents run it out of the bottom floor of a building on Fentress, lottery tickets and cigarettes behind the counter, a cooler of energy drinks that hums louder than it should, a whole aisle just for chips because apparently that's what sells. For years I thought of the register as the place I got stuck. My friends were at the lake or wherever, and I was scanning a can of Arizona iced tea for the ninth time that hour for a man who came in every single day at exactly 4:15.

Here's the thing I didn't expect, though it took me long enough to notice it that I'm almost embarrassed to admit when it happened. It was maybe two years ago, a Tuesday, nothing special about it, and Mr. Okafor came in - the 4:15 man, I finally learned his name after something like three years of ringing him up - and he was in a mood, talking fast about his daughter getting into some program, and I just stood there and listened because what else was I going to do, there was no line. And I realized I knew things about him. Not big things. That his knees hurt in the cold. That he'd started buying the diet version of his usual soda in March, which meant something, I didn't ask what. That he said "take care now" instead of goodbye, always, like a period at the end of a sentence.

I started paying attention after that, and once I started I couldn't really stop. The woman who buys a single scratch-off every Friday and never more, like she's rationing herself against something. The two brothers, maybe eight and ten, who come in after school and count out exact change for one bag of chips to split, and who I now quietly make sure gets rung up as the cheaper size if there's ever a discrepancy, don't tell my dad. The guy who used to buy a pack of Marlboros every day and then one day switched to gum and has bought gum every day since, and I have never once asked him about it because it isn't my business, but I notice, and I think noticing is its own kind of caring even when you don't say anything.

I used to think the register was where time got taken from me. Now I think it's the opposite. I can be back there for a four-hour shift and lose the whole afternoon without feeling like anything was stolen, because I'm not just standing behind a counter scanning barcodes, I'm reading a rotating cast of a few hundred people who trust me, in this small unglamorous way, to know their order and not make them repeat themselves. That's not nothing. My dad never explained this to me in words. He just did it himself, every single day, remembering who takes their coffee black and who's trying to quit smoking and who just lost someone, and I absorbed it the way you absorb anything you watch closely enough for long enough, which is slowly, and then all at once.

I don't know exactly when the shift happened in my head, whether it was Mr. Okafor's daughter or something quieter I didn't clock at the time. But I know I stopped counting down my shifts and started, without meaning to, keeping a kind of ledger of people instead of just money. And that clatter of the bell still isn't a pleasant sound. It's just become one I listen for.

text:
For fourteen months, my dad got up at 6:15, ironed one of his four dress shirts, and sat at the kitchen table by 6:45 with coffee and his laptop open to job boards, dressed like he had somewhere to be. He did not have anywhere to be. He'd been laid off from Halvorsen Machine Tool in March of my sophomore year, after nineteen years there, and for over a year there was no somewhere.

I want to say I found this admirable from the start. I didn't. For a long stretch I thought it was sad, honestly, and I told him so, once, badly, on a Tuesday in the fall when I came downstairs for school and saw him at that table in a pressed blue shirt with his cufflinks in, reading want ads for jobs he was overqualified for. I said something like, why do you get dressed up for nobody, Dad, you're not fooling anyone, you could just wear sweatpants like a normal person going through this. I remember exactly how it landed, because his face went very still, and he just said, I'm not doing it for anybody else.

I respected my dad's opinions more than almost anyone's. He'd run a floor of forty machinists for two decades and never once, in my whole life, seemed unsure of anything. So when he disagreed with me that morning - calmly, not even raising his voice - it shook me more than if a stranger had said the same thing back. I went to school still thinking I was right. Getting dressed for a job search that was going nowhere seemed, to me, like a kind of denial. I thought the honest thing, the healthy thing, was to let the front down and just be sad in your pajamas for a while, like everyone else I knew would have done.

It took me a long time, and one specific morning in January, to understand what he meant. I came down earlier than usual and caught him before he'd started the ritual - he was still in his undershirt, standing at the counter, and for just a second before he noticed me there, he looked like someone I didn't fully recognize. Not sad exactly. Loose. Unanchored is maybe the word for it. Then he saw me, and about ninety seconds later he was upstairs getting the blue shirt, and by the time I left for school he was back at the table, dressed, coffee poured, looking like my dad again.

That's when I got it. The shirt wasn't for the job search. It wasn't even really for us. It was the thing standing between him and that loose, unanchored version of himself he'd caught me seeing by accident. Nineteen years of getting up and being someone specific at a specific time had built a shape, and the shape didn't disappear just because the job did. If he'd taken my advice and let it go, I think something in him would have gone with it that might not have come back so easily.

He found a position in April, at a smaller company, for less money, and he still irons a shirt every morning, though now, at least, there's somewhere to wear it. I never told him I was wrong that Tuesday morning in the fall. I don't think I need to; I think he knew I'd figure it out eventually, the way you know a kid will understand a thing when they're ready and not one day before.

What I took from disagreeing with him isn't really about unemployment, or about shirts. It's that some habits look pointless from the outside because you judge them by what they produce, and my dad's habit was never producing a job. It was producing him, every single morning, on schedule, whether or not the day ahead had earned the effort.

text:
"You didn't even ask me," Wren said, and she said it quietly, which was somehow worse than if she'd yelled, because Wren yells about everything, Wren has yelled about socks being the wrong shade of white, and this time she just sat on the edge of her bed with the port access kit still open on the nightstand and said it like she was too tired to yell.

I had called the nurse line without telling her. Wren has cystic fibrosis, and that week her oxygen sats had been dipping in a way that scared me - not scared her, she insisted, but scared me - and I'd waited until she was in the shower and called our care coordinator, a woman named Deb who I'd spoken to probably two hundred times over six years, and asked whether we should push up her clinic visit. Deb said yes. I told my parents. By the time Wren got out of the shower, there was already a plan in motion that she hadn't been part of making.

She's fourteen. I'm seventeen. In the specific math of our house, that three-year gap has meant I've been half a sister and half something else for most of her life - the one who learned to do chest physio before I learned to parallel park, the one who can recognize a bad cough from a normal one through a closed door. I have never resented this, not really, not in a way I could point to and name. But somewhere in those six years I also started making decisions about her body without asking her first, and I told myself this was love, and mostly I still think it was, except for the part where I never checked whether it was also something else.

Our home health aide, Marisol, has worked with our family for four years, and she's the one whose opinion I trust more than almost anyone's outside my parents. She was there the day Wren found out about the call. I expected Marisol to back me up - I'd done the responsible thing, hadn't I, caught something early, gotten ahead of it - and instead she pulled me into the kitchen and told me, not unkindly, that I'd made a mistake.

"She's not a a problem you're managing," Marisol said. "She's a person whose lungs happen to be the thing you're managing. Those aren't the same, and you're old enough now that the difference matters."

I argued with her. I actually argued, standing in our kitchen with the kettle going, saying that Wren doesn't always make the safest choice for herself, that someone has to be the one who calls it in, that if I'd waited to ask permission we might have lost days we didn't have to lose. Marisol didn't say I was wrong about the sats. She said I was wrong about the asking. She said the whole architecture of Wren's illness, from diagnosis at two years old onward, has been built by adults deciding things about her body for her, doctors and nurses and parents and, now, me, and that somewhere in all that necessary managing, nobody had left her a single decision that was actually hers to make about her own health.

I didn't agree with her in the kitchen. I still don't know if I fully agree with her now. Some part of me still believes that if I'd asked Wren first and she'd said no, and something had gone wrong that week, I would never have forgiven myself, and I don't think that fear is unreasonable given what I've watched her body do to her over the years, given what CF actually does when it moves fast.

But I keep coming back to her face on the edge of the bed. Not angry. Just tired in a way that had nothing to do with her lungs.

I asked her, a few weeks later, carefully, what she would have wanted instead. She thought about it longer than I expected. She said she didn't know exactly - that she probably would have said yes to the call anyway, that this wasn't really about the call at all. She said what she wanted was to have been in the room when the decision got made, even if the decision ended up the same. Even if I was right about the sats. Even if speed mattered.

I still don't fully know what to do with that. Marisol was right about something I can name and can't yet undo, and I think about it most when Wren's oxygen monitor beeps in the next room and my hand is already reaching for my phone before I've thought to knock on her door first.

text:
The object is a tire lever, cheap orange plastic, one of three that came in a five-dollar patch kit my neighbor Mr. Duval gave me two summers ago, and it's the only one of the three that hasn't snapped yet, which feels like it should mean something even though I know it's probably just luck.

I started fixing bicycles for the kids on my street almost by accident. A neighbor's son, maybe eight years old, was standing in his driveway crying over a flat tire he had no way to fix and no money to take anywhere, and I happened to be walking past with nothing better to do that afternoon, and I said I'd take a look, mostly because I didn't want to keep walking past a crying kid and pretend I hadn't noticed. I didn't actually know how to fix a flat. I looked it up on my phone standing right there in his driveway, patched the tube badly, and sent him off wobbling but riding.

Word got around the way things get around on a street with more kids than cars. Within a month I had a rotating list of neighborhood bikes lined up against our garage most Saturdays - chains that had jumped their gears, brakes that squealed, one memorable bike with training wheels so bent they'd started digging trenches in the driveway. Mr. Duval, who'd fixed his own bikes for probably fifty years before I ever showed up, started coming out to supervise, then to help, then, eventually, to just hand me tools before I asked for them because he'd learned to predict what I'd need next.

He gave me the patch kit that Christmas, wrapped badly in newspaper, no card, just left on our porch with my name written on it in marker. I don't think he meant it as a big gesture. I think he just had an extra kit and knew I'd use it. But it was the first time an adult outside my family had looked at something I did on my own initiative and decided it was worth investing five dollars and a little bit of faith into. That's a small thing to say out loud and a much bigger thing to actually feel, standing in a driveway holding a present from a man who'd watched me ruin at least four inner tubes before I learned to do it properly.

I still use that same lever, worn smooth now where my thumb sits, even though I could afford better tools myself at this point from the little bit kids' parents have started insisting on paying me. I've fixed maybe sixty bikes over two summers, mostly small stuff, occasionally something that took me a full weekend of watching videos to figure out. None of it made me any money worth mentioning, not really, and none of it was ever going to.

What it did was give me a strange, specific kind of gratitude I hadn't expected, aimed less at the kids who thank me with a lot of enthusiasm and more at Mr. Duval, who noticed a kid trying badly at something and decided the right response was tools, not correction. He never once told me I was doing it wrong, even when I clearly was. He just kept showing up with his own hands ready, letting me be the one who actually held the wrench.

I think about that orange lever more than its five-dollar plastic self probably deserves. It's outlasted two better ones I bought myself since. I keep meaning to replace it and I never do, mostly because I think some tools earn the right to keep being used past the point where it makes practical sense, just for what they were there for the first time.

text:
I've been cut from varsity soccer three years in a row now, freshman through junior year, and somewhere in the middle of that streak I started doing something I never told my coaches about, because it felt private in a way that trying out never did: I started watching full ninety-minute matches with a notebook, pausing constantly, mapping out where players moved when they didn't have the ball.

It began almost by accident. After the sophomore-year cut, I couldn't sleep, and I put on a random match to distract myself, and instead of watching the ball the way I always had, I found myself watching the fullback on the far side of the field who never touched it for the first fifteen minutes. He was constantly adjusting his position by a few feet, shifting to cover space that didn't exist yet, reading the game two passes ahead. I paused the video. I rewound it. I watched those fifteen minutes probably six times before I understood what he was actually doing, and by the time I looked up it was past two in the morning and I had somehow filled four pages of a notebook with arrows.

This became a routine without my really deciding it should. Most nights, at least three a week, I'd watch forty-five minutes of match footage and lose an hour and a half to it, tracking one player at a time across an entire half, noting the tiny anticipatory movements that never show up on a highlight reel because nothing dramatic happens in them - a step to the left before a pass even gets played, a shoulder check over one side instead of the other. I couldn't have told you, freshman year, that soccer had this much invisible architecture underneath the visible game. I know it now the way you know something you've stared at for hundreds of hours.

What captivates me about it, if I'm honest, is that it's the one part of this sport where being smaller and slower than the players who made varsity doesn't matter at all. Spacing and anticipation aren't athletic gifts. They're a kind of literacy, something you build by paying obsessive attention over time, and I have paid that attention more consistently, I think, than most players who've actually made the roster I keep missing.

I don't have a coach for this part. I go looking for it myself - old broadcasts, post-match tactical breakdowns from analysts online, occasionally a forum where people argue for hours about a single defensive shape. Nobody assigned me this. I built the routine out of three consecutive disappointments and a lot of empty evenings, and it's become the thing I actually think about when I'm supposed to be doing homework, the notebook now on its fourth volume, still full of arrows nobody but me has ever asked to see.

text:
The duffel bag is army green, canvas gone soft at the corners, and one wheel has been missing since our third move, replaced by nothing, so it drags along one side with a scraping sound I could pick out of a crowded hallway blindfolded. There's a luggage tag looped through the handle with five city names on it, four of them crossed out in different pens, because I kept meaning to buy a new tag and never did. That bag has been packed and unpacked in six different bedrooms since I was eight, which works out to a new school roughly every eighteen months, which my dad still calls opportunity and I have, more than once, called something else to his face.

He's a civil engineer who takes on infrastructure contracts, bridges mostly, sometimes a water system, and the work goes wherever the project is, which has meant Ohio, then Texas, then back to Ohio but a different city, then Georgia, then North Carolina, then here. Every time, the duffel bag came first, packed the night before the movers arrived with whatever I couldn't stand to put in a box, and every time I told myself the same thing, that this would be the last one, that surely a person only needs to start over so many times before the universe runs out of new schools to put them in.

Two years ago, when he came home and said there was a project in Charlotte, I told him no. Not in the calm way I'd rehearsed it in my head for approximately a year, but standing in the kitchen, saying that I was fifteen years old and had exactly one friend group I hadn't had to explain myself to from scratch, and that his job had cost me every single one before that. He said, and I remember this exactly, that he wasn't going to apologize for providing for us, and that I'd adjust the way I always adjusted, like adjusting was a skill I should be thanking him for instead of a wound I was tired of reopening. I said some things back that I mostly still stand by and one thing I don't, about wishing he'd married someone whose job didn't drag us everywhere, which was cruel and aimed at my mother by accident, and he went quiet in the way he goes quiet when he's decided a conversation is over rather than resolved.

We moved. I packed the duffel bag myself that time, wheel still dragging, tag still crossed out and rewritten. We have never actually finished that conversation from the kitchen. We don't fight about it anymore, mostly because I stopped bringing it up and he stopped explaining himself, which isn't the same as agreement, just a kind of ceasefire neither of us negotiated out loud.

I'm packing that same bag again now, for college, and it will be, undramatically, the seventh time. I've gotten strangely good at making a new place feel livable within about a week, which is either the best thing my childhood gave me or the thing I resent most about it, and I genuinely don't know which, some days both at once. My dad helped me pick out the flight. He didn't mention the bag. Neither did I.

meta.topic: moving between six schools in nine years
meta.prompt: Write about an object that is important to you.

text:
My older sister ran the lighting board for our school's fall play for three years before she graduated, and I inherited the job from her the way you inherit most things in our family, without much of a ceremony, just her handing me the binder of cue sheets and saying good luck, you'll need it, on her way out the door to college.

She still comes to opening night every year, even now, home from school for exactly one weekend that always happens to line up with our production, and she still sits in the booth with me for the first act like she owns some part of it, which, in a way, she does. This year we disagreed, and it wasn't really about lighting at all, though lighting was the argument we actually had.

I wanted to run the final scene of our show - a quiet two-person dialogue at the end - with a single warm spotlight and everything else dark, hard focus, no ambiance. She thought it needed a wash of blue behind them, something softer, more atmospheric, the way she used to run comparable scenes when it was her board. I told her the show wasn't hers anymore. I didn't mean it as cruelly as it came out, but it came out that way, and I watched something in her face close a little when I said it.

She backed off outwardly. Said fine, it's your call, your name's on the program this year, not mine. But she said it in the specific flat voice she uses when she's decided not to fight about something she still thinks she's right about, and I know that voice better than almost anyone alive, because I grew up underneath it, always one grade behind her, always walking into rooms where she'd already set the expectations.

We ran it my way both nights. The spotlight, the hard dark around it, exactly as I'd designed it. And I still don't know if it was right. Some nights, sitting in the booth after the show ends, I run that final cue back in my head and picture her blue wash instead and I genuinely cannot tell you which version serves the scene better. I only know I wanted, badly, for it to be mine, uncomplicated by her opinion, even a good one.

She left Sunday afternoon, back to school, and we hugged at the door the way we always do, and neither of us brought the lighting up again. That's not unusual for us - we don't really relitigate things, we just let them settle into the pile of small unresolved disagreements that seem to accumulate between people who love each other and used to share every single thing, right down to a booth eight feet wide, and now mostly share holidays and a handful of weekends a year instead.

I think about it more than the size of the disagreement should probably warrant. Not because I regret the spotlight choice, exactly. Because I keep noticing that I wanted to win an argument with my sister more than I wanted the scene to be as good as it could be, and I don't fully know what to do with that discovery about myself, sitting up in a booth she taught me to run, using a binder she built, doing a job that will always, in some sense, still partly be hers no matter whose name is on the program this year.

meta.topic: running the lighting board for the school play
meta.prompt: Tell us about a time you disagreed with someone whose opinion you respected.

text:
My mother still keeps our old address written on a Post-it stuck inside a kitchen drawer in our new apartment, three thousand miles from the house it belongs to, and I found it by accident looking for a rubber band and didn't say anything about it, just closed the drawer and stood there for a second longer than I needed to.

We moved from outside Manchester to a suburb of Cleveland in October of my junior year, which is, as it turns out, an objectively terrible time to move a sixteen-year-old anywhere. My dad got the job offer in August. By October we were in a rental house with boxes still taped shut in the living room, and I was sitting in a new classroom being asked to introduce myself to twenty-six strangers while my accent, which I had never once thought about before, suddenly felt like the only thing about me anyone could see.

I don't lose track of time thinking about the move itself. What actually captivates me - and I recognize how strange this is going to sound - is the specific, almost geological process of how a place stops being home and a different place slowly starts being home instead, without your permission, without you noticing the exact day it happened. I've read more about migration psychology and identity formation in the last year than I've read for any actual class, which my history teacher, Mr. Alvarez, would probably find funny given how little I contributed to discussions on unrelated topics that semester. I found a study once, at eleven at night, about how people who relocate report "home" as a feeling that splits and exists in two places simultaneously for years, sometimes permanently, and I sat there reading footnotes until my dad knocked and asked why my light was still on.

My mom is the one I go to when I want to actually talk about it, which is strange, because she's also the one I fight with about it most.

She adjusted faster than I did, or she says she did, or maybe she just decided faster that adjusting was the correct thing to perform in front of me. She likes it here, genuinely, the space, the job my dad has, the quiet. I don't dislike it. That's not the disagreement. The disagreement is about whether it's allowed to still hurt this long later, whether missing a place is a thing with an expiration date on it that I've overrun.

"You have to let it go a little," she told me a few months ago, not unkindly, more like she was worried about me. "You can't keep living half in a place you don't live in anymore."

I told her I wasn't doing that. I was lying, a little. I still know the bus schedule to my old school by heart. I still, embarrassingly, sometimes go to type our old postcode into forms out of muscle memory. She thinks this means I haven't accepted where we are. I think it means something different - that a person can build a whole new life in a place and still keep a room, somewhere inside themselves, furnished exactly the way the old one was, and that this isn't a failure to move on, it's just what moving actually costs.

We haven't resolved this. We probably won't, not with a single conversation, maybe not ever completely, because I think we're both a little bit right and neither of us wants to fully concede the point. She wants me to be lighter about it than I am. I want her to admit that lightness isn't actually available to everyone on the same schedule.

What keeps me up reading isn't nostalgia, exactly. It's the mechanics of it - how identity apparently isn't a single location you can just swap out, how the research keeps using the word "liminal" in ways that finally made sense to me only after I lived it. I go looking for language that explains what's happening to me because nobody in my actual life, including my mother, including myself most days, has quite found it yet. The Post-it is still in the drawer. I don't think either of us is ready to throw it away.

text:
Room 118 has a busted thermostat. The dial goes past 80 before it clicks over to heat, so in October it's either freezing or a sauna, no in between, and for the first six weeks of chess club - my chess club, the one I begged the front office to let me start - it didn't matter, because nobody was in there to complain about the temperature except me and Mr. Boyle.

Mr. Boyle cleans that wing of the building. I knew him the way you know a custodian, which is to say I said hi and he said hi back and that was basically it, for two years. Then I started this club nobody wanted, Tuesdays and Thursdays at lunch, and it turned out Mr. Boyle unlocked room 118 every single one of those mornings before I got there. Not because anyone told him to. He wasn't even supposed to be on that hallway before ten.

I found this out by accident, on a Thursday when I showed up ten minutes early to fix something with the folding table, and the door was already open, lights on, thermostat cranked so the room wouldn't be an icebox for whatever eleven people I was still, at that point, imagining might one day appear. He was in the hallway with his cart. I asked if he'd unlocked it. He said something like, yeah, figured you'd want it warm, and kept moving.

He kept doing that. Every single meeting, all fall, whether one kid showed up or zero. I didn't ask him to. I don't think he ever mentioned it to anyone else, and honestly I might never have said anything about it either, except one day in December I caught him setting up two folding chairs across from each other at the little table by the window - a table nobody used, off to the side - and I asked why, and he told me, kind of sideways, not really looking at me, that his younger brother used to beat him at chess when they were kids and he hadn't played since his brother died, years back, and something about the room made him think of it.

I didn't know what to say to that. I still don't, really. I just said thanks, and he shrugged like it was nothing, and went back to his cart.

Here's the thing about gratitude nobody tells you: it doesn't always feel like a big warm feeling in your chest. Sometimes it just quietly rearranges what you think you're doing. I'd started that club because I liked chess and figured other people might too, eventually, if I was patient enough. After I found out about Mr. Boyle, I started showing up fifteen minutes early myself, and I started leaving the door propped even when it was just me sitting there, because it turns out an open door is a whole different message than a locked one, and I'd never once thought about that until somebody did it for me for six straight weeks without saying a word about it.

We have fourteen members now. Mr. Boyle still unlocks the room before I get there most days, out of habit I think, even though I have my own key. I never taught him to play. He's never asked, and I've never pushed it. But sometimes I set up that little table by the window anyway, two chairs, nobody sitting in them, and I just leave it like that until I lock up for the day.

None of this shows up on a transcript. There's no line for it. But if you asked me what actually taught me to keep something going when it looks like it's failing, it wasn't a coach or a book, it was a man with a cart who decided, quietly and for no credit at all, that a cold empty room deserved to be warm anyway.

text:
The object is a swim cap, navy blue, still faintly smelling of chlorine even though it hasn't touched a pool in fourteen months. I keep it in the top drawer of my desk, underneath a stack of loose pens, where I have to move things aside to get to it, which I think is intentional on my part even if I've never admitted that out loud until right now.

My shoulder gave out during a 200 fly at Sectionals the winter of my sophomore year. Not gave out like a dramatic pop, nothing you'd see in a movie - it was more like something inside just quietly stopped agreeing to do what I asked of it, mid-stroke, and I finished the race anyway because that's what you do, and then I couldn't lift my arm above my head for six weeks. The diagnosis had a long name involving my labrum that I've since memorized the way you memorize the name of a person who hurt you. Surgery, then months of a physical therapist named Deb pushing my arm through ranges of motion while I stared at the ceiling tiles and did math in my head to keep from crying. The short version is that the shoulder healed enough for regular life and nowhere near enough for competitive butterfly, and a doctor with kind eyes told me that at some point, the eleven years I'd spent in a pool were, medically speaking, over.

My father did not agree with this. He still doesn't, not really, not all the way, and this is the part I haven't figured out how to write about without it sounding like I'm blaming him, because I'm not, or I don't think I am.

He was my first coach. Before club teams, before anyone else timed me with anything more official than a kitchen stopwatch, it was him at the edge of our local pool at six in the morning, before his own workday started, and swimming was the thing we built between us instead of whatever fathers and daughters usually build. When the doctor said what she said, my dad's first instinct wasn't comfort. It was research. He found three more specialists. He asked about experimental treatments. He wanted a second surgery, a third opinion, a path back into the water that didn't involve the word "over."

I didn't want any of that. I wanted to be done, and I wanted him to let me be done, and those two things turned out to be much harder to say to him than I expected.

We had the fight - if you can call it a fight, since neither of us raised our voice, we just got quieter and quieter until the silence itself was the argument - in the car outside Deb's office. He said I was giving up too early. I said I wasn't giving anything up, I was choosing something, and those aren't the same, and he said choosing to quit is still quitting, and I said maybe quitting isn't always the wrong word for a thing.

We never really finished that conversation. We just stopped having it, the way you stop touching a bruise once you've learned exactly where it is. He still brings up swimming sometimes, carefully, like he's testing whether the door is unlocked. I still change the subject, carefully, like I'm not entirely sure it isn't.

I don't know if he thinks I resent him. I don't, not exactly, though I did for a while. What I think now, holding this cap that doesn't smell like much of anything anymore if I'm honest, chlorine doesn't last fourteen months, maybe I'm imagining it - what I think is that he loved the sport for both of us, and I only ever loved it for as long as my body agreed to let me, and neither of us has found the sentence yet that explains that difference in a way the other one can actually hear.

meta.topic: an injury that ended a competitive swimming career
meta.prompt: Write about an object that is important to you.

text:
The surveyor's spray can hisses twice before it catches, and then there's a red X on the mango tree's trunk, right at chest height, right over the spot where thirteen years of pencil notches are still faintly visible if you know where to look. My uncle is telling my father the number again, like saying it slower will make it hurt less, and my father isn't answering him, just standing there with his hand flat against the bark like he's checking the tree's pulse.

The notches are mine. Every year on my birthday, since I was four, my grandfather stood me against that trunk and cut a small line at the top of my head with his pocketknife, and then wrote the date next to it in pencil that has long since worn away, leaving just the cuts, a crooked ladder climbing the bark from somewhere around my grandfather's knee to somewhere past my own shoulder now. He used to say the tree and I were growing up together, since he'd planted it the spring my father was born and I was, in some sense he never fully explained, the second child it was raising.

My uncle wants to sell four acres to a developer building flats along the highway, enough money to cover what his son's surgery cost and what the loan he took out for it is now costing on top of that. My father wants to keep the land whole, the way it's been in the family for three generations, and every time this argument happens, which is often now, it ends the same way: my uncle asking what exactly my father thinks pride is going to pay for, and my father not answering, because there isn't a good answer, only a stubborn one.

I used to think my father would win just by refusing to lose. He's good at that, at outlasting a conversation instead of resolving it. But the surveyor was standing in our field with a can of spray paint because the bank had already sent a second notice, and no amount of my father's hand flat against bark was going to change what the four acres closest to the road were now worth on paper.

They sold it. Not all of it - my father held the line on the two acres nearest the house, including the tree, in a compromise that satisfied nobody completely, my uncle getting less than he needed and my father losing more than he wanted. The X stayed on the trunk for almost a year after, through two monsoons, fading from red to a rust-colored ghost of itself, until my father finally scrubbed it off one Sunday with a wire brush, not saying much while he did it, just working at the bark like it owed him something.

I climbed up to check the notches again before I left for school this fall. They're still there, thirteen crooked lines and a fourteenth my grandfather cut just weeks before he died, my father holding me steady that year since my grandfather's hands had started shaking too much to trust with a knife near my scalp. The tree stands maybe eighty feet from where the new boundary fence now runs, close enough that I can still see the flats going up on what used to be ours, three stories of scaffolding where the wheat used to come in gold by April.

My uncle and my father still don't really talk about it, not directly, though they sit at the same table every Sunday and pass dishes to each other like nothing happened. I keep waiting for one of them to say something that ends it properly. Neither of them ever does.

meta.topic: an argument about whether to sell the family land
meta.prompt: The lessons we take from obstacles we encounter can be fundamental to later success. Recount a time when you faced a challenge, setback, or failure. How did it affect you, and what did you learn from the experience?

text:
I learned to drive sitting on a phone book in my grandfather's 1978 Ford, bouncing across the hay field behind his barn, both of us sunburned, him working the pedals with his left foot because my legs weren't long enough yet to reach the clutch and the brake at the same time. I was eleven. What I actually fell for that summer wasn't driving. It was the truck itself - why it lurched when I let the clutch out too fast, why it ran rough until it warmed up, why my grandfather could diagnose a problem with that engine just by listening to it through the hood with his eyes closed, the way other people listen to music.

That's the thing that captivates me, genuinely, more than anything in a classroom: the internal combustion engine as a system, all those small controlled explosions turning into rotation turning into motion, and the fact that a person with the right knowledge can listen to a machine and understand what's wrong with it the way a doctor listens to a heartbeat. I've read the Chilton manual for that truck so many times the spine is cracked in three places. I've spent entire afternoons I meant to spend on homework instead pulling the valve cover off just to look at it, then putting it back exactly the way it was.

My grandfather taught me everything I know about that truck, hands-on, over eight years, and he is also the person I have the longest-running disagreement of my life with, one we have never actually resolved. He believes you learn an engine by feel - by hours, by mistakes, by your hands - and that reading about compression ratios in a manual is close to useless next to just listening to the thing run. I believe both things are true at once, that feel matters and that I also want to understand the actual physics of what's happening in that cylinder, the math behind why a slightly different timing advance changes everything. When I told him last year that I want to study mechanical engineering, he didn't discourage me exactly, but he got quiet, and later I heard him telling my uncle that school was going to teach me to explain an engine without ever really knowing one.

I love him too much to let that go, and I'm stubborn enough not to let it go either. We've had version after version of the same argument, usually while working on the truck together, him saying something like "your hands will teach you faster than any book," me saying that his hands only work because forty years ago somebody's book taught someone the theory he inherited secondhand. Neither of us has ever won. He still calls the manual "the excuse" for not really knowing a machine. I still bring it out to the barn anyway, and he still, despite himself, ends up leaning over my shoulder to look at the diagram.

We haven't settled it, and at this point I don't think we're supposed to. What I know is that I can now do both - diagnose a rough idle by ear the way he taught me, and explain in a lab report exactly why it's happening. I think, somewhere under his stubbornness, he's a little proud of that. He has just never once said so out loud.

meta.topic: learning to drive on a farm

text:
Six weeks after Priya Anand stopped speaking to me, I was sitting in the back of Mr. Halloran's room during a free period when he said, not even looking up from the stack he was grading, "You know she could have torched you on that evaluation and she didn't." I asked him what he was talking about, and he seemed surprised I didn't already know, and then he wouldn't say anything else, like he'd already told me more than he meant to. It took me the rest of the day to figure out he meant the peer contribution forms from our Envirothon project, the ones we'd each filled out alone back in March, right around the time everything between us had gone quiet.

Priya and I had been best friends since the start of freshman year, when we got seated alphabetically next to each other in biology and bonded over both hating the teacher's habit of cold-calling. By junior year we did everything together, including, unfortunately, signing up as partners for the county Envirothon regional, where our assignment was to design and build a working rainwater filtration prototype on a budget of forty dollars, using whatever we could scavenge out of her dad's garage. She was better at the engineering. I was better at explaining things to judges. It should have worked.

It didn't, not because the filter itself failed, but because we spent weeks disagreeing about whose idea the core design actually was. She said the layered charcoal-and-sand approach had been hers from the beginning. I remembered it differently, remembered sketching it on the back of a worksheet at lunch while she was still stuck on a completely different model that needed a pump we couldn't afford. By the week before the competition we were barely speaking except to argue about credit, and two days before we presented, she said, loud enough that people in the hallway turned to look, that I didn't even understand my own part of the project. Maybe I didn't, not entirely. But it was the kind of thing you don't forgive fast, and neither of us tried to.

We stopped sitting together. We stopped texting. I wrote maybe four different drafts of an apology I wasn't sure I owed and never sent a single one. In March, when Mr. Halloran handed out the individual contribution forms, the ones where you rate your partner's effort and describe what they actually did, I filled mine out honestly but carefully, giving her full credit for the design even though it still stung, because I didn't want to be someone who let a fight rewrite the truth.

I assumed she wouldn't return the favor. I assumed, if I'm being honest, that she'd use the form to write down some version of what she'd said in the hallway, this time somewhere it would count toward my actual grade. So when Mr. Halloran let that comment slip, I asked to see my own file, which technically I wasn't supposed to do, and he let me anyway. Priya had written two sentences naming the exact piece I'd built, the water-clarity testing rig nobody else had noticed because it wasn't the flashy part, and said I'd done it without being asked and without complaining once. She'd dated the form March 9th. I checked that against my own memory and realized it was four days after the hallway, four days into a silence she had no reason to end, and she'd had every opportunity to hurt me on paper and had chosen, instead, to sit there and write something true and generous about a person she wasn't speaking to.

I don't know exactly what made her choose that. I've pictured the scene more times than I probably should, her at her kitchen table with the form and a pen, still angry, still not answering my texts, deciding to be fair anyway, for reasons that had nothing to do with me finding out. I never got an explanation, because we never really talked again, not properly, not the way we used to before all this. But something in me shifted after Mr. Halloran's comment, some assumption I hadn't known I was carrying about what people owe each other once a friendship is over. I started paying closer attention to my own smallness in situations like that one, the instinct to protect my version of events even when it costs someone else something real. I started trying, in whatever form that takes outside of a classroom, to rate people the way Priya rated me instead of the way I'd been ready to rate her.

It didn't fix anything between us. Some friendships end and just stay ended, no matter how the story resolves itself later. But it changed what I thought fairness was worth when nobody's forcing you to practice it, and that lesson has outlasted the fight by years now, longer than the friendship itself lasted after it.

meta.topic: a friendship that ended over a group project
meta.prompt: Reflect on something that someone has done for you that has made you happy or thankful in a surprising way. How has this gratitude affected or motivated you?

text:
The queen had one eye missing. I'd found her in my grandfather's office drawer, buried under some old tax documents, and I knew immediately that I was going to build an entire chess club around her.

Nobody at my school played chess. That wasn't a guess - I'd asked around. I knew everyone in my small school, and none of them had ever sat down to a real game. When I tried to explain the rules to people, their eyes glazed over the way they did in math class. The idea of staring at a board for an hour seemed to physically pain them. I got that. I understood why chess seemed boring if you didn't already understand why it was beautiful.

But I had this queen with the missing eye, and I had this absolute certainty that if I could just get five people to learn the game, some of them would fall into it the way I had.

I made a poster for the club meetings using a photo I took of the queen. Blurry, probably too artsy, but it made her look like something from a mystery novel. Someone had damaged her. Someone had loved her enough to keep her anyway. I posted it outside the library before school started in the fall, and I didn't honestly expect much. Maybe one person would show up out of curiosity.

Three people came to the first meeting. By week four, we had seven. By the end of the year, we had a waiting list.

I should say they all became brilliant players or that I discovered some hidden talent in my school or that we went to regional tournaments or something inspiring like that. We didn't. We had one tournament in the spring and we did badly. Some of the kids quit after a month because, as predicted, they found it tedious. One person only showed up because their girlfriend was coming. Two of them never got past the opening moves.

But there were these two kids who came every single Thursday and by the end of the year they were playing each other with this intensity that reminded me of the feeling I had when I first understood what chess was about. They were learning the language. They were beginning to see the board the way I see it, as this universe of possibilities where your mind gets to stretch itself in ways that the rest of the day doesn't allow.

I still have the one-eyed queen in my locker. The club is still going, led by someone else now because I'm graduating. It's smaller than it was at its peak, which makes sense. Most hobbies don't last beyond the novelty. But the fact that it existed at all, that I convinced even a handful of people to care about something they had every reason to ignore - that's the thing I keep thinking about.

I found something that nobody else was looking for. And I was stubborn enough to insist it mattered until a few other people believed me.

meta.topic: founding a chess club at a school with no chess players
meta.prompt: Some students have a background, identity, interest, or talent that is so meaningful they believe their application would be incomplete without it. If this sounds like you, then please share your story.

text:
My mom's clothing business was an accident. That's how she always tells it. She didn't wake up one morning and think "I'm going to buy and sell used clothes on eBay." What actually happened is that she cleaned out her closet one Saturday and had this pile of things she'd never wear again. She'd gained weight after having me. Her style changed. Some of it was just from 2005 and didn't fit anymore. And she realized that selling it online might make a few hundred bucks for a trip or something.

She made fifteen hundred dollars in the first month. She couldn't believe it. People, apparently, wanted vintage Banana Republic and barely-worn coach bags from the 90s and early 2000s. She kept the business going, started going to thrift stores and estate sales, buying things cheap and reselling them for a markup. Within a year she'd turned it into an actual business with structure and goals. She had inventory organized in our basement with a whole system - things sorted by condition, by season, by brand. She'd wake up at five in the morning to take photos and list things. She was making real money - like, genuinely more than her part-time job was bringing in. My dad thought it was funny at first, then he thought it was impressive, then he stopped thinking about it altogether because it had become normal.

For about two years, the business was everything. She talked about profit margins at dinner. She'd calculate the cost per item and spend actual hours researching comps on eBay to make sure she was pricing things right. It was ambitious and kind of beautiful - she was building something. Making something. And it was working. We had more money. She had this thing that was hers. My younger brother joked that she loved her business more than she loved us.

I believed him completely. I thought she was avoiding her actual life by hiding in the basement with packages and business spreadsheets. I'd ask her to come to my soccer games or my school events and she'd be there physically but distracted, thinking about inventory numbers and profit margins. She'd miss dinner sometimes because she was at Goodwill hunting for deals on a Thursday night instead of being home with us. It felt selfish to me. Not evil or anything. Just selfish. Like she'd found something more interesting than us.

Then one day she just quit. She listed everything she had at basically break-even prices on the Facebook marketplace and got rid of it all in about two weeks. She was done. She said she didn't know why anymore. That she'd lost interest. My dad thought she was crazy. I thought maybe she'd finally realized what everyone had been trying to tell her - that her family was more important than a side hustle.

But here's the thing I didn't get at the time. She wasn't just quitting a business. She was grieving something much deeper. She was grieving the person she thought she could be. The version of her that was an entrepreneur, that could build something from nothing, that had these hours that belonged just to her and her own ambitions. The business had mattered to her in a way that seemed to threaten all of us. And she'd killed it because she felt like she was supposed to - like being a good mother meant abandoning that version of herself. Not because she'd stopped loving it. The opposite. She loved it so much that she felt guilty.

Years later we talked about it. She said she'd made a mistake. That she shouldn't have listened to the guilt she felt about choosing something for herself. That maybe if she'd kept going, if she hadn't let everyone make her feel like she was failing as a mother, she wouldn't spend so much time now wondering what happened to her. Not to the business - to her. To the person who wanted to build something and thought she could.

I think about that a lot. About how sometimes the unsuccessful thing is just quitting when things get hard or feel wrong. And sometimes the unsuccessful thing is not even trying, because you convince yourself you're not allowed.

meta.topic: a mother's second-hand clothing business
meta.prompt: Describe a time you were not successful. What did you do next?

text:
My mom went back to university when I was seven, and I spent the next decade convinced this was the worst thing she had ever done to me. She was forty years old. I remember thinking it was selfish. I was seven. My opinion on selfishness was not sophisticated.

She was in classes from eight until three. Then she came home and made dinner and did homework with me and did everything else she'd always done, but there was something different. She was tired in a way I blamed her education for. No vacations because of exams. Pasta for dinner because she was studying. The house was messier. She was less available.

I was furious about this on her behalf, which is what kids do when they see their parents sacrifice things. They interpret it as personal betrayal.

What I got wrong was that I thought going to university was something she did instead of being a mom. I didn't understand she was doing both. That choosing yourself doesn't mean abandoning your kid. I spent years resenting the pasta dinners and the weekends she spent studying instead of playing with me. I thought she was being selfish. I thought a good mom would just stay home.

My mom graduated last year. She's working as a consultant in environmental policy now. More importantly, she's different. She talks about her work with a confidence she never had before. Not confidence as a mom, but confidence as herself. Having something that was just hers mattered to her. It changed her.

The thing I still think about is all those years I spent being resentful. All the times I thought she was doing something wrong. All the ways I punished her in my head for not being available in exactly the way I wanted.

But now I understand what she was actually teaching me. That you can want multiple things at once. That being a mom and being a person with your own goals aren't mutually exclusive. That sometimes loving your kid means showing them you have your own life. That you matter beyond your role as a parent.

I know I'll face this myself someday. If I have a daughter, I'll want to do what my mom did. I'll want to keep growing, keep building something. And because of what my mom did, I know I can do both. I have a model of what it looks like to be a woman who doesn't stop at motherhood, who isn't satisfied with just doing the expected thing.

That's worth all the pasta dinners. I just wish I'd understood it when I was seven instead of taking until sixteen.

meta.topic: a mother who returned to university at forty
meta.prompt: What is something you have taught yourself, and what did learning it without a teacher show you?

text:
I was so committed to the pallet furniture phase. Like, embarrassingly committed. I was going to recycle materials responsibly. I was going to be creative and resourceful. I was going to make beautiful rustic pieces that would look amazing in my room and cost basically nothing. My mom thought I was insane. My dad thought I was going through a phase that would pass. But I had watched TikTok videos and Pinterest boards and YouTube tutorials of people building perfect pallet tables, and I was absolutely convinced I could do it too.

The first pallet I found was behind a grocery store. I convinced my brother to help me drag it to our house and I was already planning where it would go. Coffee table. That's what I'd make. I watched three different tutorials and then I grabbed my dad's power tools - without asking, which is maybe the first problem - and I started taking the pallet apart.

It took four hours to disassemble something that probably took fifteen minutes to put together in the factory. My hands hurt. Splinters everywhere. The wood was not as clean as it looked in the videos. There were weird stains and some of the boards were warped. But I was undeterred. I was going to sand it down and make it perfect.

The sanding took two days. My arms hated me. The patio was covered in wood dust. My mom definitely yelled about that. But then I stained it and I have to say it actually looked pretty decent. I was so proud. I put the legs on and I had a functional coffee table. It was crooked. It was uneven. But I had made it and it existed.

I was going to make ten more things. I found pallets literally everywhere once I started looking. Restaurants, stores, parking lots. I started the second project - a headboard for my bed. This was more ambitious. More failure points. And here's the thing I didn't see coming. I was getting tired. And also, I was beginning to realize that recycled pallet furniture is actually kind of ugly. Like, aesthetically speaking, it's a trend that's a trend for a reason and that reason is not that it looks good. It looks like you found wood in an alley and made furniture out of it. Which, to be fair, you did.

Halfway through the second project I just stopped completely. I looked at the half-made headboard sitting in my room and I thought about the coffee table that I'd paid forty dollars in materials to "save money" on. I thought about all the time and the actual effort that had gone into it. I thought about the fact that I could just buy actual real furniture from a store that didn't give me splinters and didn't require five different YouTube tutorials to assemble correctly.

I never finished the headboard. I don't even know where the pieces went. Probably still in our garage somewhere. My coffee table sat in my room for a few months and then I got a real one from IKEA because the pallet table was deeply uncomfortable to put drinks on.

What changed my mind wasn't failure. It was understanding my own motivation. I wasn't actually trying to recycle or be sustainable or creative. I was trying to be the kind of person who did DIY projects. I was performing. And the moment I realized that, it all felt pointless. I'd rather be authentic about not caring than fake caring about pallets.

text:
My mom started the garden in our backyard three years ago when the landscaper broke his leg and we couldn't afford to replace him immediately. She bought seeds from the dollar store and planted them in rows. Tomatoes, carrots, some kind of squash that she says came from her mother's garden thirty years ago. I helped because she asked me to, not because I particularly cared about vegetables.

For two years it worked. We'd get tomatoes in August that tasted like nothing from the grocery store could ever taste like. My dad would make salsa on a Saturday afternoon. It was fine. It was a nice thing but it wasn't essential. I wasn't someone who cared about gardening. That was my mom's thing.

Then the drought hit. I don't know if it was officially a drought or if that's just what people called it when it didn't rain for six weeks and the water department sent emails about conservation. The garden started dying. The tomato plants got brown and brittle. The carrots looked like someone had turned them to leather. My mom kept watering them anyway, dragging the hose out every evening even though it felt wasteful. She'd stand there in the heat and pour water on plants that looked like they were already dead. It seemed pointless.

I told her that. I said we should just let them go. We can buy vegetables from the store. It's not worth the water. We can replant next year when it rains again. She didn't argue. She just nodded like she'd heard this before, which she probably had, from my dad or my sister or her own brain telling her to give up. But she kept going out there anyway.

One afternoon in July I came home from work and she was kneeling in the dirt next to a tomato plant that looked absolutely dead. Like brown stick dead. And she was checking the soil and adjusting the drip line and saying something to the plant that I couldn't hear. I almost walked past her. Actually I did walk past her. But then I came back outside and asked what she was doing.

She said she read that during droughts, if you keep watering deeply but less frequently, the plants send their roots deeper to find water. They get stronger. And maybe they don't produce as much fruit. Maybe they're not beautiful. But they survive. And the next year when it rains again, they're better adapted to handle the dry spells. They're more resilient.

We didn't get tomatoes that year. We got like five sad ones that tasted slightly better than store-bought. But we kept almost everything alive. And the next year, when it did rain again, the garden came back differently. The plants were smaller but tougher. They produced more than they ever had before, even in normal conditions.

I didn't think much about this at the time. It was just something that happened in my yard. But I'm different now from the person who told my mom to give up. Not because I suddenly care about tomatoes, though I kind of do now. But because I learned something about persistence from watching her stand in the heat and tend to plants that looked like failures. About how sometimes you have to keep investing in things that seem pointless in the moment because you're not measuring for today. You're measuring for next year.

meta.topic: keeping a garden alive through a drought
