text:
I didn't learn to read music until I was fifteen, which is stupidly late in the music world. Most people learn as kids. They're taught it alongside learning an instrument. They just absorb it the way you absorb any language that people around you speak. But my childhood was not a musical one, so at fifteen I was sitting in jazz band without being able to read a single note of sheet music.

I learned by ear. That's what I told people when they asked. I learned by ear. Which sounds cool and natural and like I have some kind of musical instinct. What it actually meant was that I waited to hear other people play and then I copied them. I watched the trumpet player's fingers. I listened to the rhythm. I played back what I heard. It worked fine for jazz. It worked less fine when we played new pieces I'd never heard and everyone was sight-reading off the sheet and I was the person holding up the section.

The teacher suggested - very kindly - that I might want to learn to read music. She offered to teach me. She said it would take maybe a month to get the basics down. A month. And I think that's when I decided I was insulted. A month? I'd spent seven years playing music without needing to read it. I was fine. I could play complex pieces by ear. I understood theory. Reading music seemed unnecessary. Reading music seemed like something you had to do if you weren't naturally musical. I was naturally musical.

For about six months I remained stubbornly illiterate on the subject. Then we got a new piece that I literally could not figure out by ear because it was too complex and I hadn't heard it before and nobody could play it slow enough for me to figure out the notes individually. I bombed the first rehearsal. Completely fell apart. And that's when something shifted.

I realized that not being able to read music wasn't brave or natural or independent. It was limiting. It was like refusing to learn written English because you could speak fine. It didn't make you special. It just made you unable to access things. Sheet music is a language and I had decided I didn't need to learn it, and that decision was starting to cost me.

So I learned to read music at fifteen in about six weeks. The teacher was right - it's not that hard. The basics are simple. The note on the bottom of the staff is E, then F, G, A, B, C, D, E again at the top. Lines and spaces. Treble clef and bass clef. Time signatures. It's like learning a code. Once you have the code, everything just translates.

What changed after I learned was less about the music and more about my understanding of myself. I realized how much of my identity had been built on things I was naturally good at. When something required actual learning and effort and time, my impulse was to reject it. To convince myself that learning it would diminish the natural talent I already had. But that's not how learning works. Learning doesn't erase instinct. It enhances it. And refusing to learn isn't brave or pure. It's just fearful.

I still have good instincts with music. But now I can also read. And being able to do both things makes me better than I ever was at just doing one.

meta.topic: learning to read music at fifteen
meta.prompt: Discuss an accomplishment, event, or realization that sparked a period of personal growth and a new understanding of yourself or others.

text:
I taught myself physical therapy exercises from YouTube videos while my father relearned how to walk, and what that taught me is that the internet will teach you how to do basically anything, but it won't teach you how to stop being afraid.

He had the stroke on a Tuesday morning. He was in his fifties. He was relatively healthy. He went to the gym. And then he had a stroke and the left side of his body stopped working the way it was supposed to work. It was the kind of thing that happens to other people's fathers, not ours. But it happened to ours.

The hospital was loud and fluorescent and everyone there seemed to know what they were doing except us. They ran tests and did scans and used words like "ischemic" and "prognosis" that didn't mean anything to me. What mattered was that he was alive and his brain was damaged and nobody could really tell us what that meant for his future. The doctors talked about recovery. The physical therapists talked about neuroplasticity. Everyone talked about the "window" where recovery was most possible, and that window was weeks, maybe months, and after that it got harder.

We came home with discharge papers and a list of exercises he needed to do. Daily. Repeatedly. The exercises were simple. Arm movements. Leg movements. Balance work. The theory was that by repeating them, his brain would rewire. New neural pathways would form. His body would relearn things it had forgotten.

My mom hired a physical therapist to come twice a week. But the rest of the time, between those visits, he needed to do the work. And my mom couldn't do it alone - she had to work to keep insurance. So I started helping. I'd come home from school and we'd go through the exercises. Twenty reps of this. Hold this for thirty seconds. Do that five times.

I watched YouTube videos about stroke recovery to understand what we were doing. I learned about motor cortex and muscle memory and why repetition mattered. I learned that every single repetition was theoretically helping his brain reorganize itself. I learned that motivation mattered because people gave up too easily. I learned all of this from various physical therapists and recovery specialists on YouTube, people I'd never met explaining their expertise to a camera.

What I didn't learn from YouTube is how to watch your father try to lift his arm and not quite get there. How to see him frustrated that his body wasn't doing what he wanted. How to hear him say things like "I used to be strong" with his voice breaking. YouTube doesn't teach you how to keep showing up every single day to do something that feels like it's not working. To do fifty reps of an exercise that looks tiny and meaningless but is supposedly rewiring his brain. To believe in something you can't see happening.

I was afraid the whole time. Not the dramatic kind of afraid where you can't function. Just the persistent kind where you're doing everything right but you're terrified it's not going to be enough. That his brain wasn't going to rewire. That the neuroplasticity wouldn't happen. That he was going to be stuck like this - limited, frustrated, no longer the person he was before.

By month four something shifted. He could lift his arm higher than he could before. He could walk further. The progress was real and measurable. But that's when I realized that my fear hadn't actually changed. Even with evidence that things were improving, I was still afraid. I was still bracing for something bad. I was still preparing for the worst case scenario.

What YouTube didn't teach me is that hope and fear can exist at the same time. That you can see someone getting better and still be terrified that it's not going to last. That recovery is ongoing and uncertain and you can do everything right and things can still go wrong. You can do fifty reps every day and still not know if it's enough.

He's mostly recovered now, years later. He still does exercises. He'll probably always do exercises. But I learned without any teacher that some things just require you to show up and do the work and live in the uncertainty anyway. YouTube can teach you the mechanics. It can't teach you the faith that it matters.

meta.topic: a father's stroke
meta.prompt: What is something you have taught yourself, and what did learning it without a teacher show you?

text:
The lighting booth is in the back left corner of the auditorium, up three metal stairs and through a door that's usually locked. Before sophomore year, I didn't know this place existed. Now I can't imagine school without it.

I started running lights for the drama club kind of by accident. The technical director needed someone and asked around, and I volunteered mostly because my friend Sarah was doing the sounds and I thought it would be fun to sit with her during rehearsals. It was fun at first - just pressing buttons at the right time, watching the stage come alive when you flipped the switches. But then I actually started paying attention to what I was doing.

Every Thursday night during spring semester, I climbed those stairs and sat in a tiny booth with a lighting console that had about thirty cues marked on a printout. The director would call out the scene changes and I'd have maybe three seconds to dim the house lights while bringing up the stage lights to exactly the right level. Too bright and it washed out the actors' faces. Too dim and nobody could see anything. There's this exact point that feels right, and I got obsessed with finding it every single time.

I started coming in early to test different levels. I'd sit in different parts of the audience to see how the light looked from various angles. I made notes on my script about what each cue was supposed to convey - the romantic scene needed to be warm and intimate, the scary moment needed harsh shadows, the climactic monologue needed everything to be just slightly dimmer so the actor's face was the only thing that mattered. It sounds silly now but at the time it felt incredibly important. Like I was actually responsible for whether this performance worked or failed.

The thing is, I was right. Not because I'm particularly talented at lighting, but because once I started really paying attention, I realized that lighting isn't just turning things brighter or darker. It's telling the story. It's saying where the audience should look, how they should feel, what moment matters most. When I got a cue wrong in dress rehearsal one night and accidentally left the stage way too bright during this vulnerable scene between the two main characters, I could see it destroy the moment. The audience laughed nervously instead of sitting with the discomfort that the scene was supposed to create.

I apologized to the director afterward. She said it was fine, it was just tech rehearsal. But I spent two hours that night redoing every single cue, checking them again and again until I was sure I had it right. And when we opened the show the next week, I was positioned in that booth with my hand hovering over the controls, completely focused, and for the first time I understood what it felt like to be truly needed in something.

I've run lights for three plays now. I'm still not perfect. Sometimes I miss cues or hit them slightly off. But something changed in me that first year. I discovered this place where I can sit in the shadows and literally shine light on what matters. Where I can be invisible and essential at the same time. The lighting booth is where I feel most myself - focused, purposeful, part of something bigger than just me sitting alone.

meta.topic: running the lighting board for the school play
meta.prompt: Describe a place where you feel most yourself, and why.

text:
I believed that if I cared enough, I could learn how to do anything. That confidence made me volunteer to sew costumes for Romeo and Juliet when the designer was overwhelmed. I'd watched my mom sew a hundred times. How hard could it be?

Very hard. The first dress was a disaster. I measured wrong, cut wrong, and sewn the bodice so tight nobody could breathe. The second was slightly better. By the fifth dress, I understood how seams worked and why you backstitch. But I was also fourteen days behind schedule and the designer looked panicked whenever I showed up.

I'd been treating sewing like something I could just brute force through. Just keep going until it works. But sewing is precise. You can't will yourself through a quarter-inch seam allowance. You can't just decide that your stitches are good enough if they're not actually good enough. The costumes have to move with the actors or they're going to ruin the performance. There's no compromise space.

I told the designer that I thought I was making it worse, not better. That she should probably give the last few dresses to someone who actually knew what they were doing. She looked disappointed but not surprised, which somehow made it worse. She'd known this wasn't working for a while but was too kind to say it directly.

I quit about ten days before opening night. Someone else came in and finished the dresses in time. They looked beautiful, actually - professional in a way that mine never would have been. I went to opening night and watched Romeo and Juliet move across the stage in costumes that I had failed to create, and I felt this weird combination of relief and shame.

What I got wrong was thinking that confidence and effort were enough. That if I just cared hard enough, I could skip the actual learning part. I'd never sewn before. I didn't have steady hands or good spatial reasoning or years of understanding how fabric moves. I had enthusiasm and stubbornness, which turned out to be exactly the wrong tools for this particular job.

I still believe you can learn how to do almost anything. But I'm more careful now about understanding the difference between something being possible and something being possible for me in the timeframe I have available. Sometimes the bravest thing isn't saying yes. It's knowing when to say you're not the right person for the job.

meta.topic: sewing costumes for a community theatre

text:
Everyone got their first phone in sixth grade except me. I got mine in seventh grade, which is not a long time but it felt eternal when you were the only kid in your friend group without one.

I think my parents thought they were protecting me from something. A bad influence, maybe. Predators. Addiction. There was probably a parenting blog somewhere that said kids shouldn't have phones until they were older and my mom found it and made this decision and stuck to it even when I begged. She said everyone else's parents were making a mistake and she wasn't going to do that to me.

By the time I got to seventh grade, the friendship groups had basically formed based on group chats. People made plans in Discord and on iMessage and I found out about things after the fact. I'd overhear people talking about jokes from their group chat and I had no context. My best friend would be texting with five other people and I'd be sitting there with nothing to do. They weren't trying to exclude me. It was just that without a phone, I wasn't really part of the infrastructure of how friendships worked anymore.

I felt like I was living in a different decade. Everyone around me was having these subtle conversations constantly and I was checked out of all of it. I thought I was fine with it at first. I told myself I was more independent, more present, less addicted to technology. I judged everyone else for needing their phones. I was very smug about the whole thing.

But honestly? I was miserable. I was lonely. I felt like I was watching my friends have a life that I wasn't invited to. It wasn't even that they were doing anything particularly exciting. They were sending stupid memes and making plans and saying dumb things that aren't worth remembering. But that's what friendship was at that age - it was the accumulation of stupid small moments. And I was missing all of them.

When I finally got a phone, nothing really changed with my friends. We were still the same people. But I could finally access the random moments that made up friendship. And I realized how much I'd been judging everyone for something that I didn't actually understand until I was part of it.

What I got wrong was thinking that being above technology was the same as being above the need for connection. My parents were trying to protect me, probably, but they were also accidentally isolating me. I learned that there's a difference between being intentional about technology use and just refusing to participate in the way everyone else is participating. The first one is about making choices. The second one is about opting out while pretending you're making a choice.

I'm grateful my parents eventually let me get a phone. And I use it way too much, probably. I get it. But I also think that year without one taught me a lesson that backfired. It taught me that I need connection more than I need independence. That sometimes fitting in isn't the same as selling out. That being different for the sake of being different is just another kind of trying too hard.

meta.topic: the year they were the only one of their friends without a phone
meta.prompt: Describe a place where you feel most yourself, and why.

text:
My grandmother taught me how to be patient with someone who is slowly leaving you, and she absolutely didn't mean to do it. She didn't mean to teach me anything because the dementia had already started taking the parts of her that knew how to teach or instruct anyone. But somehow I learned anyway, just by being around her and choosing how to respond to her confusion. And what I learned through this whole experience is that my grandfather and I have very different and conflicting opinions about what that learning actually means and how we should treat her.

When she first started forgetting, it was small. She'd ask the same question twice in one conversation. She'd lose track of where she'd put her glasses. My mom would gently reorient her, telling her the story again, finding the glasses again. It seemed patient and kind. My grandfather was less patient. He'd sigh and repeat himself. He'd get a little sharp with her, the way you do when you're tired of explaining something. I didn't think much about it.

By the time I was old enough to really notice it was getting worse, we were living in the age of internet articles about dementia. My mom read them and shared them with us. The one I remember most clearly was about using validation instead of correction. Instead of saying "No, Mom, that didn't happen," you were supposed to meet her in her reality. You were supposed to say "That must have felt scary" and just let her believe what she believed. It seemed kinder than insisting on facts she couldn't access.

I started practicing this approach with her. She'd tell me stories that weren't quite right, stories that didn't match what had actually happened, and instead of correcting her, I'd just listen quietly. I'd ask her questions about the version she remembered. I'd treat her reality as equally valid even when it wasn't factually accurate. And it worked. She seemed noticeably more comfortable. Less agitated and upset. I thought I was doing something genuinely generous and wise.

My grandfather hated it. He said I was enabling her. He said by not correcting her, I was letting her disappear further into confusion. He'd argue with my attempts at validation. He'd insist on facts. "No, Mother, that's not what happened. You're confusing it with another time." And then she'd get upset and confused and he'd get frustrated that she was upset.

We fought about it. I said he was being cruel. He said I was being naive and making things worse. I said he just didn't understand how dementia works. He said I was patronizing her. The fights weren't big but they were constant, this low-level disagreement about the most loving way to be with someone who's slowly vanishing.

I still think validation is the right approach. The research backs it up. Meeting people with dementia in their reality, rather than insisting they accept ours, actually reduces agitation and improves quality of life. I've read the studies. I understand the neurology. My approach was correct.

But what I'm less certain about now is whether being right about dementia care is the same as being right about love. My grandfather was insisting on facts because he was grieving. He was trying to hold onto the person she was by refusing to accept the person she was becoming. Every time he corrected her, he was saying "No, you're still you. You still know things. You still matter." Which is a kind of love too, even if it was the wrong strategy.

What I taught myself, by learning on my own instead of taking classes, was that there are different ways to love someone and they can be in direct conflict with each other. My way was gentler. His way was more true. Neither of us was really wrong, we were just loving her in different languages and neither of us knew how to help the other person understand our translation.

He died before she did. After his death, I wondered if he'd been right all along. If his insistence on facts was actually the braver thing - the refusal to let her go all the way under. But I still did it the way I did it. And I still think she was more comfortable with me than she was with him.

We never resolved it. We just both kept loving her in our separate ways until there wasn't anyone left to love.

meta.topic: a grandmother's dementia
meta.prompt: What is something you have taught yourself, and what did learning it without a teacher show you?

text:
My uncle's radio came to me the same way a lot of broken things do - he mentioned it once and my dad said "oh, my kid might be able to fix that." Uncle Mike had found it at an estate sale for three dollars. It was from 1987. It didn't work. But it was the kind of thing you could see working again if you squinted and imagined it right.

I brought it to my workspace - which is basically a shelf in the garage with some tools and a lot of YouTube access - and I told myself I'd spend maybe an hour trying to figure it out. See if it was worth trying to actually restore. It turned into two years.

That first hour was spent just opening it up and understanding the architecture. There's this moment with old electronics where you open them and the smell just hits you - dust and age and metal oxidation. The guts were pretty simple. A speaker. A power supply. A radio tuner. Capacitors and resistors and a transformer. Nothing was broken exactly. Everything was just old and tired. The capacitors had dried out. The contacts were corroded. Nothing was talking to anything else properly.

I started small. Cleaned the contacts. Replaced the most obviously dead capacitors. Flipped the switch and nothing happened. Which was fine. It was going to take more than that.

For about six months I worked on it in fragments. A weekend afternoon here, an evening there. I'd learn something about circuit boards or transformers and then apply it. I replaced the power supply. Found replacements for the old ceramic capacitors that are just not manufactured anymore. Rewired the speaker. Cleaned every single contact with isopropyl alcohol until the radio looked almost new inside, which was funny because the outside still looked like it had been buried in 1987.

Then there was this period where I just stopped. I looked at the radio and I thought, why am I doing this? It's not my radio. Uncle Mike is never going to care about this radio. It's not useful. It's not impressive. It's just old. And I'm spending time on it that I could spend on literally anything else.

I was right about most of that. But I was also just tired. It was grinding work. It required precision and patience and there was no guarantee that even if I fixed everything, the radio would actually work. That last part, actually, that's the thing that got to me. I could do all this work and it could still just be broken in some final way that I didn't know how to fix.

I talked to my dad about quitting. He said I could. He said Uncle Mike wouldn't care. He said I could just put the radio in a box and return it. The permission to quit actually made me want to keep going. Or maybe the permission to quit meant I actually wanted to do it, and I just needed to feel like I had a choice.

I can't remember what finally made it work. Probably the capacitors. It was probably some stupid combination of old components that just decided to cooperate one afternoon. I powered it on and it crackled and there was actual sound coming through the speaker. AM radio. A distant station. Something. It worked.

I called Uncle Mike and told him it was ready. He came by and listened to it like he couldn't believe it. He said it was exactly like he remembered. And I realized that the point was never about the radio at all. The point was about the person who cared about something enough to restore it.

meta.topic: restoring an uncle's old radio

text:
Every morning for six months I would wake up and check the sales. It was literally the first thing I did before I even got out of bed or brushed my teeth or had any coffee. Pull up my phone, open the Shopify app, scroll to the orders section, see how many orders came in overnight. Usually it was zero. Sometimes it was one. Once it was three, which I genuinely thought was my breakthrough moment. Like maybe this was the day things turned around. It wasn't.

The phone case business was supposed to change everything. I'd watched some YouTube videos about print-on-demand, found a supplier, designed a few basic cases with clichéd motivational slogans that I thought were clever. "Be yourself, everyone else is taken." "Do what makes you happy." Standard stuff that you see on a thousand Instagram posts. I'd uploaded them and set the price at a markup that seemed reasonable but probably wasn't. Then I'd waited for people to buy them, which they mostly didn't.

This small repeated habit - checking the sales first thing - it became almost meditative. I'd lie in bed and just stare at the number. Zero. I'd think about what that meant. I'd think about changing the listings, adding new designs, marketing differently. I'd make a mental note to fix things. And then I'd get out of bed and go to school and completely forget about it until the next morning.

Six months of that. Six months of a slow accumulation of not-happening. I sold maybe twenty cases total, which after the supplier cost me money instead of making money. My parents didn't say I told you so, but I could see them thinking it. My friends asked how the business was going and I'd say fine, great, building it up, knowing they could tell I was lying.

What's strange is that those six months taught me more about myself than any successful business could ever have taught me. Not in a motivational way where I'm saying "failure is learning" or some clichéd thing like that. That's the kind of inspirational sentiment that makes me want to throw up. It's true, probably, but it's also the most obvious way to put it and the most false-sounding when you're actually living it.

What I mean is that the repetition of checking the sales and seeing nothing, day after day, slowly wore away my resistance to the idea that maybe I wasn't an entrepreneur. Maybe I wasn't going to be the person who built something. Maybe I was just a person. Just me. And that person liked doing homework and making art and talking to friends, not constantly trying to figure out how to sell phone cases to strangers.

At six months I just stopped. I closed the shop. I stopped checking the sales. And for like two weeks I felt sad about it, like I'd given up on myself. But then I realized what I was actually grieving was the idea of myself as someone who was doing this thing. Not the actual thing. Just the idea.

It sounds depressing but it was actually liberating. I spent so much energy maintaining the story that I was an entrepreneur when I could have been using that energy to do things I actually cared about. I could have been making art that I made for myself instead of art I was trying to sell. I could have been learning things because I wanted to learn them, not because they looked good on a business plan.

The small repeated habit of checking the sales every morning was the real thing I was building, and what I was building was resilience to not having what I thought I wanted. Or maybe I was building self-knowledge. Every morning I was confirming: this is not for you. This is not who you are. And that confirmation, repeated enough times, finally stuck.

Now I do things that matter to me without needing them to look like a business or a side hustle or an achievement. I make art when I want to. I write things just for myself. I think about things deeply without rushing to monetize the thinking. I'm not an entrepreneur and I've made peace with that. That six months of morning phone checks taught me something fundamental - it's infinitely better to do nothing than to keep performing at something that doesn't align with who you actually are. The performance is the real waste of time.

meta.topic: a failed attempt to start a business selling phone cases

text:
I started the recycling program in ninth grade because I was angry. Not angry at any one person or thing in particular, but just generally angry at the world for being wasteful and stupid and headed toward environmental collapse. I was that kid who'd watched one too many documentaries about the Great Pacific garbage patch and the rate of species extinction. And I had this rock-solid conviction that I, personally, was going to fix this through the power of my own passion and some blue recycling bins that I could convince the administration to buy.

The school's existing recycling setup was nonexistent. We threw everything in the trash. Plastic, paper, aluminum - all of it went to the landfill. It seemed like the most easily solvable problem in the world. So I did what every activist teenager does. I made a PowerPoint. I researched local waste management companies. I calculated the amount of garbage our school produced annually and translated it into environmental impact. I was going to present this to the administration and they were going to be so impressed that they'd immediately implement my recycling program.

The presentation was actually good. I knew that at the time and I know it now. I had the numbers. I had the plan. I had sources and citations and a timeline. The assistant principal listened to me politely and said they'd consider it. Three weeks later, I got approval to start a pilot program in the cafeteria. Three blue bins. That's what they gave me.

I was euphoric. This was happening. This was real.

For about a month, I was completely into it. I cleaned out the bins multiple times a day. I made laminated signs about what goes where - detailed signs with pictures and everything. I talked to the cafeteria manager about sorting and contamination. I set up an actual system where the recycling got picked up weekly and actually transported to a facility instead of just sitting in a closet accumulating smell. It was working. The bins were getting genuinely full with recyclables. People were using them. Students I didn't even know were walking past and putting things in the right bins. It felt like proof of concept.

Then I got busy. Sophomore year hit with classes and clubs and actual schoolwork and I had less time to babysit the bins. And that's when the system broke down. People started putting trash in the recycling. The bins were overflowing. Without someone actively managing it, nobody cared enough to recycle correctly. And if it's contaminated, the facility won't actually recycle it anyway. It all goes to the landfill. My whole system failed because I wasn't there to enforce it.

I didn't notice at first. I was in physics and struggling to understand waves and I just kind of forgot about the recycling bins. When I finally went back to check on them, months had passed. They were disgusting. Clearly nobody had sorted properly since I stopped paying attention. And the administration decided that since the pilot program had failed, they weren't going to expand it. They weren't even going to keep the pilot going. The bins disappeared.

I should have just owned it completely. I should have gone to the administration and said "I started this and I failed to maintain it and I need help making it work" and asked for actual support or resources. But instead I got angry. I got angry at students for not taking it seriously enough. I got angry at the administration for not caring enough. I got angry at the entire system itself for being designed in a way that required an individual's constant effort and attention to function properly.

The anger was misplaced. The truth is that I hadn't actually solved a problem. I'd created a system that couldn't function without me, and then I abandoned it. That's not activism. That's just performance. I wanted to be the person who saved the environment. What I actually was the person who made a mess and then left.

I'm not against environmental action or sustainability. But I learned something real about how change actually works. Systems need buy-in from multiple people and infrastructure and actual institutional support and funding. One passionate teenager with a PowerPoint and good intentions cannot fix anything sustainable on their own. That's a genuinely hard lesson but it's absolutely true. I wish I'd learned it sooner, and I definitely wish I'd learned it with less collateral damage to the program and the school's willingness to try other initiatives.

meta.topic: starting a recycling programme that the school cancelled

text:
The final project was supposed to be a collaboration. That's what the assignment sheet said. You will work in groups of three to four to create a multimedia presentation about an assigned historical event. The goal is to combine research, design, and presentation skills while learning how to work effectively with your peers.

I was paired with my best friend Maya and two other kids I didn't know as well, and I genuinely thought this would be great. Maya and I had been doing everything together since freshman year. We'd stayed up late countless times talking about college plans and relationships and why our calculus teacher seemed to hate us specifically. Surely we could handle one group project.

I still have the rubric they gave us, printed and marked up with annotations and deadlines. We were assigned the American Civil War, and we split up the work pretty evenly at first. I did the research on causes. Maya did the research on major battles. The other two kids, Jason and Sarah, were supposed to put together the design and presentation.

The presentation was due on a Thursday. By the Tuesday before, I'd sent Jason and Sarah everything I'd found. They sent back drafts of the slides. They were fine. Not perfect, but fine. Then Wednesday rolled around, and Maya called me in what I can only describe as a panic. She said the presentation was terrible, that Sarah had redesigned everything using the wrong color scheme, that it wasn't academically rigorous enough, that we were going to fail. She said we needed to stay up all night and fix it ourselves.

I said I thought it was fine. That it was a group project and we all had to accept some level of compromise. That Jason and Sarah had done their part and we couldn't just rewrite everything the night before without acknowledging that.

Maya said I was being lazy and a bad friend. We fought for twenty minutes on the phone. She said if I wasn't willing to perfect the presentation, then I clearly didn't care about our grade or about our friendship. That ultimatum was the thing that broke something. I realized I was supposed to prioritize her vision of the project over everyone else's work. I was supposed to agree that her standards were the right ones.

I didn't stay up all night. I didn't rewrite the presentation. And we did fine on it anyway. Got a B+, which is solid.

But Maya didn't talk to me for a month after that. When she finally did, it was about the presentation and how it should have been perfect. She couldn't understand why I'd chosen the group over her. I couldn't understand why the group wasn't as important as her.

We're cordial now. We see each other sometimes. But we're not best friends anymore, and we both know it. What I learned from that whole thing is that sometimes the people closest to you are the ones who can't actually let you grow beyond what they've decided you should be. I grew, and Maya couldn't accept that I was becoming someone who made decisions she didn't approve of.

meta.topic: a friendship that ended over a group project
meta.prompt: Discuss an accomplishment, event, or realization that sparked a period of personal growth and a new understanding of yourself or others.

text:
The business lasted three weeks. I thought that was something I'd be ashamed of, but mostly I just think about that three weeks as the place where I finally understood myself.

It started the way a lot of stupid ideas start - with me thinking I had discovered something nobody else had thought of. Phone case designs. But not boring designs. Cool designs. Designs that meant something. I'd learn design software, I'd commission artwork from artists, I'd sell them online, and I'd make thousands of dollars. It was obvious. Why wasn't everyone doing this?

I made the business plan on a Saturday. It was meticulous. I calculated margins, researched suppliers, created a whole marketing strategy. By Sunday night I'd registered as a business, created an Instagram account, and ordered a bulk supply of phone cases from a wholesaler. I was so confident. I've never been more confident about anything.

The first two weeks I was doing everything. I was learning Adobe Illustrator at midnight. I was designing cases that I thought were clever. I was setting up the online store. I was trying to convince artists to work with me. I was telling everyone I knew about the business. I was this person who was doing something. Finally, after years of talking about business ideas and never doing anything, I was actually doing something.

Then I sold two phone cases. To friends. Out of pity, I think, looking back. And I realized that the designing part was taking hours and the selling part was not working at all. And the business plan I'd been so proud of had an assumption that just wasn't true - that people actually wanted unique artistic phone cases badly enough to pay a premium for them.

I could have pivoted. That's the entrepreneurship advice - pivot, adapt, find the right market. But instead I just stopped. I felt this sudden exhaustion that wasn't physical. It was existential. I realized I didn't actually care about phone cases. I didn't care about business. What I'd cared about was the idea of myself as a person who was building something. The actual building was just unpleasant.

I told myself that it was fine, businesses fail all the time, that wasn't a reflection on me. But the truth is I was embarrassed. Not because it failed but because I'd put so much energy into the idea of it while simultaneously not caring at all about the actual work. I wanted the success without the grind. I wanted to be seen as someone who was doing something without actually having to do the something.

I left the website up for a few months, thinking maybe something would happen. Nothing did. Eventually I took it down. I wrote off the bulk order of phone cases as an expensive lesson.

What changed my mind wasn't a single moment but a slow realization. The place where I feel most myself is when I'm not performing a version of myself. When I'm not trying to look like a person who's building something. It's when I'm actually interested in something, when the doing and the identity are the same thing, not performing as a person.

Now when I have an idea for a business or a project, I ask myself whether I care about the actual work or just about being seen doing it. Usually it's the latter, and I just don't do it. Sometimes it's genuinely the former, and then I'm willing to put in the time. The business taught me that filtering mechanism. It taught me to be more honest with myself about my own motivations.

meta.topic: a failed attempt to start a business selling phone cases
meta.prompt: Describe a place where you feel most yourself, and why.

text:
I learned to fix bicycles because my own had broken and my family couldn't afford the repair shop. I watched YouTube videos and taught myself how to align the chain, patch tubes, true wheels. Once I fixed it, I felt capable in a way I hadn't before. So when kids in the neighborhood started asking if I could help with theirs, I said yes. I was fourteen and I thought I was doing something good.

What I got wrong is that I thought understanding the mechanics was enough. One Saturday I spent three hours working on a bike belonging to a nine-year-old named Arun. The brakes had been grinding, and I replaced the pads and adjusted the cables. I was proud of the work. Arun rode it away, and for two days nothing happened. Then his mother came to our house. She was calm about it, which somehow made it worse than if she'd been angry. She said the bike had started pulling to one side, and when Arun swerved to compensate, he'd hit a car parked on the street. He wasn't badly hurt, but he could have been.

I realized that I'd aligned the wheels wrong. When I rushed through that final step, checking them against a wall instead of doing it properly with a true, I'd created an asymmetry that only showed up under real riding conditions. I had assumed that because I understood the theory, the execution didn't matter as much. I had been overconfident in the way that young people often are about things they've only just learned.

It shook me. For a while I didn't want to touch another bike. But Arun's mother asked me to try again, to fix it properly this time, and I did. I also changed how I approached the work. I stopped rushing. I started keeping a notebook where I wrote down what I'd done to each bike, so if something went wrong I could trace my steps. I asked kids to bring their bikes back a week later to check if anything had shifted. I looked up the actual specifications for different wheel sizes instead of guessing.

What changed isn't that I became perfect at it. There's still a lot I don't know about bicycles. But I learned that the thing I was offering mattered more than I'd understood. These were kids who needed their bikes to get to school or to friends' houses. They were trusting me with something that affected their safety. That knowledge made me slower, more careful, less certain. It made me better.

This still bothers me sometimes, how easily I could have seriously hurt someone. But it also taught me something important about the difference between knowing something and doing something. Watching a video and understanding the principle is one level. Actually building skill takes repetition and attention and humility. It takes accepting that you're going to make mistakes, and that other people's welfare depends on you catching them before they do.

I still fix bikes for neighborhood kids. I've fixed maybe forty of them now, and I've gotten much better. I still mess up sometimes - a cable routing that seemed right but wasn't, a bolt not tightened quite firmly enough. But I catch those things now because I'm looking for them. I'm slower. I'm more aware. I think that's what real accomplishment actually looks like, not the confident moment at fourteen, but the sustained attention that comes after you've learned what confidence can cost.

meta.topic: fixing bicycles for neighbourhood children
meta.prompt: Discuss an accomplishment, event, or realization that sparked a period of personal growth and a new understanding of yourself or others.

text:
My grandmother stood at the stove and added salt without measuring. Not a pinch - she used her three fingers to gauge it, a gesture as precise to her as any teaspoon could have been. I watched her make dal, the same way I'd watched her make it for my entire childhood, but this time I was fifteen and I had started to believe that real cooking required precision. I had been watching cooking shows where ingredients were weighed, timed, stated in exact fractions. To me, her method looked like guessing.

I asked her to measure the salt. I said she could write it down so I could learn properly. She looked at me without seeming to understand. She didn't speak much English and I didn't speak her language fluently - another barrier I barely noticed then, just a fact of our relationship. She pointed to the stove. The dal needed attention. The salt was in the dal. This was how you learned to cook, apparently. Not by noting things down but by paying attention.

What I did wrong is I decided she didn't know what she was doing. I didn't think this consciously, but I believed it underneath - that her lack of instruments and measurements meant her method was informal, imprecise, less good than the methods I was reading about. So I started cooking at home when she wasn't there, following recipes from websites. I measured everything. I cooked three versions of dal with different salt quantities to find the "correct" one. I was pleased with myself. I was being scientific about it.

Then one day I made it for my grandmother and she tasted it and said nothing, which was worse than criticism. She went to make a pot of dal herself, using her fingers, that gesture I had started to see as careless rather than skilled. I watched her this time, actually watched instead of judgment watching. I saw that she tasted the cooking water before the dal went in. I saw that she kept the lid off for specific periods because she knew by sight when the moisture had changed. I saw that she added the salt in stages, tasting as she went, adjusting based on what the dish needed in that moment, not what a recipe from the internet had decided it should need.

Her dal was better than mine. It wasn't just salt. It was the entire thing - the depth, the texture, the way the flavors came together. My versions tasted correct, which meant they tasted like nothing. Hers tasted like home and knowledge and something that had been refined over decades.

I think a lot about what I got wrong, which is assuming that my way was more rational just because it was measurable. I didn't see that her precision was real, just not expressed in numbers. She had learned from her mother and her grandmother, refining the method through repetition until it became instinctive. When I measured the salt, I was rejecting not just her technique but her knowledge. I was saying that what she knew didn't count because she couldn't explain it in the language I was learning to speak.

I still cook with recipes sometimes, and I still measure things. But I cook much more with her now, and I've started to understand what she's doing. I watch her hands instead of looking away. I taste as I go instead of following steps. The precision is still there - it's just expressed through attention rather than instruments. She never directly told me this was wrong, what I did. But she let me watch until I figured it out myself.

meta.topic: learning to cook from a grandmother who spoke little English

text:
I've moved six times before I turned seventeen. My parents' job situation meant schools in three different countries and four different cities. Most people ask if it was hard, and the answer is that it was normal because I never knew anything else. What's harder to explain is what I started doing during these moves, something so small it barely counts, but something that has turned out to be the truest thing about who I am.

I keep the first drawing made at each school. Not the best drawing, not the one I'm proud of - the very first one, usually something quickly done in art class or a notebook, crude and unrefined. From my first school in London I have a pencil sketch of a playground. From the school in Singapore I have a watercolor landscape painted in the first week. From the school in Mumbai I have a charcoal study of my classroom. From each transition, one drawing.

I didn't plan this as some kind of project. It started with the drawing from London, which I kept because I didn't know I was leaving until suddenly I was packing. I found it at the bottom of a folder and something made me save it instead of throwing it away. When I moved to Singapore, I realized I was looking for the equivalent - that first artifact of being somewhere new. I started collecting without naming it as a collection.

What these drawings taught me is how much the first moment of arrival matters. Each one captures not the place but my relationship to the place at the instant I arrived in it. The London drawing is careful and precise because I was nervous. The Singapore one is loose and experimental because I was trying too hard to seem fine. The Mumbai one is dense with detail because I was paying attention in a way that I didn't in other places. Over time, I started to notice this before I finished the drawing - that I was drawing from a particular place of arrival, not from skill.

This habit became something bigger when I realized what it was actually doing for me. Moving is something that happens to you, something you don't choose. But collecting these drawings was something I chose. It meant I was taking ownership of the transition. Instead of just enduring the move, I was marking it. I was saying: this is where I arrived, this is what I saw, this is how I felt about being somewhere new.

By the time I moved to my fifth school, I was doing it deliberately. I would arrive and spend the first week looking for that first drawing. It became my anchor. On days when everything felt overwhelming or unfamiliar, I would go back to that drawing and remember that I had been new before. I had moved before. The panic of not knowing anyone, the weight of being the new person, these were things I had survived. The drawing was proof.

Now I have a collection of six. I keep them in a folder in my backpack. They're not good drawings, most of them. They're not impressive or technically skilled. But they're incredibly important to me because they represent something I've learned from being displaced repeatedly. I've learned how to arrive. I've learned that the new place, the strange school, the unfamiliar city - these aren't things that have happened to me. They're things that I have practiced handling, that I've gotten good at, that I carry evidence of surviving.

This matters to me for university because moving between schools has taught me something that doesn't show up on a transcript. I know how to adapt. I know how to find my place when there isn't an obvious place for me. I know how to look around a new environment and find something to anchor myself to, someone to befriend, a class or activity that makes sense. Most of all, I know that the arriving is a skill, and it's one I'm good at.

meta.topic: moving between six schools in nine years

text:
My uncle taught me to drive in a farm truck on the dirt roads that ran between his property and his neighbor's. I was fourteen, which is young, but nothing about farming is done at the right age. My uncle said I needed to learn because one day there would be an emergency and nobody would be around to drive. He was right about this in the abstract, but what he was really doing was teaching me something else, something he couldn't quite name.

At first I thought learning to drive was boring. The truck lurched and stalled. I couldn't coordinate the clutch and the accelerator. My uncle sat in the passenger seat and didn't correct me much - he would reach over and adjust my hands on the wheel, shift my foot position, but mostly he let me fail. We drove up and down the same stretch of road for weeks, nothing changing except my frustration and my confidence, which rose and fell in alternating measures.

Then one day I realized I hated this. I hated being outside in the heat, hated the grinding of the gears when I messed up, hated that it felt pointless. I had decided that driving was a tedious skill and that learning it this way, out here, in an old truck with my uncle watching, was a waste of time. I could drive anywhere, I thought. It didn't matter. If I needed to drive, someone could teach me somewhere air-conditioned and sensible.

My uncle didn't argue when I said I wanted to stop. He just drove us back to the house. The next week he asked if I wanted to go out again and I said no. He didn't push. He asked again a few weeks later and I said no again. For months I refused, and he didn't make a big deal of it.

Then the day came when the truck wouldn't start, and my uncle was in a lot of pain from an injury to his shoulder. He needed to get to the far field to check on the irrigation system. Nobody else was there. It was the middle of the day and he was suffering and the work needed doing. He looked at me and didn't say anything because we both knew what this was. This was the emergency I had laughed off. This was why I had learned.

I drove him to the far field. My hands knew exactly where to go - they had learned in all those seemingly pointless weeks. The truck responded to me now. I knew the roads well enough that I didn't have to think about them. What had felt tedious became automatic, which freed up my mind to think about what I was actually doing. I was helping. I was useful. My uncle was in pain and I was capable of removing one thing from his list of worries.

Driving back, I realized that I had been wrong about what I was learning. It was never really about the mechanics or the skill, though those had mattered. It was about understanding why things are worth learning even when they're boring. It was about the difference between boredom and purpose. The same act - turning a steering wheel, working the pedals, navigating a road - had felt pointless when I was learning it casually. It felt essential when someone depended on it.

That year I started driving regularly. I helped my uncle on the farm. I realized the driving itself wasn't the interesting part either - it was how it connected me to the work and to his life. I was no longer just his nephew visiting. I was someone he could rely on. I was part of the operation.

When I think about learning now, I think about this. I think about how all those boring weeks were necessary. You can't rush into purpose. You have to be bored first, have to do the repetition when you don't see the point, so that when the moment comes where you do see it, your body already knows what to do. Your mind is free to focus on mattering.

meta.topic: learning to drive on a farm

text:
I swam for fourteen years. My entire identity was tied to it. I woke up at five in the morning to go to practice. I spent my afternoons at the pool. I competed at tournaments every other weekend. Swimming was what I did, not just something I did. It was who I was.

The injury happened during my junior year of high school. I touched the wall wrong during practice and something in my shoulder gave out. Not dramatically - I didn't cry out or collapse. I just knew something was fundamentally wrong. The doctors eventually said it was a labrum tear. Surgery was required. I would need months of physical therapy. I could never return to competitive swimming at the level I had been at.

I quit the team. I stopped going to the pool for months. I thought that chapter of my life was finished. I grieved it in the way you grieve the loss of identity. I had been a swimmer. Now I wasn't. I didn't know who I was without that.

After a while, I went back to the pool. Not to train, but just to swim. I would go on weekends and swim slowly, moving through the water in a way that didn't hurt. I would never be fast again. I would never race. But I could still be in the water. Still move through it. This became a regular habit. Every Saturday or Sunday I would go to the pool and swim.

What I realized is that the habit of being at the pool, the repetition of it, the weekly return to the water - this became more meaningful than the competitive version ever was. When I was competitive, swimming was about performance. It was about time trials and rankings and whether I was getting better than I was yesterday. When I couldn't compete, swimming became something else. It became meditation. It became the one place where my body didn't hurt and my mind went quiet.

I've been swimming this way for three years now. I'm not training for anything. I'm not trying to improve. I just go to the water and I swim because it's where I feel most myself. The injury took away my identity as a competitive swimmer, but it gave me something else. It gave me a relationship with swimming that isn't about achievement. It's about presence.

What this taught me is that the most meaningful parts of who we are aren't always the ones we're proud of. The performance, the competition, the external validation - those things felt important while I was doing them. But what actually shaped me was the quiet habit of returning to something even after the reason I had been doing it disappeared.

I think I'm better for having been forced to let go of competitive swimming. I was obsessed with it in ways that weren't healthy. I measured my worth against my times. I couldn't imagine a version of myself that wasn't a competitive athlete. The injury forced me to find out who I was without that, and what I found was someone who loves swimming in a different, quieter way.

I still have the muscle memory of competition. Sometimes I time myself without meaning to. Sometimes I feel competitive about my pace. But mostly I just swim. I'm in the water and it's where I belong, and that's enough. The injury that was supposed to take something away from me ended up giving me something better. It taught me that sometimes the smallest repeated actions matter more than the big achievements. And that's maybe the most important thing I've learned about myself.

meta.topic: an injury that ended a competitive swimming career
meta.prompt: Some students have a background, identity, interest, or talent that is so meaningful they believe their application would be incomplete without it. If this sounds like you, then please share your story.

text:
I was holding the camera up to the bright afternoon light and I still couldn't tell if I had the exposure right. There was no light meter. The dial on top of the camera told me the shutter speed and the aperture but nothing about whether enough light was reaching the film. I had to guess. I had been guessing for weeks.

My father gave me the camera after I showed interest in photography. It was an old Pentax from the eighties, film, no automatic settings. He said it would teach me to actually think about light instead of just letting the camera figure it out for me. I thought he was being difficult. He was being brilliant, but I didn't realize it yet.

The first roll of film I shot was mostly failure. Pictures too dark or too bright or somewhere in between and I had no way of knowing until I developed them. I took notes on every exposure. The time of day, the lighting conditions, the settings I had chosen. Then I would get the prints back and I would see which of my guesses had been right. It was the slowest possible feedback loop.

What I did was look at the sun and try to estimate how much light was bouncing off my subject. I learned about the Sunny Sixteen rule - f/16 on a sunny day with ISO 100 film. I started to understand that exposure is about the relationship between light and sensitivity and the time the film is exposed. It's mathematics and it's also art. It's physics and it's also intuition.

By the second roll, I was getting better. By the fourth roll, I was predicting correctly most of the time. And then something shifted. Instead of thinking about exposure as a problem to solve, I started seeing light as the thing itself. I started noticing how light changed throughout the day. How it bent around objects. How it created shape and shadow and dimension. The camera became a tool for capturing what I was actually seeing.

The Pentax is sitting on my desk right now. It's scratched and worn. I've used it for maybe five years now and I've gone through dozens of rolls of film. I have a digital camera too. Most of the time I use that. It's faster and it lets me see the results immediately. But I still pick up the Pentax sometimes. Not for results - the digital camera gets better pictures. But for the discipline of it. For the reminder of having to think before I shoot.

Photography changed for me because of that camera without a light meter. I learned to see light instead of just recording it. I learned that limitations can be a gift. I learned that the slowest feedback loop sometimes teaches you the most.

Now when I use my digital camera, I think about what I learned on film. I'm more intentional. I pay attention to the actual light instead of trusting the camera to handle it. The absence of a light meter taught me to develop my own sense of light. In a way, it gave me something that automatic cameras never could.

meta.topic: learning photography with a camera that had no light meter

text:
I failed at something I thought I was good at - understanding Priya. We have been best friends since we were six years old, and I know her better than I know anyone. So when she started expressing political views that I completely disagreed with, I thought I could convince her. I thought I could explain to her why she was wrong, and she would see it, and everything would be fine.

It didn't work that way. What started as a conversation became an argument. Then it became a recurring argument. We would be eating lunch or walking home from school and one of us would bring something up and the conversation would ignite. I would present facts, articles, statistics. I was very sure of myself. She seemed to be choosing not to listen, or worse, not to care about the facts. What frustrated me most was that she is a logical person. We both care about the world and justice. How could we see things so differently?

I kept trying. That's what I did next, which was probably the wrong choice. I sent her links to articles. I brought up the topic strategically during conversations, thinking if I just presented the information right, she would change her mind. I was still operating on the assumption that this was a knowledge problem, that she just needed better information. I couldn't see that I was doing the opposite of listening - I was trying to make her understand me instead of trying to actually understand her.

The argument escalated. Not in the sense that we started fighting or saying cruel things, but in the sense that we were both digging in. She started sending me articles too, from her perspective. I would read them and think they were missing the point. She would do the same with my articles. We were both convinced the other person was willfully ignorant. We were both equally confident. And I was failing to reach her, which meant failing at something I had always believed was my strength - connection with people I loved.

We didn't have a dramatic ending to it. We just stopped talking about politics. It sounds like a small compromise, but it represented a significant shift for me. I had to accept that I couldn't convince her. That's when I actually started listening. Without the pressure to convert her or the goal of winning the argument, I could actually ask her why she believed what she believed. Not why she was wrong, but why this particular political worldview made sense to her.

What I learned is that her beliefs come from different values than mine, not from different facts. We both care about people suffering. We just disagree about the root causes and the solutions. She comes from a place of trusting institutions and gradual change. I come from a place of skepticism about institutions and belief in structural transformation. Neither of us is ignorant. We just built different frameworks.

This doesn't mean we agree on politics now. We still see things differently. But I'm no longer trying to fix her beliefs. When something political comes up, I ask questions. I listen to her reasoning. Sometimes I challenge her gently, not to convince her but to understand her better. And she does the same with me.

I think I was not successful because I defined success wrong. I thought success meant convincing my best friend to agree with me. I measured my failure in her continued disagreement. But that wasn't actually the point of our friendship, even though I had been operating like it was. Real success was figuring out how to love someone even when you see the world completely differently. Real success was learning that deep connection doesn't require agreement on everything.

The argument is still unresolved in the sense that we never reached consensus. But I resolved something else - I resolved my need to win. And that might have been the more important thing to learn.

meta.topic: an argument with a best friend about politics
meta.prompt: Describe a time you were not successful. What did you do next?

text:
I have a desk that I don't use anymore. It's pale wood, ordinary, the kind of thing you buy from a store because it's functional and not expensive. My mother set it up in the corner of my bedroom before I started the homeschool program, and I spent eleven months at that desk. Almost a full year of high school happened there.

I was sick in a way that nobody could quite diagnose for the first few months. Fever that came and went. Joint pain. Exhaustion that was disproportionate to anything I was doing. Doctors ran tests. Tests came back normal or abnormal in ways that didn't quite add up to anything. Eventually it was diagnosed as some kind of viral aftermath, the sort of thing where the virus was gone but your body was still processing what it had done to you.

Homeschooling was supposed to be temporary. That's what everyone said. You'll feel better soon and then you'll catch up with the regular school. You'll be fine. But I didn't feel better soon. The months went by. I watched videos of classes instead of sitting in classrooms. I took tests alone at the desk. I did worksheets. I read books that my teachers had recommended or assigned or just thought I should read. The desk became the container for my education. It was where high school was happening.

What nobody tells you about chronic illness in high school is how isolating it is. Not just physically, but in the way time moves. While I was at the desk, my friends were forming the kind of memories that matter in retrospect. They were eating lunch together in new configurations. They were dealing with whatever drama was happening that year. They were bonded by the experience of actually being there. I was having a completely different experience.

The desk represented that year in a way that's hard to explain without sounding dramatic. Some days I would wake up and feel almost fine and I would be furious at having to be at the desk instead of at school. Some days I would wake up and feel terrible and the desk was the only place I could be. It was neutral territory between the person I had been before I got sick and the person I was becoming after it.

What I learned at the desk was different from what I would have learned at school. I learned how to be alone with ideas. I learned that education doesn't require an audience. I learned that I could structure my own learning, and sometimes my structure was better than someone else's would have been. I learned how to persist through monotony and doubt.

I got better eventually. Slowly at first, then more noticeably. I went back to regular school for my junior year. I was a year ahead in some classes because of the way the homeschool program had worked out, and behind in others. I was more confident in my own understanding of concepts, less confident in my ability to handle the social dimensions of school.

Now I don't sit at the desk anymore. I use it sometimes to do college applications or write essays, but it's not the center of my life anymore. It's just an object in my room. But I think about that year a lot. I think about who I was when I was sick. I think about how circumstances shaped me in ways I didn't choose. The desk is ordinary. What happened there was not.

meta.topic: a long illness that meant a year of school at home

text:
I taught myself to read music the way most people learn things alone - slowly, with a lot of frustration, and only because I was too embarrassed to ask for help. I was fifteen and I had decided I wanted to play guitar in a real way, not just the three songs I already knew. Real musicians read music. So I had to figure out what those lines meant.

What I did was sit on my bed every day after school with a music theory workbook I bought for almost nothing at a used bookstore. The book was from the nineteen-eighties and smelled like mold and someone's old apartment. I didn't take it to school or work through it during scheduled study time. It was something I did alone, half-hidden, the way you do things when you're not sure you're smart enough to learn them. If I had somehow failed at reading music, nobody needed to know I had tried.

The first week I learned the treble clef. The lines from bottom to top are E, G, B, D, F. Every Good Boy Deserves Food. The spaces are F, A, C, E. I remember being frustrated because these mnemonics seemed patronizing, but they worked. I would look at a line of music and say the mnemonic out loud and the notes would come. Then I would look at a guitar and have no idea what to do with this information. The guitar has six strings. Music notation doesn't account for there being six strings. So I had to figure out what each string meant and how the dots on a staff corresponded to positions on the fretboard.

This is where teaching yourself gets hard. In a lesson, a teacher would show you this. You would understand the connection. Alone, you're drawing connections in the dark, guessing if you're right, not able to verify until later. I would learn something, try it on the guitar, get it wrong somehow, go back to the book and search for where my understanding had broken down.

I did this for weeks. Months. Every single day I would work through the workbook and then try to play simple melodies from printed sheet music. Most of what I played sounded wrong. But over time the number of things that sounded right increased. I started to understand patterns. The same note appeared in different places on the guitar. There were shapes to chords that made sense. The music notation began to feel less like a code I was cracking and more like a language I was learning.

By the time I was comfortable with it, I realized something important had happened. I wasn't just learning to read music. I was learning about how I learn. I was learning that I could work through confusion if I did it slowly enough. I was learning that the time investment wasn't punishment for not knowing something already. It was the actual cost of knowing something. There was no shortcut. There was just the daily work.

I started applying this to other things. When I took up coding later, I didn't ask for a teacher immediately. I sat alone with online resources the way I had sat alone with that music theory book. When I struggled with a concept, I didn't panic. I knew from experience that the panic would pass and understanding would come if I kept working. I knew this because I had lived it with music.

What teaching myself to read music showed me is that there's a particular kind of confidence that comes from learning something alone. It's not the confidence of having been taught well. It's the confidence of knowing you can persist through confusion. You've done it before. You've sat with not understanding and kept showing up anyway, and eventually the thing made sense. That feeling doesn't go away. Once you've learned it once alone, you know you can do it again.

I play well now. I read music fluently. I can pick up a score and know what it will sound like before I play it. But I think what I really learned was that reading music was just the excuse. The actual thing I learned was how to learn by myself. And that's a skill worth infinitely more than being able to play any song.

meta.topic: learning to read music at fifteen
meta.prompt: What is something you have taught yourself, and what did learning it without a teacher show you?

text:
The place where I feel most myself is my bedroom with the door closed and my supplies spread out in front of me. I make jewelry, mostly rings and bracelets from wire and beads. I've been doing it for years, and it's the only thing that quiets my mind when everything else is loud. But I did it badly once, which is something I still think about.

I decided to sell what I made. This seemed natural. I was making beautiful things. People complimented them. Why shouldn't I make money from something I was already doing? I set up an online shop and started listing my work. I was confident because I had been making jewelry for so long that I thought I knew what I was doing.

What I was wrong about was the difference between making something for yourself and making something for someone else. When you make something for yourself, you know all the details. You know the wire is sturdy. You know the clasp will hold. You know how long it lasts because you've worn it. When you make something to sell, you have to guarantee these things about every piece, and I didn't really understand that yet.

I made the products, but I didn't test them properly. I sold a bracelet to someone and she wore it twice and the clasp broke. I sold a ring and the wire loosened over time. I sold earrings and the hooks bent. Every issue would result in someone messaging me angry, and I would feel terrible, but I would also feel defensive. These were handmade. Some imperfection was natural.

The problem is that wasn't fair to the people buying from me. They paid money for these things. They expected them to work. My personal standards for my own jewelry were lower than the standards I should have had for something I was selling. I was in my bedroom with my supplies, but I wasn't treating it like a real business. I was treating it like playing.

What I did after this realization was I stopped selling online. I went back to making jewelry just for myself and for friends as gifts. But I changed how I made it. I tested everything twice before considering it done. I upgraded my materials. I took the time to understand what makes jewelry durable versus what makes it pretty. I spent weeks on this education, treating it seriously.

The place where I feel most myself is still my bedroom, still surrounded by my supplies. But now when I make something, I make it right. I'm not selling online anymore, but I could if I wanted to. The difference is I know how to make something worth buying.

I think a lot about that person who came back to me about the bracelet. I think about how she was spending money on something I made and I didn't respect that enough to do the work properly. It's a small failure in the scheme of things, but it taught me something important. You don't have to sell something to give it value. But if you do sell it, you have to respect the transaction. You have to care about the person on the other end enough to do the work right, not just well enough.

meta.topic: selling homemade jewellery online
meta.prompt: Describe a place where you feel most yourself, and why.

text:
The pasta was somehow both mushy and crunchy, the sauce had separated into an oily layer on top of tomato paste, and the garlic bread was so dark it was almost black. I stood in the kitchen looking at what I had made and felt the specific shame of someone who had tried very hard and failed in front of the only audience that mattered.

My mother had been sick for a week. My father had been working late. My siblings were hungry. I had said I would cook dinner, imagining something simple and impressive. I had imagined my family eating food that I made and being grateful. What actually happened is I made something barely edible and served it anyway because what else was I going to do.

Nobody said anything critical. My parents were kind about it. My siblings ate around the worst parts. But I could tell they were disappointed. Not angry - disappointed is worse somehow. They had believed I could do this, and I had let them down.

The next day I tried again. I picked a simpler recipe. Pasta with tomato sauce and roasted vegetables. I paid attention. I didn't rush. I tasted things as I went. It wasn't perfect but it was significantly better. My family seemed more genuinely pleased this time.

What I did after that first failure is I started cooking dinner once a week. Every Friday night I would make something. The first few months I was still mostly failing. I would overcook things or undersalt them or burn the rice. But I kept doing it. Every week I made dinner and every week I learned something from how it turned out.

Gradually the failures became less frequent. By the end of a year, I could reliably make meals that the family enjoyed. I started experimenting. I tried different cuisines. I asked my mother for her recipes and learned how to make the things we ate when I was growing up. Cooking became something I actually understood instead of something I was just guessing about.

What's interesting is that this habit of cooking weekly ended up being more meaningful than I expected. It became a time when I was doing something for the family that they couldn't easily do themselves. My parents both worked. My siblings had school. But on Friday nights, food appeared because I had made it. It was a small thing but it mattered.

My father started requesting things he wanted me to cook. My mother would eat my food and sometimes suggest improvements. My siblings came home early on Fridays because they knew dinner would be ready. What started as a failure became a tradition. What started as trying to impress my family with a big dinner became a small repeated action that ended up mattering more.

I still don't make perfect food. I still have failures. But they're the kind of failures that lead to learning. A sauce breaks and I figure out how to fix it. Vegetables get overcooked and I adjust the timing next time. The failures are just part of the process. What I learned from that first night is that trying and failing repeatedly is how you actually get good at something. The initial failure wasn't the end. It was just the beginning.

meta.topic: the first time they cooked dinner for the whole family alone
