text:
We moved from Bangkok to Stockholm when I was nine. My parents didn't ask me if I wanted to move. They didn't ask my younger sister or my older brother either. It was a job opportunity for my father. It was one of those adult decisions that children are simply expected to absorb without complaint. So we absorbed it.

The first winter was the thing that I don't think we were prepared for. Not prepared in the practical sense - we bought coats and boots and heating systems worked fine. We were unprepared in a different way. We didn't know what being cold all the time would do to us, to our family, to the way we related to each other.

My mother hated it. She said it from the first week and kept saying it every day after that. The darkness. The snow that was beautiful for the first month and then just kept existing, kept needing to be moved and walked through and dealt with. The way the city looked like it was shutting down at three in the afternoon because the sun went down. The way people seemed to disappear into their houses and there was no street life, no spontaneous gathering of neighbors, no flowing in and out of public spaces the way there had been in Bangkok.

My father loved it. He said the snow was beautiful and the winter air was crisp and the skiing was incredible and people were friendlier than he expected. He would come home excited about things he had done, places he had been, and my mother would listen with visible irritation. She didn't want to hear about how wonderful winter was. She was stuck inside because of winter. She was isolated because of winter. She was slowly being erased by winter, or at least that's how she talked about it.

What made it an argument is that they couldn't leave it alone. They didn't have one conversation about whether we would stay or go. They had fifty conversations. My mother would suggest moving back to Bangkok or maybe to somewhere warmer. My father would say we had committed to three years. My mother would say she couldn't do three years. My father would point out that the kids were adapting. My mother would argue that adapting to something terrible was not a virtue. On and on. Through that entire winter and into the spring.

My brother tried to stay out of it. My sister cried sometimes but didn't really understand what the argument was actually about. I understood that my mother was lonely and my father was happy, and that these two things were directly opposed to each other. If he stayed happy about Stockholm, she had to stay sad about it. If she convinced him to leave, they could both be home. But he wasn't convinced.

What's unresolved is that my mother's sadness and my father's joy both turned out to be true. She really was isolated. Winter really was hard for her. And he really did love it. Really did find something there that he wasn't finding elsewhere. Neither of them was wrong. They just had irreconcilable experiences of the same place.

We ended up staying the three years. Then we ended up staying longer. Now we've been here for seven years. My mother learned Swedish. She found community. She's not happy exactly, but she's built a life. My father got promoted. He has friends. He takes every opportunity to ski.

But that argument never fully resolved. It just stopped being active. It's still there underneath, the feeling that my mother sacrificed something to make my father happy. That my father was insensitive to her suffering. That they made different choices about this place and they're both correct about it.

I think about it now because I'm applying to universities and some of them are far from home. I keep thinking about my mother's winter, about being somewhere that doesn't fit you, about the cost of loving someone who loves something you hate. I don't know if I'm afraid of becoming my mother or afraid of becoming my father. But that first winter taught me something about the difference between compromise and resentment. Between staying somewhere and staying somewhere while being angry about it. My parents stayed together through that winter, but they never quite agreed about it. That's a kind of way to live, I guess. I just know it's harder than it looks.

meta.topic: the family's first winter in a cold country

text:
My grandmother has a vegetable garden that has been in the same spot for thirty years. When the drought came, I started watering it. This was supposed to be temporary, just helping while the water restrictions were in place. But it became a daily habit that taught me more about persistence and care than I expected.

The garden is in her backyard, maybe four hundred square feet. She grows tomatoes, squash, peppers, beans, and herbs. The plants had survived dry seasons before, but this drought was different. The city imposed watering restrictions. Watering between nine and eleven in the morning, twice a week. That's not enough for a garden that needs consistent moisture.

So I woke up early and hand-carried water from the house in buckets. Before my school started, I would fill buckets and pour them into the garden. It was inefficient and took maybe forty-five minutes every morning. But it worked. The plants survived.

What I realized over the course of that summer is that this daily action mattered more to my grandmother than I understood. She had lived through the Depression and through economic hardship. She had a tendency to worry about resources disappearing. She watched me water the garden and it seemed to calm something in her. The fact that the garden was alive mattered to her in a way that went beyond food production.

The drought lasted four months. For four months I woke up and carried water. On days when I slept late or was busy with school or just didn't feel like doing it, my grandmother would mention it gently. She never demanded it, but I could tell the routine mattered to her.

By the end of the drought, I had learned something about consistency. About showing up for something that doesn't really benefit you directly but benefits someone you care about. About the difference between doing something because you have to and doing something because it's the right thing to do. I was doing this by choice. I could have refused. The garden might have died back and eventually recovered. But I kept watering because my grandmother needed the garden to be alive.

I also learned about what plants actually need. I learned to feel the soil and know when it was dry. I learned which plants were more resilient. I learned that the garden was more fragile and more resilient at the same time than I expected. Everything was struggling but everything was determined to survive.

After the drought ended, I stopped watering the garden every day. But I still help my grandmother with it. I still wake up early sometimes and water before school. What was an emergency habit became a real relationship with the garden and with my grandmother's connection to it.

My grandmother is seventy-five now. She'll probably do the garden for many more years, but at some point, someone will need to take it over. I think it will be me. I think that summer of hand-carrying water woke something up in me about inherited responsibility. About the things that our families maintain and why we maintain them. The garden isn't just plants. It's continuity. It's proof that something can survive even in difficult times.

meta.topic: keeping a garden alive through a drought

text:
That summer we decided to build a canoe. My father and I. This wasn't something we had discussed for years or planned carefully. He saw a video online and decided we should do it. I said okay because I didn't have anything better to do and because saying okay to his sudden projects was the way we had always operated. He gets ideas and I go along with them.

The canoe plan was take scrap wood and instructions from an old book and create something that would actually float and carry people. My father was excited in that way of his where excitement means he immediately starts buying supplies without thinking through the full scope of what he's committed to. He would come home from the hardware store with twenty dollars of materials when we needed two hundred dollars worth. This happened multiple times. I mentioned this multiple times.

What frustrated me is that I wanted to build it right. I had spent the previous summer learning about carpentry. I understood the principles of construction and stress distribution. I knew that some of his shortcuts wouldn't hold up. When I tried to point this out, he would listen politely and then ignore what I said. He had a specific vision and I was questioning it.

About halfway through the project, we had a real argument. I had tried to fix something he had built poorly, and he saw me taking it apart and told me to stop. He said I was overthinking it. He said the whole point was to do it fast and see if it worked, not to engineer it perfectly. I said the whole point was for it to actually work, which meant taking the time to build it right. He said I was sucking the fun out of it.

This disagreement never really resolved. We kept working on it through August, but there was tension. I would do a part carefully and he would make quick fixes over my work. He would do a part carelessly and I would worry it would fail. We didn't fight about it again, but the argument hung there between us. He thought I was overly cautious. I thought he was reckless.

In early September, we finished the canoe. We took it to the lake to test it. I was terrified it would sink. He was confident it would float. Both of our predictions were partially right. The canoe did float. But it was heavy and hard to paddle and not balanced properly. We took it out for maybe twenty minutes and then came back to shore. My father seemed disappointed but not crushed. I felt vindicated but not pleased.

What I didn't expect is what happened over the following months. He wanted to fix it. Not in a quick way, but methodically. He looked at balance and weight distribution. He asked me for advice about some of the structural issues. Together we made modifications. It took the rest of the fall and into winter, but by next spring, the canoe was actually good. We went out on it and it handled beautifully.

The thing is we never actually discussed what had changed. He didn't say I was right about taking time. I didn't say I was wrong about his approach. We just both started doing the work the way I had wanted to do it from the beginning. It was like the argument got resolved by action instead of by conversation.

What this taught me is that people you love can disagree with you fundamentally about how to approach something, and you can still end up in the same place. My father and I see things differently. He's an idea person and I'm a details person. In that moment, both ways of being had value. His excitement got us started. My attention to detail made it work. We couldn't have done it alone.

I think about that summer a lot when I'm doing other things. When people disagree with me. When I want to insist on my way. The canoe reminds me that the disagreement doesn't have to be resolved for the work to succeed. Sometimes you just keep moving and at the end you're at a place you didn't expect, and you realize you were both right the whole time, just in different ways.

meta.topic: the summer they built a canoe
meta.prompt: Discuss an accomplishment, event, or realization that sparked a period of personal growth and a new understanding of yourself or others.

text:
My grandfather told me I shouldn't take shop class. He said it was beneath me. I was smart - I should be doing academic things, thinking about colleges that cared about that kind of smart. Shop class was for people who couldn't do academics. That's what he believed, and he had opinions about what I should believe too.

But I had already signed up. The welding class had started and I was interested in a way I couldn't quite explain to him. Something about taking metal and heat and making something solid appealed to me. I had always been good with my hands but never interested in expressing that at school. Welding seemed different.

My grandfather didn't forbid me from taking it. He just made his disappointment clear. He would ask if I was still doing that welding thing and the way he said it made it sound like a phase I would outgrow. He suggested I join the robotics team instead, which he considered more respectable. I kept taking welding.

What happened is I started to actually care about it. My teacher, Mr. Hassan, had this quiet way of explaining things that made sense. He didn't talk down to us. He treated welding like a real skill, like something worth taking seriously. I learned that welding requires precision and understanding and an ability to visualize three-dimensional structures. It's not mindless. It's mathematics and physics and art combined.

I made a series of progressively harder projects. I made simple boxes. Then I made a three-dimensional sculpture. By the end of the year, I made a table that my teacher kept in the shop because he said it was well done. I was proud of it in a way I wasn't proud of most of my schoolwork.

The argument with my grandfather was that he couldn't see why I would want to do this. He still doesn't, really. He's asked if I'm planning to be a welder professionally, like there's no point in knowing how to do something unless it's your career. I'm not planning that. I'm planning to study engineering, which appealed to me partially because of welding, because understanding how things are built matters for designing them.

But the fundamental disagreement is still there. He thinks trades are less valuable than intellectual work. I think that distinction doesn't make sense. Intellectual work that produces nothing is less valuable than skilled work that produces something real. Building a table matters. Understanding how to build things matters. These are intellectual activities.

We haven't resolved this disagreement. He still makes comments when I mention the welding class. He still suggests I focus on things he sees as more important. I still keep taking the class and keep being interested in it regardless of what he thinks. It's a stalemate of sorts.

What the class taught me is that people can be smart and wrong about what counts as intelligence. My grandfather is a brilliant person in many ways. But he's got this particular blind spot about manual skills. He doesn't see that thinking with your hands is still thinking. That creating something physical is still creating. That the binary between intellectual and manual work is false.

I'm not going to convince him of this. We're probably not going to have a conversation where he admits he was wrong. But I keep welding anyway. I keep coming to class and learning and making things. Not to prove him wrong exactly, but because I know he's wrong. And that knowledge is enough to keep going, even though we disagree about something I care about and someone I love thinks I shouldn't.

meta.topic: learning to weld in a school shop class
meta.prompt: Reflect on a time when you questioned or challenged a belief or idea. What prompted your thinking? What was the outcome?

text:
The basketball court behind the community center was demolished the summer I turned sixteen. It's gone now and there's just the empty lot, dirt and weeds, occasionally used for overflow parking. But for seven years before that, it was the place where I learned to play basketball, and more importantly, it was the place where I had a significant disagreement with my father that we never resolved.

I taught myself to play on that court. My father used to play when he was young, but he stopped before I was born. He didn't push me to play. I just started shooting around on the court one summer and I liked it. I kept going back. I watched YouTube videos about footwork and shooting form. I practiced the same moves over and over until they became natural. I taught myself the game from the ground up, learning through repetition and failure and gradual improvement.

My father came by the court sometimes and watched me play. He would give me tips, small corrections. He saw potential in me that I didn't see in myself. He started talking about high school basketball programs, about scouts, about the possibility that this casual thing I was doing could become something bigger. He wanted me to get serious about it.

Here's where the disagreement starts. I didn't want to get serious about it. I loved playing basketball on the court with my friends, but the moment it became something my father was invested in, something with expectations, I liked it less. I kept playing, but not with the intensity he wanted. I didn't join any traveling teams. I didn't work with a trainer. I just kept playing casual games on the court.

My father was frustrated by this. He would ask why I wasn't trying harder, why I wasn't joining competitive leagues, why I was wasting potential. I would tell him I was playing because I liked it, not because I wanted to be a basketball player. This made him angry in a way I didn't fully understand. He said I was being lazy. He said I was throwing away an opportunity.

What he couldn't see was that he was trying to make my thing into his thing. He had been a player and had to stop for reasons he never fully explained. I think he saw me as his second chance. But I didn't want to be anyone's second chance. I wanted to just play basketball on a neighborhood court with my friends on summer evenings. That was enough for me.

The court closure made this argument different. Suddenly it wasn't theoretical anymore. The court was actually gone. I couldn't just go back. The city decided the land was more valuable as parking. They took down the basketball hoop and the asphalt and made it a lot. My father seemed almost relieved. He suggested I join a gym, get a trainer, take it seriously now that I didn't have the distraction of casual play.

But I didn't. I was done playing basketball. That sounds dramatic, but it's true. Once the court was gone, I realized how much of my attachment was to that specific place. To the friends I played with there. To the freedom of just showing up and playing without it meaning anything beyond the game itself.

My father never said he was sorry for pushing me. I never said I was sorry for disappointing him. The argument just stopped being active because the condition that created it was gone. He wanted me to be a serious player and I wanted to play casually and now neither of those things was possible on the court that had started it all.

What I learned from teaching myself basketball on that court was something my father couldn't teach me. I learned that the best things are often the ones that happen without external pressure. I learned to play because I wanted to, and that was enough. The moment someone else wanted me to play, it became something else. Something I didn't love anymore.

I think about that court sometimes. I think about my father still wanting me to play competitively even after the court was gone. I think about how some disagreements don't get resolved because they're based on fundamentally different values. He values potential and achievement. I value freedom and pleasure. Both are fine. We just never agreed on which one should matter in this situation. And now the court is gone and we'll probably never resolve it, which is okay. It's just one of those things that remains unresolved between us.

meta.topic: the neighbourhood basketball court that was demolished
meta.prompt: What is something you have taught yourself, and what did learning it without a teacher show you?

text:
My uncle had this radio from the 1950s that he kept in his garage. It was broken, had been broken for years, sitting on a shelf next to bottles of old paint and tools he didn't use anymore. When I was fifteen, I asked him if I could try to fix it. He said sure, go ahead. He didn't think I would make any progress. I don't think he cared much whether I did or not. It was just something that lived in his garage.

What started as a one-afternoon project became something I did every Saturday for six months. I would go to his place and work on the radio. I had no formal training in electronics. I looked things up online. I watched videos of people restoring old radios. I learned what different components did. I learned how to carefully unsolder things and resolder them. I learned what a capacitor was and why they fail over time.

This routine of going to my uncle's place and working on the radio became important in a way I didn't anticipate. My relationship with my uncle was fine but distant. He worked a lot. We didn't see him as much as we saw my other relatives. But by working on the radio in his garage, I started spending time with him. He would come out and watch what I was doing. He would tell me stories about the radio, about when he had used it, about music he had listened to on it as a teenager.

Over those six months, I learned the history of the radio through him. I learned things about my uncle I had never known. He was different in the garage than he was anywhere else. More relaxed. More willing to talk about his own past. He would sit on a stool and tell me about his high school years while I worked on capacitors and tubes.

Restoring the radio also taught me something about time. Every component had failed for a reason - things degrade. But they can be renewed if you have patience and care and the right knowledge. Nothing is actually broken beyond repair. It just requires understanding the problem and taking the time to fix it.

By month four, the radio worked. It was the most satisfying moment. I plugged it in and the tubes glowed and a station came in clear. It was an AM station playing oldies, which felt right. My uncle listened to it and for a moment I saw him as a teenager, the person who had bought this radio and loved it enough to keep it all these years even after it stopped working.

What happened after that is my uncle asked me to look at other broken things in his house. A lamp that didn't turn on. A toaster that was temperamental. A clock that had stopped. Every weekend I would fix something else. Not because I had to, but because I wanted to. I had found something I was good at and a person who valued it.

My relationship with my uncle completely changed. He started calling me asking my advice about things. He told my parents to have me look at their broken devices. He gave me tools. He treated me like someone who knew how to do things, like someone with skills that mattered. This probably sounds small. But for me it was huge. It was the difference between being a distant relative and being someone he actually valued and wanted to spend time with.

The radio still works. My uncle keeps it on his nightstand now instead of in the garage. Sometimes when I visit he'll turn it on and we'll listen for a few minutes. He never says this explicitly, but I know the radio means something different to him now. It's not just a broken thing that couldn't be fixed. It's evidence that his broken things matter. That someone cares enough to fix them. That restoration is possible.

This process taught me about myself. I learned I have patience and focus. I learned I can solve complex problems if I take time to understand them. I learned that small routines can become meaning. Every Saturday in the garage was just me working on electronics, but it was also me building a relationship. It was me growing into someone my uncle respected. These big changes happen through small repeated actions.

meta.topic: restoring an uncle's old radio
meta.prompt: Discuss an accomplishment, event, or realization that sparked a period of personal growth and a new understanding of yourself or others.

text:
My mother decided to become a citizen when I was fourteen. She had lived in the country for fifteen years, worked, raised a family, paid taxes, but she had never formally become a citizen. One day she decided it was time. She bought a study book and asked me to help her prepare for the test.

I thought I would be good at this. I'm a good student. I understand how to study and how to teach. What I didn't understand is that my mother's relationship to this test was completely different from my relationship to academic tests. This wasn't something she was doing to get a grade or to satisfy requirements. This was something she was doing to claim full belonging to a country she had already sacrificed a lot for.

I approached it like an academic problem. I made flashcards. I organized the material into categories. I drilled her on facts about the Constitution and the history of the country and the structure of government. She studied. She got most of it right when I tested her. I was confident she would pass.

But when she took the real test, she failed. Not on the academic part - she got the questions about government right. She failed on the spoken English portion. The evaluator said her pronunciation was too difficult to understand. Her grammar wasn't perfect. Her accent was too thick.

I felt like I had failed her. If I had been a better teacher, if I had coached her on her accent, if I had practiced the speaking portion with her more, maybe she would have passed. I had treated the test like it was about knowledge and it turned out to be about something else too. It was about sounding American enough.

What I got wrong is I didn't acknowledge that this test wasn't neutral. It wasn't just measuring if she understood the material. It was measuring if she could communicate in a way that felt comfortable to the evaluator. My mother had done the work. She had learned the material. But she had an accent that the test couldn't accommodate.

She studied again and took it a second time. Same result. I remember her crying after that test, not about the material but about the fact that her way of speaking was being used to measure whether she deserved to be a citizen. She had been here fifteen years. She had built a life here. Her way of speaking shouldn't be the barrier.

She took a third time. I coached her differently. Not on the material - she knew that. I coached her on pacing, on enunciation, on how to make herself sound like what the test expected. It felt wrong to teach her to change herself, but I also knew she deserved this status. The test was going to stay biased so we had to work around it.

She passed on the third attempt. She's a citizen now. She went through the citizenship ceremony and got her certificate. I was proud of her in a way that goes beyond normal pride. I was proud that she didn't give up even when the test was measuring something unfair.

But what I still think about is how I initially approached this as purely academic when it was actually personal and political. How I treated her preparation as if knowledge was enough when the barriers were bigger than knowledge. This taught me something about how I use my education - that sometimes using it to help someone means understanding what the real barrier is, not just the official one. That's something I carry into everything I do now.

meta.topic: helping a mother study for a citizenship test
meta.prompt: Some students have a background, identity, interest, or talent that is so meaningful they believe their application would be incomplete without it. If this sounds like you, then please share your story.

text:
The jacket has been in our hallway closet for seven years now, and I know exactly when my father stopped wearing it. He bought it for his last job interview before the layoffs started, a charcoal gray thing with a subtle weave that made him look sharper, more hopeful. He wore it to exactly three interviews. After that, he stopped going.

I found it last month while looking for my winter coat. The fabric still smells like his cologne from back then, the specific one he wore to work. I pulled it out and held it like it was evidence. Which, I guess, it is.

My father worked for the same company for eighteen years. He was good at what he did. Efficient, reliable, the kind of employee who didn't make waves and produced consistent work. When the restructuring happened, they let go of everyone over fifty in his division. He was fifty-two. They gave him a severance package and a letter wishing him well in future endeavors.

For the first month, he treated job-searching like a job. He woke up at six in the morning anyway, wore the new jacket, sent out resumes, made calls. He was optimistic in a way I hadn't seen him before, talking about this as an opportunity to find something better. But nothing came. The interviews dried up. The callbacks stopped. By month three, he was applying for positions he was overqualified for and still not getting offers. By month six, he'd stopped applying altogether.

The jacket stayed in his closet. He started staying up late watching television instead of sleeping, and going to bed after we'd all left in the morning. He stopped shaving on weekends. My mother started working overtime, her salary becoming the thread that held us together. My brother and I didn't have to change our lives visibly, but we knew. We could feel the weight of it, the way everything had shifted without any of us being consulted about it.

What I understand now, and what I didn't fully grasp then, was that losing a job after that many years wasn't just losing money. It was losing the structure that organized his whole identity. He was the person who went to work. He was good at his job. And then suddenly he wasn't anyone's employee and wasn't good at anything that seemed to matter in the job market.

The jacket represents all of that. It was meant to signal a comeback. It was the physical thing that said, "I am still a professional. I still matter in this world." When he stopped wearing it, he wasn't just giving up on the job search. He was giving up on the idea that he still fit into that world.

He's been working part-time at a hardware store for the last two years. It pays less than half what he made before. Sometimes I catch him looking away when we talk about money, and I know he's thinking about all the years of contributions he made, all the loyalty that apparently meant nothing when the company decided to restructure.

I've never asked him why he doesn't wear the jacket anymore. I think we both know the answer. Wearing it would require believing again that he might need it, that there's still a version of his life where he's interviewing for something that values what he's learned to do. The jacket hangs in our closet like a memorial to that hope. I don't think he could bear to put it on and then take it off again.

He's still my father. He still makes breakfast on Sunday mornings, still listens when I talk about school, still cares about the things that matter in our house. But there's something in him that's quieter now, something that moved aside to make room for a hurt I'm still learning to see clearly. And that jacket is the artifact of that moment when he stopped believing it would work out.

meta.topic: a father's long unemployment
meta.prompt: Share an essay on any topic of your choice. It can be one you've already written, one that responds to a different prompt, or one of your own design.

text:
I learned to translate for my parents by accident, one misunderstood appointment at a time. My mother's English was basic - survival English, acquired through years of watching television and talking to neighbors. My father's was worse. When they had doctor's appointments, they took me, and I sat between them like a bridge, carrying words back and forth.

The first time I made a real mistake, I was thirteen. My mother had been having migraines, and the doctor was asking detailed questions about the pain. Where exactly? How long? Did it come with other symptoms? I translated quickly, thinking I understood, but I confused the word for "sharp" and said her pain was "dull." It seemed like a small thing at the time. The doctor nodded and wrote something down. My mother didn't correct me, and I didn't think to check what I'd said.

She got prescribed the wrong medication. It didn't help. When she went back, the doctor looked confused. He asked more questions. This time my mother spoke slowly in her limited English, trying to make herself understood. The doctor listened carefully. She got different pills. They worked.

I realized I'd failed her. Not catastrophically, not in a way that caused permanent harm, but I'd failed. I was the bridge and I'd constructed it wrong. She'd trusted me to carry her words accurately, and I'd gotten lazy or careless or just not careful enough.

After that, I started learning seriously. Not from a teacher - I taught myself. I sat in waiting rooms and made myself translate everything correctly, asking my parents to repeat things so I could be sure. I read medical terms online at night. I wrote down words I didn't know. I asked my mother to use different descriptions of her symptoms and practiced translating all the variations.

What I learned was that translation isn't just knowing two languages. It's knowing the culture inside the words. When an American doctor asks "How are you feeling?" they want an answer about pain or weakness or specific symptoms. When my mother described her symptoms, she talked about them philosophically, about imbalance and disruption of her normal self. Those aren't the same thing. A literal translation would sound vague to a doctor trained to think in specific medical terminology.

I got better at bridging that gap. I learned to ask my parents probing questions that helped me understand what they were really experiencing, and then translate that into medical language the doctor would understand. I learned when to ask the doctor to repeat something, to be specific about what they meant. I learned to notice when my mother looked confused and to ask her, in Punjabi, if she understood what was being said to her.

But I still carry that first mistake. I know what it feels like to hold someone's health in your hands and not be sure you're holding it right. I know what it's like to realize, after the fact, that you got it wrong. Every time I translate now, even for small things, I feel that weight. I check myself. I ask for confirmation. I make sure.

It took me years to tell my mother about the migraine medication confusion. I expected her to be angry, or to lose confidence in me. Instead, she looked sad. She said she'd wondered about that visit, but she'd trusted me, so she didn't push back. She'd just assumed she was wrong about her own pain.

I learned something important in that moment, something I wouldn't have learned if I'd gotten it right the first time. Being the translator isn't just about knowing languages. It's about understanding that you're responsible for someone else's safety. That they're placing their trust in you to be accurate, to be careful, to care enough to get it right. It's a bigger responsibility than I realized when I first started doing it. And I think about it every time I see another bilingual kid in a waiting room, translating for their parents, and I wonder if they're making the same mistakes I did, or if they'll learn faster than I did to understand what accuracy actually costs.

meta.topic: translating for parents at doctors' appointments
meta.prompt: What is something you have taught yourself, and what did learning it without a teacher show you?

text:
The acceptance letter sits on my desk in an envelope that still has someone else's name on it. Not someone else, exactly. A name I made up. A name that isn't mine.

I had written the essay for the National Young Writers Competition, and I knew it was good. But I also knew something else: my name is unusual. Not bad, but noticeable. In a blind competition, it shouldn't matter, but I'd seen enough to know that judges are human. Names carry assumptions. They carry baggage. They carry the weight of where you're from and what language your parents spoke and what they might unconsciously expect from you based on that name alone.

So I created an alternative. A normal name. A name that was mine in the sense that I had written the essay, but not mine in the sense that my parents would recognize it. I filled out the form with it. I printed the pages with it at the top. I sealed the envelope with it addressed to the organization.

The letter came back saying I'd won a regional award. Good money for college. Recognition from the organization. Everything I'd wanted.

I was sitting with the envelope when my brother found me. He asked what it was, and I told him it was a competition result. He congratulated me, not noticing anything wrong, and left me alone. But I couldn't open it. The name on the envelope felt like a border I'd crossed and couldn't cross back over.

The essay was about learning to trust my own voice. It was about having something to say and saying it anyway, even when the voice you use to say it isn't the voice everyone around you uses. It was deeply ironic, which is why I kept the envelope and never opened it, never claimed the award, never mentioned it to anyone who might have asked.

What I taught myself through that experience wasn't what I'd expected to teach myself. I thought I'd learn that it's okay to hide parts of yourself to succeed. I thought I'd learn that the system is rigged and you have to be strategic. I thought I might learn some validation from that award.

Instead, I learned something messier. I learned that I knew, on some level, that what I was doing was wrong. That my essay's argument - about trusting your own voice - was built on a foundation I'd undermined the moment I submitted it under someone else's name. The essay wasn't dishonest. But the submission was. And I couldn't reconcile those two things.

I've never claimed that award. I didn't put it on my resume. I didn't mention it on college applications. The money sits in a separate account that I rarely look at. Every time I think about using it, the same feeling comes back: this isn't mine. I earned the essay, but I didn't earn the right to claim it.

Sometimes I wonder what would have happened if I'd submitted it under my real name. Maybe it still wins. Maybe the judges don't care about names. Maybe my fears were completely unfounded. Or maybe it doesn't win, and someone else's essay takes that slot. Both of those possibilities feel true now, feel equally likely, and I'll never know which one was actually real.

meta.topic: an essay competition they entered under a false name
meta.prompt: What is something you have taught yourself, and what did learning it without a teacher show you?

text:
The computer lab at our school is in the basement, in a room that used to be storage before someone decided it could be something more useful. It's small, poorly lit, with a radiator that clanks unpredictably and a window that looks out onto the parking lot. There's no air conditioning. In the summer, it's sweltering. In winter, the radiator overheats it. Most students avoid it when they can.

I found myself spending every free period there, which is where I learned that half the laptops the school had purchased were broken.

It started because I was hiding, to be honest. The main computer lab was where everyone hung out between classes, and I wasn't good at belonging to that scene. But the basement room was empty most of the time. I could work on assignments there without the noise and without the specific anxiety of being in a space full of people I didn't quite know how to be around.

One day I noticed that one of the laptops wouldn't turn on. I poked at it idly, not expecting anything, and the case fell open. Inside, I could see the problem immediately - a loose cable. I pushed it back in, and the laptop started up. It felt like a small magic trick.

After that, I couldn't stop noticing all the other broken ones. Keyboards with stuck keys, screens that wouldn't respond, machines that ran so slowly they were useless. I started bringing tools downstairs - a small screwdriver set, some cleaning supplies. I taught myself using YouTube videos and a lot of trial and error. Some things I fixed, some things I didn't. But slowly, the lab went from having maybe six working laptops to having twelve.

The school's IT person eventually noticed. Mrs. Chen came down one day, looked at what I'd done, and asked why. I told her I was just killing time, which was true and also not true. She offered to show me more. She didn't ask permission; she just started teaching me, showing me how to diagnose problems methodically, how to replace components, how to know when something was worth fixing and when it was time to order new equipment.

That basement became different after that. It went from being the place I hid to being the place I chose to be. Mrs. Chen would leave me a list of machines to work on, and I'd work through them during lunch. Other students started coming down because they'd heard the laptops actually worked now. The room filled up. The noise increased. But it was different noise than the main lab. It was quieter, more purposeful.

What I realized was that I don't feel most myself in crowds or in socially active spaces. I feel most myself when I'm fixing something. When my hands are working on a problem that has a solution. When I can see the exact moment something stops being broken and starts working again. When someone comes up to me with a laptop that won't turn on and leaves with one that does, I understand my purpose in that moment with complete clarity.

The basement computer lab is still poor, still hot in summer and too warm in winter, still has a radiator that sounds like someone's dying in the walls. But it's mine in a way that feels true. I'm there most days after school, working on machines, learning more every time I approach a new problem. The school ordered better equipment once the budget allowed it, but I still maintain the old ones. They're held together by small fixes, by the kind of care that doesn't look glamorous.

I feel most myself there because I'm not trying to be anyone. I'm just solving problems with my hands while other people use the machines I've fixed. It's simple and necessary and, for the first time in school, it feels like that's enough.

meta.topic: learning to fix the school's broken laptops
meta.prompt: Describe a place where you feel most yourself, and why.

text:
I'd been at Lincoln High for exactly six weeks when I realized that this new school smelled the same as the one before it. Industrial cleaner, cafeteria grease, and the specific adolescent musk of seventeen hundred teenagers crowded into one building. The familiarity was depressing.

I'd moved between schools the way other kids moved between classes. My mother had always been looking for something better - better neighborhoods, better schools, better job opportunities. Every two or three years, we'd pack up and start over. By the time I was seventeen, I'd attended six different schools. I'd learned how to be the new student. I could navigate it efficiently. But I'd also learned to not bother.

My previous school had been my third or fourth - I'd stopped counting exactly. I had the skills. First week, find the quiet spaces. Don't push too hard on friendships because you'll be leaving. Learn where things are. Keep your head down. Get good grades because that's something consistent you can control. By week six at Lincoln, I'd already figured out that the cafeteria had a decent quiet corner in the back where I could eat alone, that the library had chairs by the windows where I could hide between classes, that Mrs. Hammond in the English department was one of the few teachers who actually noticed when I wasn't there and seemed to care.

She asked me to stay after class one day, about a month in. I assumed I was in trouble. Instead, she asked me if I wanted to help her with the school's literary magazine. I said no. Not in a rude way, just automatically. Why would I commit to something here? I'd be gone before the magazine came out. I'd learned that lesson at the school before this one.

Mrs. Hammond didn't accept that. She told me, very bluntly, that I was the most talented writer in her senior class and that it would be a shame if I didn't do anything with that. She said the magazine would be published in March. She asked if I could commit to staying until March. Just March. She wasn't asking for forever.

I told her I couldn't make any promises about where I'd be living. She said that wasn't what she was asking. She was asking if I could commit to March as if I'd be here for March. That's different, she said. That's just committing to now, not to the future.

Something about that landed differently. Maybe because Mrs. Hammond was the first teacher at Lincoln who seemed to see me instead of seeing the new kid. Maybe because she was asking me to invest in something small instead of something permanent. Maybe because, for the first time, I realized that I'd been using the fact of my impermanence as a shield. As long as I didn't commit, I couldn't lose anything. But I was also not gaining anything.

I helped with the literary magazine. I submitted three of my own pieces and also took on the role of senior editor. I went to meetings. I had conversations with other students about writing and about their work. I started to know people not just as classmates but as writers with specific things they were trying to say.

In February, my mother mentioned that a new job opportunity had come up and we might need to move after graduation. She was giving me time to prepare, to understand that this school, like all the others, was temporary. She looked guilty about it, the way she always did when she broke this news.

But something was different this time. I felt disappointed, which was new. I wanted to stay until the magazine came out. I wanted to see it finished. I wanted to see how the contributions came together, how the final product would look with all of our work in it.

That's when I understood that I'd been afraid, not practical. I'd been protecting myself from loss by refusing to commit. But refusing to commit meant refusing to live anywhere, really. I'd been moving my whole high school career and not actually being anywhere at all.

meta.topic: moving between six schools in nine years
meta.prompt: Describe a place where you feel most yourself, and why.

text:
I spent four years at St. Augustine's, which was supposed to be building my character and my faith in equal measure. Every morning, I woke up at six to make it to school by 7:15 for the morning service. Every evening, we said grace before dinner. Every Sunday, my family went to church. This was the rhythm of my childhood, from age eight to age twelve, the routine so consistent that I never really thought to question it.

The questioning started small. A friend at St. Augustine's stopped going to the optional Friday night youth group, and when I asked her why, she said she just didn't believe it anymore. Just like that. She didn't believe. I was shocked, partly that she could say it so casually and partly that no one seemed to punish her for it. She still came to school. She still participated in everything else. She just wasn't at youth group on Friday nights.

After that, I couldn't stop questioning. Not in an angry way at first, just noticing things that seemed odd. The contradiction between what we were taught about charity and the way the school excluded students whose families couldn't afford tuition. The way the religion class was taught as doctrine rather than theology, as if there was one right answer rather than centuries of different interpretations. The way doubt was framed as a sin rather than as a natural part of thinking about anything important.

Every morning, I would sit in the chapel and listen to the readings. It became this ritual of internal debate. I'd hear something that made sense, and I'd also hear something that made me uncomfortable. The cognitive dissonance started to feel like the most honest thing in my life. I wasn't pretending to believe. I was genuinely sitting with the contradiction, morning after morning, trying to work it out.

By the end of ninth grade, I'd decided I didn't believe anymore. Not dramatically, not in a moment of rebellion, but gradually, like a door closing quietly. I kept going through the motions. I still attended the services, still said grace, still wore the uniform and followed the rules. But I was going through it as a practice rather than as an expression of faith.

My parents knew something was wrong before I told them. I think they could see it in how carefully I was performing, how deliberate every action had become. When I finally said I wanted to leave St. Augustine's, my mother was disappointed but not surprised. My father took longer to come around.

Leaving the school was harder than I expected. It wasn't just leaving the academic environment. It was leaving the identity I'd had since I was eight years old. I was a St. Augustine's kid. That was part of how I understood myself. Leaving meant rebuilding that entire sense of who I was supposed to be.

The interesting thing is what stayed with me from those four years. Not the doctrine or the specific teachings, though I respect them more now than I did when I was sixteen and angry about contradiction. What stayed was the habit of spending time thinking about big questions. The morning services, which I resented so much, had given me a practice of sitting quietly with complicated ideas. I didn't know how valuable that was until it was gone.

At my new school, public and secular and utterly different, I missed the chapel sometimes. Not because I missed God or the faith, but because I missed the built-in time to think. Everyone at my new school seemed to be rushing from one thing to the next without ever stopping to wonder about the foundational questions of how to live.

I'm grateful for St. Augustine's now, which surprised me. I'm grateful that I was given the structure and the language to question faith in the first place. I'm grateful that they didn't punish me for my doubt. And I'm grateful that it forced me to actively decide what I believe rather than just inheriting it.

My parents and I still don't talk about it very much. My mother remains quietly disappointed. My father has made peace with it. And I've learned that faith, whether religious or otherwise, requires active belief. It can't just be something you do because you've always done it. At some point, you have to choose it or let it go. I let it go, but I kept the part that mattered - the habit of sitting with hard questions and not rushing past them.

meta.topic: leaving a religious school
meta.prompt: Reflect on a time when you questioned or challenged a belief or idea. What prompted your thinking? What was the outcome?

text:
I met Kai in a Discord server for people interested in digital art, which seemed like a safe way to make friends without the complications of actual proximity. He lived in Japan. I lived in the Midwest. The distance meant we could be friends without it being complicated by the social hierarchies of real life.

For the first year, it was exactly what I wanted. We'd talk about art, about school, about the specific experience of being a teenager in completely different contexts. He'd tell me about Japanese high school. I'd tell him about American high school. It was interesting precisely because it was removed. There was no possibility of this friendship becoming something more complicated.

But somewhere around month fourteen of knowing him, that distance stopped feeling like a feature and started feeling like a problem.

It started when he mentioned he was applying to American colleges. He asked me what my town was like, whether there were good schools nearby. He was thinking about California, he said, but he was also thinking about the Midwest. He'd researched it. It seemed like there were good options.

I think that's when I realized I'd fallen into the specific trap of online friendships where you can like someone without having to actually deal with them. Kai was perfect at a distance. But if he actually ended up an hour away from me, in the same geographic reality, I'd have to figure out whether I actually wanted a real friendship with him or whether I was just comfortable with the version of him I'd created in my head.

I became weird. I stopped responding to messages as quickly. I made excuses not to video call. I told myself it was because I was busy, but actually I was scared. Scared that if we became real-life friends, I wouldn't like him as much. Scared that he'd realize that the version of me I presented online was edited and curated and wasn't fully real.

He called me out on it, which was both the kindest and most difficult thing someone's ever done. He said he could feel me pulling away, and he wanted to know why. He asked if I didn't want to be friends anymore. He asked if I was embarrassed by him.

I had to tell him the truth, which was messy and complicated and made me look selfish. I told him I was scared of ruining something by making it real. I told him I'd gotten comfortable with the distance. I told him that if he actually came to the same continent, I wasn't sure I was brave enough to be his friend in a way that required actual showing up.

He didn't get mad. He just got quiet for a few days. When he came back, he'd decided not to apply to American colleges. He was going to stay in Japan. He said that if our friendship meant I had to be afraid, then it was better to keep it the way it was.

I don't know if that was the right call. I think about it sometimes, about whether I made a choice that was about protecting myself or about protecting our friendship. I think about the version of reality where he came to the same country and I was brave enough to show up, and I wonder what that friendship would have looked like.

What actually happened is that I changed my mind about what I wanted from friendship. I stopped trying to have relationships that were safe and started valuing relationships where I might get hurt or disappointed or have to be vulnerable. Kai stayed in Japan. We're still friends. But there's this specific thing between us that we never resolved, this acknowledgment that I chose to protect myself over choosing him.

I think that taught me something, but I'm not sure I can explain it clearly. Something about how love - all kinds of love, not just romantic - requires risk. Something about how you can't actually connect with another person if you're also always protecting yourself from connection. It's either real or it's not.

meta.topic: an online friendship with someone in another country

text:
I couldn't sleep for a year, and that year fundamentally changed how I understand myself and what makes me who I am.

It started junior year with ordinary stress - tests, friend drama, the general anxiety of being sixteen in a world that demands you figure out your future. I'd lie in bed and my mind would just start racing. Not about anything specific, just a constant low-level anxiety that made sleep impossible. I'd lie there for hours, watching the clock, getting more frustrated as it approached midnight and then one a.m. and then two.

I tried all the standard things. No screens before bed. Exercise. Meditation. Melatonin. Warm milk. Chamomile tea. I'd read about sleep hygiene and implement it perfectly and still lie awake, my brain running at full speed while my body was exhausted.

By month three, the insomnia had become its own kind of anxiety. I was anxious about not sleeping, which made sleeping impossible. It was a cycle. I'd go to bed, lie awake for hours, get frustrated, get more anxious, sleep stay impossible. During the day, I was exhausted and irritable. I could barely focus in school. I was falling apart.

My parents took me to doctors. There was nothing physically wrong with me. A psychiatrist wanted to prescribe medication, but I resisted. I don't know why exactly, except that I felt like fixing the insomnia with medication would mean I was giving up on figuring out the actual problem. I felt like there was something I was supposed to learn from the inability to sleep.

By month six, I'd stopped fighting it. I accepted that I wasn't going to sleep eight hours a night. On good nights, I got four. On bad nights, I got two. I started structuring my life around what I could do on two hours of sleep. I lowered my expectations. I stopped trying so hard. I stopped seeing myself as someone who was broken and needed fixing.

That's when everything shifted.

Once I accepted that I was awake, the anxiety about being awake went away. I could be awake without the narrative that this was something wrong. I'd lie in bed and instead of fighting it, I'd just... think. About my life. About who I was. About what mattered to me. It was like the constant noise of the day went away and I could finally hear my own thoughts.

I realized during one of those sleepless nights that I'd been living my life based on what I thought I was supposed to want rather than what I actually wanted. I was supposed to be ambitious, to know my future, to be working toward college. And I did want some of those things. But I also wanted other things that seemed less impressive or important - time to think, time to create, time to just be without doing.

I realized I'd been anxious about sleep because I'd been anxious about everything. And the insomnia was actually my mind's way of forcing me to slow down and pay attention to things I'd been ignoring.

By month ten, my sleep had started to gradually improve. I wasn't "fixed," exactly. I still only got five or six hours on average. But it was better. And more importantly, I wasn't suffering about it anymore. I wasn't seeing myself as broken.

The year of insomnia taught me something about myself that I think is important. I'm someone who needs quiet and space to process. I'm someone whose mind works better when I'm not fighting my own nature. I'm someone who needed permission to not be constantly productive.

Now, a year later, I sleep mostly normally. Sometimes the old patterns come back for a week or two, and I panic briefly before reminding myself that I survived a year without sleep. One week is nothing.

But the person I became during that year is still here. That's my baseline now. I'm someone who understands that anxiety about being anxious is often worse than the actual anxiety. I'm someone who believes that sometimes our minds know something our conscious minds don't, and it's worth listening to that.

My identity now includes the fact that I went through that and came out the other side different. It's not a tragedy that scarred me. It's not a triumph that I overcame. It's just something that happened that changed how I understand myself. And that turned out to be necessary.

text:
I made him coffee every morning even though he couldn't taste it anymore, which is how I know something fundamental about myself had shifted.

He came home from the hospital on a Tuesday with half his body recovered and half of it still not talking to him. The stroke had happened fast - early morning, my mother finding him confused and unable to move his left side. The neurologists were optimistic. He'd regain function. Time and physical therapy would heal most of it. The rest he'd have to accept.

The coffee became the thing I did while he was learning to use his body again. I'd wake up early, make it the way he'd always liked it, bring it to him while he was sitting in his chair trying to get his hand to close on the mug. Half the time, the coffee would spill because his grip wasn't there yet. I'd clean it up and make another cup.

I told myself I was doing it to help him practice using his hands. To build strength through repetition. That's what the physical therapist recommended, after all. Repetition. Practicing the small movements over and over until the pathways rebuilt.

But that wasn't why I was really doing it. I was doing it because my father couldn't do it anymore, and I needed to fix something. He was unfixable. The left side of his face was still slightly slack. His left arm would never be quite right. His speech had returned but he got tired easily and his words came slower. These were permanent. But I could make coffee. I could try to make the small thing work.

By week three, I realized I'd never noticed him making coffee before. It was just something that happened. He'd wake up before everyone else and the coffee would be made when we came downstairs. I'd taken it for granted. Now that it was gone, I understood it had been his daily small act of care for all of us. Making coffee was how he started the day. It was his ritual.

So I took it over. Every morning, even after my mother started making coffee again, even after he eventually recovered enough to make it himself. Every morning, I'd wake up and make his coffee exactly the way he used to, in the order he used to, at the time he used to. It became my ritual now. It became the way I told him that I'd noticed, that I understood what he'd been doing.

He never acknowledged that I was doing this. Or he did, but indirectly. He'd sit in his chair and wait for the coffee. He'd accept it from me when I brought it to him. After a few months, his hand could hold it without spilling. After six months, he could make it himself. But I kept making it anyway. Every single morning.

My mother asked once why I kept doing it if he could do it now. She meant well. She was pointing out that the help wasn't needed anymore, that I could go back to sleeping an extra twenty minutes. I didn't answer her. How could I explain that it wasn't about functionality? That it had become about something else entirely?

meta.topic: a father's stroke

text:
The first time I saw the lighting board for the school play, I thought it looked like something from another world. All those switches and dials, the thick cables running along the ceiling, the way the light technician moved through it all with such certainty. I was in tenth grade, and I'd volunteered for the job because I needed community service hours, not because I actually wanted to do it. I figured I'd learn the basics, show up on performance nights, push some buttons.

By the third rehearsal, I realized I'd been completely wrong about what this job meant. The lighting board wasn't just equipment you operated. It was a language the director used to tell the story. A single cue could make the audience feel something entirely different about what they were watching. When the actor arrived at the crucial moment in the second act, if the light came up even a half-second late, it ruined the whole impact. If it came up too bright, it killed the intimacy.

I remember the moment I changed my mind about the whole thing. We were running through a scene where the main character realizes something devastating about her family. The director had gone over this moment with me maybe five times. The lights needed to dim slowly, very slowly, while staying warm. Not cold, not dramatic, just warm and human and sad. I'd been thinking about it technically, like checking off a task. But then I actually watched the actor's face as the light changed around her, and I understood what it was really supposed to do. It was supposed to make the audience feel what she was feeling.

That's when I stopped thinking of it as a favor I was doing to get my hours done.

The work became incredibly demanding after that. The show was complex, with forty-seven lighting cues across two acts. I had to memorize every one, understand the exact timing, know which combinations of channels would create which effects. I started asking the director questions during rehearsals instead of just showing up to run cues. Why does this moment need to be brighter? Why is this transition happening over two seconds instead of five? She never made me feel stupid for asking.

There were nights I messed up. During dress rehearsal, I missed a transition in the third scene and had to scramble to catch up without the director stopping everything. I sat there during intermission feeling absolutely sick about it, convinced I'd ruined everything. But then the technical director came by and said it was fine, most people wouldn't have noticed, and we just needed to clean it up for the next run. The show went on.

Opening night, I was more nervous than the actors probably were. I sat in the dark booth with my script and my cue marks and my muscle memory of forty-seven moments when the stage needed to transform. I thought about how many things could go wrong, but I also thought about how if I did this right, I was helping to create something that mattered to a lot of people. Families were going to come watch. People were going to feel things.

When the final light cue came in the last act, and the stage went dark on exactly the right beat, and the applause started, I felt something I hadn't expected. It wasn't just relief. It was something closer to pride, or maybe accomplishment, though those words seem too small for what I actually felt. I'd been part of creating an experience for hundreds of people. I'd done that with my attention and my effort and my willingness to care about details that most people would never even notice.

I'm still doing lighting for the school productions. I'm the head technician now, and I help train new people who come in wanting community service hours. I always tell them what I wish someone had told me on my first day: this job sounds like it's about pushing buttons, but it's actually about seeing how light can change what people feel. Once you understand that, you can't do it any other way.

text:
I don't know how to explain to my parents what I feel in the sitting room on Thursday afternoons when I'm supposed to be watching my brother. It's not anger exactly, and it's not love exactly either. It's something sharper and more confused than either of those things, and I've been angry at them both for making me feel this way, for being the kind of family where I have to feel this way at all.

My brother has lupus. He was diagnosed in eighth grade, and now he's in tenth grade, and the disease is still the third person in our house, the one who gets the most attention even when we're not talking about it. His medication has to be taken at specific times. His appointments have to be scheduled around his energy levels. When he has a flare, everything in our family reorganizes itself around the fact of his suffering, and sometimes - I know this is terrible, I know this is wrong - I resent him for it.

On Thursday afternoons, I sit in the sitting room while he rests upstairs, and I'm supposed to be available if he needs something. I'm sixteen years old, which is old enough to understand that resentment toward a sick sibling is the kind of thing good people don't feel, but young enough to feel it anyway, acutely and without any way to process it. He didn't choose to be sick. I understand that. But he also gets to rest while I sit here, and he gets to miss school without it being a reflection on his character, and he gets to be tired in a way that's acceptable, whereas my tiredness from taking care of him is something I'm supposed to just absorb quietly.

My parents think I'm noble for helping. My mom has actually used that word. She said, "You're so noble, the way you look after your brother." And all I could think was how I didn't feel noble at all. I felt trapped and resentful and like I was being made into a better person against my will, which isn't nobility, it's just coercion dressed up in love.

The thing I don't tell anyone is that I love him. I love him so much that sometimes when he's having a flare and lying in bed in actual pain, I feel guilty for the resentment I've carried around, and that guilt makes me even angrier because now I'm angry at myself for being angry, and there's nowhere for any of this to go. He's my brother. He didn't make himself sick. He didn't make me be born first, or older, or more able-bodied. He didn't decide that our family would structure itself around his illness.

But he benefits from the fact that it did, and I think we both know that, and I think that's what I'm really angry about. Not that he's sick. Not that he needs help. But that the help I give him is treated as this beautiful act of sibling love rather than as labor, and labor that I didn't consent to perform. I love him. I also didn't choose this.

I don't know how to reconcile those two things. And I don't know if my parents have ever stopped long enough to ask me how I'm doing in all of this, or if they assume that love is enough to carry me through. Maybe it is. Maybe I'm being selfish and cruel for feeling the way I feel. Or maybe it's possible to love someone and still resent the situation that love has placed you in, and maybe nobody ever talks about that because it makes us all look less noble than we want to be.

meta.topic: caring for a younger sibling with a chronic illness
meta.prompt: Describe a place where you feel most yourself, and why.

text:
Mr. Kapoor lived three doors down from us, and he'd been asking for help with his smartphone since probably the day smartphones were invented. My parents kept saying I should go help him - he was elderly, he was lonely, and his daughter lived overseas and wanted him to stay connected with his grandchildren through video calls. I put it off for months.

When I finally agreed, I thought it would take maybe an hour. I figured I'd show him how to open apps, send a text message, maybe video call, and I'd be done. It turned out to be far more complicated, and not in the way I expected.

The technical part wasn't the problem. Any seventeen-year-old can show someone how to navigate a screen. The problem was that Mr. Kapoor's entire relationship with technology was based on fear. He believed that if he pressed the wrong button, he would break something permanently. He was terrified of the internet - not in a reasonable, "I'll be careful about what information I share" way, but in a deep, existential way, like it was this dangerous wilderness he might wander into and never return from.

I tried to be patient. I really did. I showed him where the app store was, how to search for things, how to download an app safely. I explained that nothing he could do with his thumb would break the phone. I said it probably a hundred times in different ways.

But he couldn't actually believe it, and I got frustrated.

There's one moment I keep thinking about. He'd asked me to help him send a message to his granddaughter in London, and I'd shown him exactly how to do it. Then he looked at the keyboard and said he was afraid he'd spell something wrong. I made some comment like, "People spell things wrong in messages all the time, it's fine," and I could see him physically retreat from the phone. He literally didn't pick it up again.

I realize now that what I interpreted as him being unable to learn was actually him being afraid, and I'd responded to his fear with impatience instead of understanding. My comment wasn't mean, exactly, but it was dismissive. It was the kind of thing that confirmed for him that he couldn't do this, that this world of technology was too complicated for someone his age.

We spent three sessions working through things. By the end, he could send messages and make video calls and access his emails. Technically, I taught him what he wanted to know. But I'm pretty sure he still feels like he doesn't understand how it works, like he's just following a script of steps that I'd outlined and that if anything goes wrong, he'd be helpless. That's not actually learning. That's just being coached through something.

Last week, I saw a video call notification pop up from him when I was in his house. He'd successfully initiated one on his own without asking for help. It was a tiny thing, and he seemed embarrassed about it, like he'd probably done something wrong even though he'd obviously gotten it exactly right. I told him it was perfect and that he was doing great. I meant it, but I also wish I'd said things like that more often during our lessons.

I still think about what I should have done differently. I should have moved slower. I should have taken his fears seriously instead of treating them like something to brush past. I should have realized that for someone in his seventies, this represents a genuinely significant challenge - not because he's not smart enough, but because technology is designed by young people for young people, and it doesn't naturally make sense to someone from a completely different era.

I messed that up. I taught him the mechanics of how to use a phone, but I didn't teach him to actually feel capable with it. And I'm not sure that's something I can fix now.

text:
There's this thing that happens when someone lives in your house for a year. They stop being a guest and they become a person. That's what I learned from having an exchange student stay with us.

Her name was Akiko, and she was from Japan, and my parents thought it would be great for our family to host an exchange student. They thought it would expose us to different cultures, that she'd learn English, that we'd all benefit from the experience. I thought it would be fine. Probably boring. Definitely an intrusion on my space.

I was very wrong about most of this.

The first few months were awkward, which was expected. Akiko's English was okay but not great. There were communication gaps. We didn't have much in common. I showed her around school and introduced her to my friends, but I kept a lot of distance. This was still a guest situation. This wasn't real life.

By month four or five, something shifted.

We started actually talking to each other. Not about school or Japanese culture or anything performative like that, but about the actual things we cared about. She was interested in chemistry. I was interested in music. We'd stay up late and talk about our families and our worries and our hopes for the future. She'd make me tea the way she liked it. I'd help her with homework. We developed inside jokes. We had an actual relationship that went beyond the surface-level exchange student experience.

By month ten, I had completely forgotten that she was temporary.

I think that's the thing that got me wrong. I'd thought of hosting an exchange student as this discrete experience - a year-long project where we'd learn about each other and then she'd go home and life would return to normal. But human relationships don't work that way. You can't spend a year living with someone, eating meals with them, supporting them through difficult times, and then just return to normal when they leave.

When she left, it was one of the hardest things I've experienced.

Her last week, I was in this constant state of low-level sadness that I couldn't quite manage. We did all these farewell activities, saw her favorite places one more time, took a million photos. But nothing really prepared me for the fact that she was actually leaving and I wouldn't see her for years, if ever.

The morning she left, I didn't cry until she was actually gone. Then I cried for probably three hours straight. My parents didn't really know what to do with how devastated I was. They tried to make it better by pointing out that we could stay in touch, that it was just a year and she'd go on to her next experience and her life would move forward. All of that was true. None of it made me feel better.

What I got wrong was thinking I could protect myself from missing her by not getting too close in the first place. By the time I realized I'd failed to protect myself, it was because I'd already fallen into a real friendship with her. So the loss was genuine.

I still talk to Akiko, though less frequently now. She's in university and her life is busy. We're still important to each other, but we're also living completely separate lives. Every time we do talk, there's this moment where I remember how much I missed her after she left and how much she meant to me.

I think about what that year taught me about connection and loss and the fact that you can't actually protect yourself from caring about people by staying distant. The caring happens whether you're trying for it or not.
