text:
I'd spent my entire childhood in a religious school. Catholic education, which meant uniforms, mandatory chapel, religion classes mixed into every subject. By ninth grade, I'd started asking questions. By tenth grade, I was certain that I didn't believe the things the school was teaching me. By eleventh grade, I was sure I needed to leave.

The decision to actually leave was harder than I expected.

My parents were shocked. They'd chosen this school specifically because it was religious, because they wanted me to have that education and that foundation. My mother actually cried when I told her. My father said I was throwing away the education they'd worked to provide. My little sister thought I was making a huge mistake. The school's administration tried to convince me to stay, said that leaving in the middle of high school would hurt my record.

Everyone seemed invested in me not leaving.

But I felt like I was suffocating. Every religion class felt like being forced to accept something I didn't believe. Every chapel service felt like pretending. I was spending six hours a day in a place that I'd outgrown, and I was angry about it in a way that was affecting everything else. I wasn't focusing in my actual classes. I wasn't participating the way I used to. I was just waiting for the day to end.

So I pushed to transfer schools. I found a public school that would take me mid-year. I filled out the paperwork. I told my parents this was happening whether they were happy about it or not.

What I didn't expect was that once I left, I'd miss it.

Not the religion classes. Not chapel. Not the uniforms. But I missed my friends, who all stayed at the religious school. I missed the structure and the clear expectations. I missed knowing exactly what the rules were and what would happen if I broke them. The public school was bigger and more chaotic and had so many more social hierarchies that I hadn't anticipated.

More than that, I realized that I'd been so focused on what I was leaving that I hadn't thought about what I was moving toward.

The first month at the new school was disorienting. The second month was actively lonely. By the third month, I'd made some friends and I was adjusting, but I kept having this weird feeling that I'd made a mistake. Or not a mistake exactly, but I'd made a choice without fully understanding it.

Looking back now, I think that moment of wanting to leave, the thing that felt so clear and obvious and necessary at the time, was also the moment I stopped believing I had to have everything figured out. I left the religious school because I was certain I was right about needing to leave. But I left not really knowing what came next, and that uncertainty was actually okay. I adapted. I found a different path. My life didn't end because I made a big change.

What changed my mind about the whole thing is that I realized the leaving was actually the right choice, even though the transition was harder than I'd anticipated. The religious education wasn't for me. The religious school wasn't for me. And that was fine. Other people should have religious education if they want it. But I didn't. I needed something different.

That feels obvious now, but it wasn't obvious at the time, when everyone around me seemed to think I was making a terrible mistake.

text:
I believed India was my home in the way people believe facts. It was the place I had always been, where my family lived, where school was a comfortable routine I had learned to navigate without thinking. I didn't think of myself as someone with a home - home was just the air around me, invisible and constant. Then my father's company told us we were moving to Singapore, and I had to revise that belief, which turned out to be harder than I expected.

The news came in May, right in the middle of tenth grade. We would leave in July. I told my friends and their responses ranged from jealousy to sympathy, but nobody really understood what I felt, which was a kind of panic I couldn't name. Singapore was a real place on a map, a place I could find in my geography textbook, but it was also a theoretical place, not a place where I had memories.

I spent the first month there in a fog. The school was clean and organized in a way that made everything feel sterile. The students were nice in a polite way that felt distant. My accent, which I had never noticed before because everyone around me had always sounded the same, suddenly announced itself constantly. Teachers would ask me to repeat things. Classmates' heads would turn when I spoke. For the first time I could remember, I sounded like someone who didn't belong.

But something happened around month three. I was walking home from school - we lived close enough to walk, which surprised me because I expected Singapore to be different, but it was just a place where people walked and lived and complained about homework like anywhere else. A girl from my English class caught up with me and asked if I wanted to get food. Her name was Iris and she was from Hong Kong and had moved there last year. We went to a place that made noodles, and she told me that the weird thing about moving was that you don't get to choose when you stop feeling like a visitor.

"You just wake up one day and you're not," she said, eating her noodles carefully to avoid dripping them on her uniform. "It's not a moment exactly. It's just the first day you don't think about how much you miss home."

I thought that was the most depressing thing I had ever heard, and I said so. Iris laughed and told me I was thinking about it wrong. "You don't stop missing it," she said. "You just learn that your brain isn't big enough to hold two places with the same amount of reality. So one of them gets smaller. That doesn't mean it's not real. It just means you're not living in it anymore."

That was in October. By the time winter break came around, I noticed something strange. When I video-called my friends in Delhi, I could barely imagine the places they were calling from. The streets I had walked a thousand times looked flat and distant on my screen. And when I looked at where I was living - the apartment, the park near school, even the noodle place where I had first started to feel maybe okay - it had become realer than the place I used to be. I wasn't sure if that made me a traitor to my own past or just a person living forward into my own life.

I still miss Delhi. But I stopped believing it was the only place I could belong. Home turned out to be more portable than I thought.

meta.topic: moving countries in the middle of high school

text:
I was the only girl on the robotics team, which at first seemed like it might be a problem and turned out to be a different kind of problem than I'd anticipated.

The team had nine people - eight boys and me. The boys were nice enough, mostly. They didn't overtly exclude me. But there was this constant low-level thing where I had to prove myself in ways they didn't. When they wanted to test a new design, they just tested it. When I suggested something, there'd be a beat where they seemed to be evaluating whether my suggestion was worth considering. Not always - sometimes they just did the thing I suggested. But often enough that I noticed it.

The worst part was that I wasn't sure if I was being paranoid. Maybe they were just deliberate about every decision and I was reading too much into their deliberation. Maybe the fact that I was the only girl on the team wasn't actually creating a dynamic, and I was just bringing anxiety into a space where none existed.

There was one project where I suggested we approach the problem differently than they were planning to. They'd been thinking about it as a power management issue, and I suggested it was actually a balance issue. I had reasons for this - I'd studied the problem and I thought I was right. They listened to me and then kind of moved on. They went ahead with their plan.

Their plan didn't work. Three weeks of building and testing, and the robot still couldn't move efficiently. I remember sitting there thinking, I told you so, but also feeling genuinely awful about it because I didn't want to be right in a way that proved me difficult or made things awkward.

They did eventually come back and ask if I still thought it was a balance issue. I said yes. We tried it my way. It worked. The robot moved smoothly. Problem solved.

I should have felt vindicated. Instead, I felt kind of sad about the whole thing. I felt sad that I had to be more right than everyone else just to be considered equally credible. I felt sad that there'd been this moment where my observation could have saved them three weeks of work, but they didn't consider it seriously enough to try it right away. I felt sad that by the time we figured out I was correct, I just wanted to move past it rather than prove a point.

What I think I got wrong was assuming that this dynamic was something I should bear alone, that me being frustrated about it was somehow selfish or would make me unpopular. I should have said something to the team. I should have named what I was observing - that my suggestions seemed to get less weight than my counterparts' suggestions, and that if they wanted the best solutions, they probably shouldn't dismiss an idea based on who suggested it.

But I didn't say that. I just worked harder to be undeniably correct so that my credibility wouldn't ever be questioned.

The thing that bothers me still is that I'm not even sure if the problem was real or if I invented it. Maybe I was just more insecure than the boys and I was reading into normal team dynamics. Maybe if I do robotics in the future I'll find that this was a one-time thing specific to that particular team. Or maybe it's a real pattern that I'll keep running into and I'll have to keep figuring out how to navigate.

What I know is that I learned how to make myself indispensable, which was effective but also exhausting. I wonder if there was a way to belong without doing that. I wonder if I'll ever find it.

meta.topic: acting as the only girl on a robotics team

text:
My family has owned the same small orchard for thirty-seven years. It's not big - maybe two acres of land with apple trees, a few plum trees, one lonely pear tree that mostly produces disappointment. My grandfather planted most of them. My parents have maintained them. Last summer, when I was sixteen, my father asked if I wanted to take over the summer care of the orchard.

I said yes without really thinking about what that meant.

It meant showing up at seven in the morning before it got too hot. It meant understanding what each tree needed - which ones were diseased, which ones had pests, which ones were stressed by drought. It meant pruning dead branches. It meant managing the weeds that grew around the base of each tree. It meant being alone in the orchard for several hours each day, just me and the trees and the work.

The key to understanding any summer of orchard work is understanding the notebook.

My grandfather had kept a handwritten garden journal for thirty years. When my father gave it to me, I opened it and found pages and pages of notes in his handwriting. "Apple tree, east row, fertilized." "Plum tree attacked by insects, treated with sulfur." "This year's harvest light, probably the frost." Every entry was dated. Every entry was specific.

I started my own journal that summer, and I found myself writing the same kinds of things. "The third apple tree lost a major branch, probably to wind damage." "The pear tree has some kind of fungal growth on the trunk, treating it with copper fungicide and watching carefully." "Best year for apples in several seasons, probably because we had good rain in June."

The notebook became a physical object that mattered. It wasn't just a place to track data. It was the conversation I was having with my family's land, written down. It was proof that I was paying attention. It was evidence that the work I was doing mattered and would be remembered.

Looking back now, I realize that the notebook was also how I fell in love with the orchard. I'd grown up knowing the trees existed, but I'd never actually understood them until I started writing down what I was observing. The act of writing it down meant that I had to really see it - not just notice that something was wrong, but understand what was wrong and what might fix it.

In September, when school started and my official orchard work ended, my father asked if I wanted to keep doing it into the fall. I said yes. In October, he asked about winter pruning. I learned how to prune correctly instead of just randomly cutting things. Every season had its own demands, and the notebook evolved with it.

The notebook sits on my desk now, and there are forty-six pages of my handwriting in it. It's not beautiful handwriting. I'm not particularly eloquent. But every single page represents hours of time in the orchard, noticing things, recording things, caring about things. It represents a relationship with a piece of land that I didn't know I wanted until I started paying attention to it.

What I think it means is that sometimes you inherit something and you don't understand its value until you spend enough time with it to really see it. The orchard isn't just a place my family owns. It's a living thing that requires attention and knowledge and care. I'm part of maintaining it now in a way I wasn't before.

meta.topic: a summer of caring for a family orchard

text:
We lost every single game that season.

Our baseball team went 0-14. Zero wins. Fourteen losses. The kind of record that becomes a legend at the school in a way that's not exactly flattering. People made jokes. "Are you trying to set a record for worst team?" that kind of thing. By the end of the season, we'd stopped showing up expecting to win. We showed up expecting to lose, and then we'd lose, and that was the story.

The thing nobody talks about is how demoralizing it is to be part of a team that loses constantly. It's not inspirational. It's not something you laugh about the way adults sometimes claim you will later. It's just disheartening. Every game feels pointless. Every practice feels pointless. You show up because the schedule says you have to show up, but the actual hope that things will be different is long gone.

The last game of the season, we were playing against the team that was in first place. We were supposed to lose. We'd probably lose by ten runs. We went into that game with basically zero expectations.

And then my father had the audacity to tell me, the night before that last game, that he was proud of me for sticking with the team through the whole season.

I remember being genuinely angry at him. I said, "What are you proud of? We won nothing. We didn't accomplish anything. I quit at some point - I've been going through the motions for weeks." I felt like he was patronizing me by acting like just showing up was worthy of pride.

He said something like, "You're right. You lost every game. And you kept coming back. Not because you thought you'd win, but because you'd made a commitment to be there for your teammates. That takes more character than winning when you're the best team."

I wanted to tell him he was wrong. I wanted to tell him that character was for people who won something. Character was for people who actually mattered. Character wasn't what we had. We just had failure.

But then the last game happened and something strange occurred.

We were up by three runs in the final inning, which has never happened before in our entire season. The other team started scoring, and suddenly we were in a position where the game could actually go either way. The pressure completely changed. We were no longer the team that was supposed to lose. We were the team that had a shot.

They ended up beating us by one run. We lost our last game just like we'd lost all the others. But the margins mattered that time in a way they hadn't before, because we'd actually been in position to win.

Walking off the field, I felt something different than I had after the other fourteen losses. I didn't feel crushed. I felt like something had shifted in how I understood our season. We'd been terrible. But we'd shown up. We'd tried. And in that last game, we'd actually competed.

My father's comment made more sense to me after that game than it had before. He wasn't saying losing was good. He was saying that my character wasn't measured by my wins and losses. My character was measured by whether I showed up when things were difficult, whether I could keep caring when caring didn't immediately produce results.

That's an argument I think we're still actually having, not just about baseball but about bigger things. Whether effort matters if the outcome isn't successful. Whether commitment to something is valuable even if you fail. I still think success matters. But I think I understand better now that it's not the only thing that matters.

meta.topic: the last game of a losing season

text:
I spent an entire year preparing for the mathematics olympiad.

Not just preparing - consumed by it. I'd wake up at five in the morning to work through problem sets. I'd stay after school to meet with the olympiad coach. I'd do problems until my eyes hurt and my hands cramped. I convinced myself that winning the olympiad was going to define my entire future, that it was the most important thing I could do in high school.

My parents were supportive, which meant they asked me every evening if I'd practiced, if I was making progress, if I thought I was going to win. My friends got used to me canceling plans because I had to study. I turned down social activities, skipped parties, missed events I actually wanted to go to because I was supposed to be training for this competition.

The week before the olympiad, I was confident. Not cocky, but genuinely confident. I'd solved so many problems that hard problems didn't feel as hard anymore. I understood the concepts deeply. I was ready.

I wasn't ready.

The actual olympiad was harder than anything I'd practiced. Not just slightly harder - completely different in a way I hadn't anticipated. The problems required approaches I hadn't developed. They tested edges of mathematics that I had gaps in. I left the competition feeling devastated, knowing I'd failed before the results even came out.

When the results were published, I was even further down the rankings than my worst fears had predicted. I was in the bottom half. My score was below average. All of that year of work, all of those early mornings and canceled plans and single-minded focus, and I'd still failed at the actual thing.

I think I spent about a week being genuinely depressed about it. I remember my mum trying to tell me that it didn't matter, that I'd learned so much through the process, that failing at the olympiad didn't mean I was bad at math. None of that landed. I'd failed at the thing I was supposed to succeed at. That's what mattered.

What messes me up still is that I don't think the failure was necessarily about my intelligence or my work ethic. I think I just didn't have the kind of creative problem-solving brain that makes you good at olympiad math. I could memorize techniques and solve problems I'd seen before. I couldn't generate novel approaches to problems I'd never seen. That's not a failure of effort. That's a limitation of my brain.

But also, I don't regret the year I spent training. I learned mathematics at a depth that I probably wouldn't have otherwise. I developed stamina for difficult problems. I learned how to sit with the feeling of not knowing something and work through it anyway. Those things are useful. They're real.

What I'm still wrestling with is how to think about effort when effort doesn't result in success. There's this narrative that if you just work hard enough, you'll achieve whatever you want. But I worked as hard as I could, and I still failed. So either the narrative is wrong, or I didn't work hard enough, or I'm not capable of succeeding at this thing. I'm not sure which one it is.

My friends don't really know how much I still think about this. They probably think it's weird that I'm sad about something from a year ago that I ultimately overcame. But I think about it because it taught me something that nobody wanted me to learn: that there are real limits to what hard work can achieve. That sometimes you try your absolute best and you still fail. That has to be okay if I'm going to actually be okay.

meta.topic: the mathematics olympiad they trained for and failed

text:
Mr. Chen let me use the lab after school, which seems like a small thing but actually transformed the entire trajectory of my high school experience.

I got to know him in Chemistry when I was in tenth grade. I was genuinely interested in chemistry - not just in the classes, but in the actual science. I'd ask questions that went beyond what we were covering in the curriculum. I'd read about chemistry research that was being done at universities. I asked him if there was any way to do actual experiments outside of the standard lab schedule.

He said yes. He gave me a key and told me I could come use the lab after school, as long as I cleaned up after myself and didn't do anything dangerous. The only real condition was that I had to document everything I did.

That key changed my life. I mean that sounds dramatic, but it's true.

I started spending hours in that lab. I'd work on experiments that nobody was asking me to do. I'd test hypotheses that I was curious about. I'd read papers and try to replicate the experiments. I'd fail at things and then figure out why I'd failed and try again. There was nobody watching me, nobody grading me on whether I was doing it right. There was just me and the science and the need to understand something.

The only conflict I had with Mr. Chen about this was when he wanted me to slow down.

I was probably doing too much. I was coming in every single day. I was staying for two or three hours. I was getting obsessive about this one experiment where I was testing crystal growth rates under different conditions. He pulled me aside and said I seemed like I was burning out, that I should maybe take it easier, do the lab work less frequently.

I remember being frustrated with him about it. I felt like he was trying to limit me, like he was being parental in a way that I hadn't asked for. I told him I was fine, I wanted to keep going. I understood the risks of burnout, and I was managing it.

We had a sort of argument about this, or not an argument exactly, but a real disagreement. He was worried about me. I was annoyed that he was worried about me.

But he was right, which I only realized later.

I did eventually get burned out. I got into an experiment so deeply that when I hit a wall I couldn't get past, I fell into this spiral of self-doubt about whether I was actually capable of doing this kind of research. I didn't want to go to the lab anymore. I felt like I'd failed, and everything else felt tainted by that failure.

It took me about a month to climb out of that hole. Mr. Chen was patient about it. He didn't say anything. He just let me come back when I was ready, and we went back to our routine.

What I understood later is that he wasn't trying to limit me. He was trying to teach me something about how to be a person who does science in a sustainable way. He was trying to show me that burnout is real and that protecting yourself from it is part of being a good scientist, not a sign of weakness.

We're still in disagreement about some things. He wanted me to focus more on the coursework and less on the lab work. I wanted to do everything. But I think he was right that I needed to learn how to care about something without letting it consume me entirely. That's a lesson that goes way beyond science.

meta.topic: a science teacher who let them use the lab after hours

text:
The insomnia started around junior year and it just didn't stop.

I couldn't fall asleep at night. I'd lie in bed for hours and just stare at the ceiling. My mind would start racing about things - school, college, whether people liked me, random conversations I'd had in the cafeteria that I'd suddenly realize sounded awkward. I'd check my phone and see that it was two in the morning and I had to be up at six, and that anxiety about not getting sleep would make it even harder to fall asleep.

After about a month of this, I went to the doctor. She said it was probably stress and prescribed some relaxation techniques. Meditation. Progressive muscle relaxation. Keeping the room cool. All the standard advice.

None of it worked.

By month four of insomnia, I was a mess. I was falling asleep in classes. I was getting sick more frequently - apparently sleep deprivation tanks your immune system. I was emotional about stupid things. I was struggling to concentrate. My grades were slipping. My parents were worried. I was convinced that I'd permanently broken my brain somehow and I'd never be able to sleep normally again.

I went back to the doctor. She referred me to a sleep specialist, but the first appointment was three months out. I was supposed to just suffer through this.

So I developed a routine.

Around eleven at night, I'd start getting ready for bed even though I knew I wouldn't sleep. I'd take a warm shower. I'd make tea. I'd read something that was boring - not something I wanted to read, something deliberately tedious. I'd sit in my room with soft music playing. I'd journal about whatever was keeping me awake. I'd do breathing exercises. I'd lie there and just accept that I might not sleep, and somehow that acceptance made things slightly better.

I still didn't sleep very well. But I moved from getting maybe two hours to getting maybe four or five. And the routine itself became something I could count on, something predictable in a period where sleep felt absolutely random.

About six months in, something shifted. I still wasn't sleeping perfectly, but I was sleeping more consistently. My body had adapted to the routine. The anxiety about not sleeping had decreased because I had an actual process for managing the insomnia instead of just lying there panicking.

What I realized later was that the insomnia had been the symptom of a bigger stress issue that I eventually addressed - I talked to a therapist about test anxiety and perfectionism and all the things that were making my brain unable to shut off at night. That's what actually fixed the underlying problem.

But while I was waiting to address the underlying problem, the thing that helped me survive was having a routine. Having something I could do every single night that felt like I was taking action, even when the action wasn't actually making me sleep. Having a process made the insomnia less terrifying.

I still have nights where sleep doesn't come easily. But I'm not afraid of those nights anymore because I know I have tools and I know my body can function even on less sleep than I'd prefer. The insomnia taught me something about resilience and adaptation that I probably wouldn't have learned otherwise.

meta.topic: a year of insomnia

text:
My parents opened the restaurant when my older brother was two years old. I have a photograph from the opening week: my dad standing in front of a small storefront with a handwritten sign, my mum in the kitchen wearing an apron that says someone's name I don't recognize. They looked exhausted and proud in equal measure.

By the time I was born, the restaurant was established enough that I essentially grew up in it. My earliest memories are of being underneath the tables during lunch rush, playing with pots in the kitchen while my mum cooked, falling asleep in a corner booth while my parents closed up for the night. The restaurant was what my family did.

Twenty-two years after my parents opened it, my father decided to close it.

The decision didn't come suddenly, though my brother tried to argue that it had. My father had been quieter for the past year, staying up later looking at the accounting books, talking to my mother in low voices about rent and staffing costs and how much the delivery platforms were taking. The restaurant was still doing okay, still had regular customers, still had a purpose in the community. But it wasn't thriving the way it once had, and my father was tired in a way that didn't improve even on his days off.

My brother was furious. He'd started talking about taking over the restaurant eventually, about eventually leaving his job in finance to come back and run it. He thought my father was giving up. He thought they should fight harder to keep it alive. I remember him saying, "Dad's just burned out. If he took a month off, he'd feel differently about this."

I think my brother was wrong, and I've been angry at him for not seeing it, which is probably why I'm writing about this instead of just moving on.

The thing my brother didn't understand was that for my father, the decision to close wasn't a failure - it was a release. He'd given the restaurant twenty-two years. He'd been there at four in the morning to start prep. He'd listened to customers' problems and their stories and their complaints. He'd watched food trends change and rent increase and his own back and knees start to give out from standing all day. The restaurant had given my family stability and purpose and a living, and then it had also started taking more than it was giving back.

My brother wanted my father to keep sacrificing himself for something that was also sacrificing him.

That's where we disagreed, and that's where we still disagree. My brother thinks I'm being disloyal by understanding our father's decision. He thinks I should have fought with him to keep the restaurant open, like that somehow proves I care about the family legacy or understand the value of what our parents built. But I think understanding that my father deserved to be tired, that he'd given enough, that sometimes the most important thing you can do is choose yourself - I think that proves I understand what family actually means.

The closing happened over several weeks. My father reduced hours gradually, stopped taking on new catering projects, started saying goodbye to regular customers. We held a final service on a Saturday, and it was packed with people who'd eaten at the restaurant over the years. People brought their kids and their grandkids. Someone brought a cake. The whole thing was sad and celebratory at the same time.

My father cried afterward, and I held his hand.

I haven't resolved this with my brother. He's still sort of angry about the whole thing, still mentions sometimes how the restaurant could have been saved if my father had just held on longer. But I've made peace with it, or I'm making peace with it. I've realized that loyalty to your family doesn't mean asking them to keep destroying themselves for something they built. Sometimes it means letting them rest.

meta.topic: the family restaurant closing after twenty-two years

text:
I set up my stall at the weekend market at six-thirty in the morning, before the sun was fully up and before most of the other vendors had arrived. I was selling jewelry I'd made myself - mostly beaded necklaces and bracelets, some earrings. I'd been making jewelry for about a year by that point, and I thought I was ready to actually sell it to strangers.

I was very, very wrong.

The first person who came to my stall asked how much for the big necklace. I'd spent six hours beading that necklace. I'd chosen each bead carefully and arranged them in a specific pattern. The materials had cost me maybe eight hundred rupees. I'd never actually calculated what I should charge for the labor and the expertise and the time. I just knew I wanted to make some money, so I said, "Five hundred rupees."

The man immediately left. I didn't sell anything to him.

Over the course of the three-hour market, I sold three pieces. I made 1,200 rupees total, which sounds decent until you realize that two of those sales were at prices I'd set randomly and one was to a friend's mother who was being nice to me. By the time I packed up, I was exhausted and demoralized. I'd done all this work, spent six hours just on one necklace, and I'd essentially made two hundred rupees per hour for the time I'd actually spent selling things. That was lower than minimum wage. That was worse than my regular babysitting gig.

I spent that whole week thinking about how I'd failed at this. Everyone talks about entrepreneurs starting with a product and a market, and I'd had both, and it hadn't worked. Or I hadn't worked, which seemed to be the actual problem.

So I went back the next Saturday determined to do better.

The first thing I did was actually cost out my pieces properly. I looked at how much time I'd spent, how much materials had cost me, and I decided on prices that were realistic. The necklace that I'd originally priced at five hundred rupees? It should have been 1,200 rupees at least. My earrings should have been 300 rupees per pair, not 150.

I thought if I was going to fail, at least I'd fail at a fair price.

The second thing I did was make my stall look better. I got a small backdrop and arranged my pieces more carefully. I made a sign that said the pieces were handmade. I didn't have any capital to invest in this, so I got creative with things I had at home.

I sold eight pieces that Saturday at the new prices. One person actually bargained with me instead of just accepting my prices, which made me feel like I was doing something right. Two people bought multiple things. One woman asked if I did custom orders.

By the fourth week, I was actually making decent money. Not a fortune, but enough that it was worth my time, and enough that I could reinvest in better materials and supplies.

What I'm still realizing, even now, is how much of that initial failure was on me. I had come to the market unprepared. I had underpriced my work. I hadn't thought about what I was actually doing from a business perspective - I'd just thought about it as me trying to sell jewelry. Once I actually treated it like a real endeavor, it worked better. Not perfectly, but better.

The other thing is that I'd quit after one bad day. I'd let that failure convince me that I wasn't good at this, when what actually happened was that I wasn't good at pricing and presentation. Those are learnable things. Once I learned them, the whole thing got better.

I haven't continued with the market stall - I got busy with school and other things. But I've continued making jewelry, and I've continued thinking about what that experience taught me about failing at something and then actually examining why you failed instead of just accepting the failure as final.

meta.topic: running a stall at a weekend market

text:
My family had owned a piece of land outside the city for as long as I can remember. It wasn't really developed or valuable - mostly it was just empty land with some trees on it and a lot of emotional weight from generations of family history. My grandfather bought it. My father was born there, technically, before they built the house in the city. My grandmother has spent every summer there for fifty years.

When I was fifteen, there was a real-estate developer who approached my father about buying the land. The offer was substantial - a lot more money than my father had expected. He was actually considering it seriously, which shocked everyone in my family.

My grandmother was absolutely furious. She said the land was not his to sell, that it belonged to the family, that selling it would be betraying everything it meant to own something that had been in the family for decades. She said my father should be ashamed for even considering it.

My father said the land was his legally and financially, and if he wanted to sell it, he had every right to. He said my grandmother needed to accept that people change and priorities change, and what had made sense to keep fifty years ago didn't necessarily make sense now. He said they couldn't afford the property taxes forever and that the money would actually improve our family's financial stability.

They had a real argument about this. My grandmother stopped speaking to my father for several weeks. The family was divided. Some aunts and uncles sided with my grandmother. Others thought my father was making a rational financial decision.

I sided with my grandmother, which I think was unfair to my father.

I remember telling him that he was being selfish, that some things matter more than money, that he should value what the land meant to the family rather than what some developer was willing to pay for it. I was righteous about it. I was absolutely certain that he was wrong.

But I was also sixteen, and I didn't have to pay property taxes or worry about financial stability or manage complex decisions that affected multiple generations. I was just holding onto nostalgia.

My father ended up not selling the land. He decided that what the land meant to my family outweighed the financial benefit of selling it. He made that choice not because I convinced him, but because he went through his own process of deciding what mattered.

The thing I was wrong about was assuming that I knew what should matter to him. I was wrong about thinking that the fact that I loved the land and had memories there meant he was wrong for considering selling it. Just because something mattered emotionally didn't mean it made financial sense to keep it. Those two things can both be true at the same time.

And even though my father ended up keeping the land, I still think he should have felt free to sell it if he wanted to. I think I should have supported his right to make that decision even if I disagreed with the decision itself. I was so busy being upset about the potential loss that I didn't consider what he actually needed from his family in that moment.

We've never really resolved this, and I'm not sure we will. My father kept the land partially because of family pressure. That's not a great reason to keep something. But I'm also not sure what would be different if I'd handled it differently - if I'd been less judgmental, more curious about his reasoning, more willing to acknowledge that his needs and concerns were legitimate even if they conflicted with what I wanted.

I think about this whenever I'm tempted to judge someone for a choice they're making with their own resources. I remember how certain I was that my father was wrong, and how little I actually understood about the full picture.

meta.topic: an argument about whether to sell the family land

text:
I hadn't ever seen snow until I was sixteen years old.

My family had moved around a lot, staying in warm places, and I'd grown up in India, which doesn't have snow basically anywhere. So I'd seen photos of snow, read descriptions of it, imagined what it would be like. But I'd never actually experienced it in person.

When we moved to a city that has real winters, I was expecting to be disappointed. Snow, I figured, would be like most things that are hyped up - less impressive in reality than in the anticipation. But then winter came and the temperature dropped and we woke up one morning and everything was covered in this thick white blanket.

The first thing that hit me was the quiet. It's weird that I remember that most, but snow changes how sound travels. The whole world seemed muffled and soft. The second thing was that it was beautiful in a way that photos really can't capture - this particular quality of light bouncing off white surfaces, the way individual flakes catch the sun.

But what really changed my mind was the coldness of it.

I stood outside for maybe thirty seconds and my hands started to hurt. My face went numb. The cold wasn't romantic or picturesque from inside the cold - it was urgent and demanding and real. My body was having a genuine reaction to this weather in a way I hadn't anticipated. This wasn't a nice aesthetic experience. This was something that mattered physically.

I came inside convinced that snow was actually terrible and I was going to hate the whole winter.

But then something shifted. I started paying attention to how my body adapted. My hands got less sensitive to the cold. I learned to dress properly. The shock of the cold in the morning started to feel invigorating instead of painful. By week two of the snow season, I was actually enjoying being outside in it.

The thing that changed my mind was going sledding with some kids from school. It was absolute chaos - there were probably twenty of us on this hill and half of us couldn't sled worth anything. People kept falling off and sliding into other people and laughing hysterically. I fell, like, three times and every time I laughed harder than the last time.

At one point, I was sitting on the sled at the top of the hill and I remember thinking, A month ago I thought I was going to hate this place because of the weather, and now I'm sitting on a hill in the snow genuinely having one of the best times I've had since we moved here.

It was this realization that my initial judgment had been wrong. I'd decided that snow was going to be this romantic thing, and when it turned out to be actually cold and uncomfortable, I'd decided it was bad. But neither of those judgments was quite right. Snow was just snow - cold and wet and beautiful and inconvenient all at the same time. The experience of it depended entirely on whether I was willing to be present in the actual experience rather than comparing it to what I'd expected.

That seems like a small thing to learn from seeing snow for the first time, but it stuck with me. I think about it now when I encounter something new and I'm tempted to write it off as disappointing because it doesn't match my expectations. I think about that day sledding and I remember that reality is usually more complicated and more valuable than I expected.

meta.topic: the first snow they ever saw

text:
My mother started the business from our garage six years ago, and I thought it was foolish. She spent weekends hunting through thrift stores and estate sales, hauling back bags of used clothes that smelled like other people's closets. She'd bring home racks and racks of fabric, and I'd see her hunched over a sewing machine late into the evening, mending seams and replacing buttons on vintage dresses that seemed to have no future.

I was twelve when she started and skeptical in the way twelve-year-olds are. My friends' parents had real jobs, jobs with office buildings and salaries and business cards. My mother had a used sewing machine and a dream about making unwanted clothes beautiful again. I was embarrassed by it, if I'm being honest. When people asked what my mom did, I'd say she worked in fashion without mentioning the part about the secondhand garage.

The belief I held was simple and unexamined: used things were inferior. They had been rejected once already, worn out by previous owners, marked by use. The fact that they were cheap was the proof of their worthlessness. Only new, untouched, purchased items from stores were worth owning or wearing. This seemed like basic truth to me, not really an opinion at all.

That belief started to crack when I was fourteen. I had to help my mother with the business for a school project, and I found myself actually looking at the clothes she was restoring. There was a 1950s wool coat she'd found, navy with damaged lining and one broken button. She replaced the lining with bright patterned fabric, fixed the button, and suddenly it was beautiful. She sold it on her small online shop for forty-five dollars to a college girl who left a review saying she'd been searching for a coat exactly like this her entire life.

There was a silk slip dress, cream-colored, that had yellowed slightly. My mother carefully dyed it a soft blush and added lace trim to the hemline where it had torn. A woman bought it and sent a photo of herself wearing it to a wedding. In the photo, she looked radiant.

I realized that my mother wasn't selling used clothing. She was seeing potential in things that others had discarded. She was understanding that something worn didn't mean something worthless. It meant something was waiting for a second chance.

By the time I was fifteen, I was actively helping. I learned which fabrics could be dyed, which could be altered, which needed to be left alone because their damage was part of their beauty. My mother taught me that a vintage leather jacket with a patina wasn't damaged - it was lived in. A dress with a small stain could become a unique upcycled piece if you worked with the imperfection rather than against it. The previous owner's story wasn't a mark of shame; it was part of the object's character.

This shift in thinking changed how I see the world. I realized I'd been taught to believe that newness equals value, that use equals damage, that handmade meant inferior. But watching my mother restore old clothes, I understood that those beliefs were wrong. Things that had been rejected could be reimagined. Things that were worn had stories. Things that were imperfect could still be beautiful, perhaps more beautiful because someone had chosen to care for them.

Now I work in her shop on weekends, and I think about the people on the other end of the sales. Someone will buy something that was unwanted and make it part of their life. A teenager might find a coat that makes her feel like herself. Someone will wear something handmade and vintage to an important event and feel like it was chosen just for them.

My mother wasn't foolish. She just saw value where others saw waste. That's the belief I had to let go of, and in letting it go, I began to understand the world differently. Used things aren't failures. They're just waiting for someone to see what they could become.

meta.topic: a mother's second-hand clothing business

text:
The register sits at the counter of my family's convenience store like it has for twenty years. It's not one of those modern touchscreen systems that looks sleek and efficient. It's mechanical, heavy, with worn plastic buttons and a metal drawer that slides out with a satisfying click. The number pad is rubbed smooth from the thousands of fingers that have punched in prices and codes and quantities. Some of the numbers are barely legible anymore.

I've been working behind that register for four years, since I was thirteen. On Saturdays and after school, I ring up chips and milk and lottery tickets and energy drinks for people I've started to recognize by face. Mrs. Chen comes in Wednesday mornings for her coffee. The teenager from down the street always buys the same gum, same time. The man with the dog stops by most evenings.

This register has taught me something unexpected about the ordinary. When you stand behind a counter and interact with hundreds of people over thousands of transactions, you start to see the small stories embedded in what they buy. A father buying formula and diapers and looking exhausted. A girl buying supplies for a craft project, her hands already paint-stained. An elderly woman who always chats for five minutes and seems to have nowhere else to be. A teenager buying ice cream after, presumably, a bad day.

I used to think working this register was just a way to make money. Something temporary, something I'd move past quickly. My parents owned the store, and helping out was just what you did in a family business. But standing at this register, I've watched how it sits at the center of a lot of people's days. Someone's morning routine. Someone's emergency stop. The place where a neighbor is briefly visible as a whole person, not just a voice or a face passing on the street.

The register is old and imperfect. It gets stuck sometimes. The receipt printer jams and I have to coax it. The drawer occasionally doesn't close smoothly. Nothing about it is elegant or efficient in the way modern things are supposed to be. But every day it works. Every single transaction, it rings up, the drawer pops open, the receipt prints out. It's reliable in a way that feels important.

Working this register has made me think about value differently. The convenience store isn't glamorous. The job isn't impressive in the way that summer internships or college-application-looking volunteer work is supposed to be. But it's real work that helps real people, and the small relationships that form at this counter have mattered to me more than I expected.

My father still works this register too. He knows the regulars' names, their orders, something about their lives. He's shown me that there's dignity in this work, that knowing your community and serving it well is a form of contribution that's worth doing. That a job you show up for, day after day, quietly and reliably, matters even if no one external is keeping score.

This worn-out register has been a teacher in its own way. It's taught me that the ordinary things, done consistently with attention and care, add up to something meaningful. That showing up for people matters. That even a simple transaction can contain a moment of genuine human connection.

text:
I met Sofia through a forum about literature when I was fourteen. She was in Portugal, same age, and we started messaging about books we were reading. That was four years ago. She's the person I send screenshots to, the person I think of when I want to share something I've found. The person who knows my bad jokes and laughs anyway.

Our friendship exists entirely online. We've never met. We probably never will, at least not for several years. But this digital space, this place where our conversations happen, has become where I feel most myself.

The internet can feel like a lot of places to different people. For some it's performative, a stage where you're always aware you're being watched. For others it's escapism, a break from reality. For me, it's become the most honest place I know. And that's almost entirely because of Sofia.

With Sofia, there's no pretense. We started talking at an age where we were both still figuring out who we were, and we've done a lot of that figuring out together. She knows about the anxiety I get before presentations. She knows which teachers I dislike and why. She knows my family drama, my friend conflicts, the things I'm insecure about. And I know the same about her - her immigrant parents' pressure, her love of math, the boy she's been quietly in love with for two years.

We have a ritual. Every Sunday evening, my time, we video call and just talk. Sometimes for ten minutes. Sometimes for hours. We might be doing homework in the background or making tea or just lying on our beds looking at the ceiling. Often we don't even talk much. We just exist in the same space, digitally, and it's enough.

This friendship has taught me something about belonging. I have friends here, at school. I'm not isolated or lonely in the way that questions sometimes imply. But there's something different about Sofia. She sees me when I'm not performing. When I'm not thinking about how my words will land or what impression I'm making. She knows me when I'm tired or frustrated or just being weird.

What strikes me most is that none of this requires physical proximity. We don't hang out. We don't have memories of doing things together. We exist through conversation alone, and somehow that's been enough to build something real. It's made me question what friendship actually requires. It turns out it doesn't require shared geography or weekly meetups or even being able to grab coffee. It requires attention. It requires someone who chooses to know you.

When I think about where I feel most myself, I keep coming back to my bedroom, late evening, calling her. To the feeling of being able to say whatever I'm thinking without editing. To the knowledge that someone in another country has chosen to know me thoroughly, to witness my confusion and growth and weirdness, simply because they want to.

It's changed how I think about connection. I used to believe that real friendship had to look a certain way, had to happen in person, had to include the markers I'd been taught to recognize. But Sofia and I have built something that feels more authentic to me than friendships that follow all those rules.

She's probably the person who knows me best, even though we've never sat in the same room. In some ways because of that. There's an honesty in a friendship that exists purely through words and choice. No social pressure. No pretense. Just two people deciding, over and over, to keep choosing each other.

meta.topic: an online friendship with someone in another country
meta.prompt: Describe a place where you feel most yourself, and why.

text:
I started keeping score at my father's cricket matches when I was eight because he asked me to, and asking me to do things was how we spent time together. He played in a weekend league on Saturday mornings, and keeping score seemed like a job important enough for me to take seriously. He gave me a small notebook and showed me how to mark each run, each wicket, each boundary. It had a language and a system that made sense.

For years, that's what I did. I sat in the stands behind the players' families and I tracked the game in my notebook. I learned the rules so I could understand what I was tracking. I learned to anticipate moments. I knew when someone was building a real innings and when they were just hitting lucky boundaries. I could feel the momentum of the game the way other people read sports instinctively.

My father loved that I was doing this. He'd ask me at dinner about the match, about how close it had been, about what I'd noticed about certain players. I was the keeper of the record. I had information he wanted. It made me feel useful and important in his world.

But when I was fourteen, I realized something uncomfortable. I wasn't actually enjoying the cricket. I was enjoying the feeling of being useful to my father. The cricket itself was background. I showed up Saturday mornings not because I cared about the game but because the game was an excuse to be near him, to have a job to do that made me feel necessary.

There was a particular match that clarified this for me. I was fifteen, sitting in my usual spot with my notebook, and the weather was terrible. It was unseasonably cold, and I was miserable. I wasn't interested in the game. I wasn't interested in being there at all. And I realized, sitting there shivering and annoyed, that I had no idea what was actually happening on the field. I was keeping score on autopilot while my mind was elsewhere, wishing I could be at home.

That evening, I told my father I didn't want to keep score anymore. I said it was boring and I was too old for it. What I didn't say was that I felt trapped by my own habit, by something that had started as connection but had become an obligation.

He looked genuinely hurt. I think he had believed that I actually cared about cricket, that I was developing a real passion for the sport we shared. But the truth was I had been performing interest to keep him happy.

I didn't go to matches for about a month. He didn't ask me to. But then one Saturday, I woke up and realized I missed it. Not the scoring, but something about being there. Being part of something he cared about. And I went back to the pitch, but this time without the notebook.

I sat and actually watched. I learned cricket not because I needed to track it, but because I wanted to understand the game he loved. And it turned out, when I stopped doing it for him, I actually liked it. The strategy interested me. The beauty of a well-timed shot interested me. The social aspect of the league interested me.

That's when I realized that my father had been trying to teach me something the whole time, and I'd completely missed it. He didn't want me to keep score. He wanted me to see what he saw. He wanted me to learn not because I was obligated, but because the thing itself was worth knowing.

Now I go to his matches without keeping score, and we talk about the game differently. Real talk, about what we actually noticed. And I understand that what I taught myself wasn't cricket, but the difference between doing something for someone and doing something for yourself.

meta.topic: keeping score at a father's cricket matches
meta.prompt: What is something you have taught yourself, and what did learning it without a teacher show you?

text:
My mom used to say that I would never make it in another country because I was too used to things being a certain way. The comment stung when she said it, though she meant it as a challenge, not an insult. What I didn't tell her was that staying the same way in a new country is what I had chosen to do, and it took her six months to figure out that the choice itself was what changed me.

When we moved to Singapore in the middle of tenth grade, I brought my stubbornness with me like luggage. I woke up every morning at six-thirty, which is what time I had always woken up. I packed my lunch the same way I had always packed it. I bought the same brand of shampoo that I had used in Delhi, at an expensive expat store, because switching felt like giving up. These tiny habits were the only things that felt like mine in a place where everything else was unfamiliar.

But here's what happened, and I still don't fully understand the mechanism of it: those small routines became the bridge from the life I had known to the life I was actually living.

Every morning, waking at the same time, I would open my window and notice something new about the humidity or the light or the sound of people starting their day outside. Every time I made the decision to pack my lunch the same way, I became slightly more confident that I could be consistent somewhere, even here. The shampoo, which I bought at an expat store, led me to talk to the shop owner, who mentioned a study group at a different school, which led me to meet people outside my immediate circle.

These weren't glamorous changes. They were the kind of thing you don't even notice happening while it's happening. I was just trying to stay the same, and in doing so, I became someone new. It sounds paradoxical, but it's not really. It's just that small repeated actions accumulate in unexpected ways.

My mom brought it up once, maybe three months into the year. We were eating dinner, and she said, "You've settled here, haven't you?" And I realized that I had. Not because I had made some big decision to integrate or be brave or open my mind to new experiences. I had settled because I had been too stubborn to change my morning routine, and my morning routine had eventually changed everything else.

I still prefer some of my Indian brands. I still think of Delhi when I smell certain spices or hear certain songs. But I also have a favorite place to eat near school now, and friends who text me random things, and a version of myself that makes sense in this place.

The irony is that my inflexibility was what made me flexible. By refusing to change the small things, I had the stability to change the big things. Every routine morning, I had enough solid ground beneath me to step into something unknown. And now, looking back, I think that's maybe what it means to actually grow somewhere new. Not to abandon who you were, but to bring that person along steadily, habit by habit, until you're suddenly somewhere else entirely without having planned the journey.

text:
I rode a bus for two hours every morning to get to school, and I spent three years convinced that this was evidence that my parents didn't care about me. The bus route was crowded and stopped at every corner and took a detour through neighborhoods that seemed to have nothing to do with the school. The drive straight there was twenty minutes. The bus made it an ordeal.

My parents had offered to drive me. They had offered to let me transfer to the closer school. I said no to both, which was the teenage equivalent of cutting off your nose to spite your face. Instead I took the bus and I was angry about it, this anger that was diffuse and didn't have a clear target but seemed to blame my parents for making me suffer for reasons I couldn't articulate.

The bus ride wasn't actually bad. It was just long. By sophomore year, I knew the driver's name. I knew the usual passengers, the ones who got on at the same stops every day. There was a guy in a maintenance uniform who always brought coffee. There was an elderly woman who read the same book for three months. There was a teenager who practiced violin in the back of the bus, which sounds obnoxious but was actually kind of beautiful.

I convinced myself that hating the bus ride was justified. Two hours a day that I could have spent sleeping, or doing homework, or literally anything else. But looking back, I don't think I actually hated the bus ride. I hated the idea of the bus ride, which is different. I hated what it represented, which was something about my family not being the kind of family where parents drove you to school, where you had a car, where things were easy.

One morning, six months into senior year, the bus broke down. We all got out in the rain and stood there while the driver called for a replacement. An older woman - the one with the book - stood next to me and said, "Well, this is inconvenient." And I said yes, and she said, "But it's not the worst thing, is it? At least we got farther than usual."

And something shifted. I realized I had spent three years riding this bus with all these people, building these small routines, and I had hated all of it without ever actually experiencing it. I had been too busy resenting the bus route to notice that the bus ride was fine. Boring sometimes, but fine.

I started actually being on the bus after that. I read. I talked to people. I started sitting by the window and watching the city unfold in a way I hadn't noticed before. There was a park that appeared around mile seven. A mural that changed every month. A building that was being demolished and rebuilt. None of this was new - it had all been there the whole time. I had just been too angry to see it.

I still think about the bus ride sometimes now. I think about how much time I wasted being resentful about something that was actually fine. The bus wasn't the problem. My assumption that difficulty meant something was wrong with my family was the problem.

When I got my license, I stopped taking the bus. But I never felt like I won. I felt like I had lost the opportunity to understand something, which took me a while to articulate. Which was that sometimes we make ourselves suffer by refusing to accept the shape our lives actually take. We convince ourselves that if things are hard, we're being victimized. We don't notice that hard and fine can be the same thing.

The bus ride taught me that, eventually. Took me three years to learn it, but it's one of those lessons I actually remember now.

meta.topic: the bus route that took two hours each way

text:
My uncle had a farm two hours outside the city, and every summer starting when I was nine, my family would drive out there for a week. The farm was the kind of place where there was always work to do, and the work was often physical in a way that felt both tedious and necessary. By the time I was fifteen, I had done enough of the tasks to know the rhythms - when things needed watering, when animals needed feeding, when the fencing needed checking.

Learning to drive started as the smallest of habits. My uncle had a tractor, and he used it to pull a trailer around the property, moving equipment and feed and whatever else needed moving. One summer, he asked if I wanted to help, and helping meant driving the tractor while he guided from the back. I was fourteen, far too young to legally drive anywhere, but on his property, nobody was watching.

That first time, I was terrified. The tractor was huge and loud and nothing like the car I would eventually learn to drive in. My hands shook. I couldn't figure out the gears. The tractor lurched forward and I nearly threw my uncle off the trailer. He laughed and told me to try again. So I did.

The second time was less terrifying. The third time, I knew which gear I needed. By the end of that first summer, I could drive the tractor smoothly enough that my uncle stopped holding on and just sat in the trailer, letting me take him where I needed to go. It was the first time I had felt competent at anything physical, which sounds strange, but I had always been a clumsy kid. Bad at sports, bad at any activity that required coordination. But something about the tractor made sense to me.

For three summers, the first thing I did when we arrived at the farm was ask my uncle if he needed the tractor moved. He always did. There was always a reason to drive it - moving hay, clearing a field, pulling out stumps. It became this small routine between us. We didn't talk much while I drove. We just existed in the comfortable silence of people doing necessary work together.

I think what happened is that something in me shifted without me noticing. I stopped being the kid who was learning to drive the tractor and became the person who could drive the tractor well enough that my uncle trusted me with it completely. The habit wasn't just about the driving. It was about showing up every summer and doing the same task over and over until it stopped being a task and became just something I did.

This sounds small, like it doesn't matter. But when I actually learned to drive a car at sixteen, it was almost boring. I already knew how to operate a machine, how to think about space and speed and what was happening around me. I already understood that learning something took repetition and patience and that most days it wasn't going to feel dramatic or special.

My uncle died when I was seventeen, before I had a chance to show him that I had learned to drive a real car. He never got to sit in the passenger seat of something I was driving legally. But I think about those summers a lot, about how the most important thing I learned from him was that showing up over and over, doing the small things that nobody notices, is actually what makes you capable of doing the big things when they matter.

text:
The pool at Hamilton High has never been the same since I left, or at least that's what I tell myself when I pass it on my way to school now. The water still looks blue and calm through the glass doors, but I don't see myself there anymore. I used to spend more time in that pool than I did in my own house. From 6 a.m. to 7 a.m. before school, then again after classes until dinner, my life orbited around lane four, the one closest to the left. The coach knew exactly when I would arrive and which goggles I would wear - the black ones with the clear lenses, never the tinted ones because I liked to see the bottom of the pool.

Then junior year, three months before regionals, I tore my rotator cuff. It happened on a Tuesday during a set of butterfly drills, a movement I had done thousands of times. One moment my arm moved through the water the way it always had, and the next moment something inside my shoulder just gave way. The pain was sharp but strangely small, like someone had put a single wrong note in a song I knew perfectly. I kept swimming for another lap before I told Coach.

Everyone said I would come back. The doctor said maybe six months of physical therapy, maybe a year. My parents whispered about surgery in the kitchen, their voices reaching my room as a low hum of possibility. But what I heard underneath all of that was the unspoken thing: maybe not. Maybe the thing that had defined me, that had made me who I was supposed to become, would not be something I did anymore.

For three months after the injury, I didn't go near the pool. I couldn't watch from the deck because it would hurt too much, not in my shoulder but somewhere deeper. My teammates would text to ask how I was doing, and I would respond with thumbs-up emojis that felt like lies. I started sleeping in. I picked up books I had meant to read. I learned to bake bread, actually bake it, not just help my mom measure flour. One Tuesday morning, when I would normally have been in the pool, I went back to that same place and sat on the side for the first time since the injury.

That sounds like a small thing, I know. But sitting there, watching the water and the swimmers moving through it, I realized something unexpected. I wasn't watching them and thinking about what I was missing. I was just watching them, the way a person might watch anything beautiful they weren't part of. And that felt like freedom, which made me angry and then guilty for feeling angry.

The physical therapist asked me eventually if I wanted to try swimming again, just for fitness, just for the feeling of it. And I said yes, and it was strange, learning to move in water like someone who had never been trained, like someone who was just discovering what their body could do. It's been six months now. I still swim, but I'm not training toward anything. The pool doesn't own me anymore. I'm there because I want to be, and somehow that matters more than all the medals I never got to earn.

meta.topic: an injury that ended a competitive swimming career
meta.prompt: Describe a place where you feel most yourself, and why.

text:
I have a collection of forty-two subway maps from cities around the world. They live in a portfolio folder under my bed, and my dad thinks they should mean something about my future, like they're evidence that I'm going to be an urban planner or a geographer or something that makes sense. He's wrong. They mean that I got obsessed with something and nobody in my family knew how to talk to me about it.

The obsession started with the Tokyo Metro map, which my friend Priya brought back from her family trip. It was beautiful in a way I didn't expect a map to be. The lines were color-coded perfectly. The geometry of it was almost perfect - not perfectly symmetrical, but organized in a way that felt intentional. I asked her if I could keep it, and she said yes, probably assuming I would look at it once and forget about it.

I looked at it every day. I studied it. I tried to understand the logic of why certain stations existed, why the lines crossed the way they did, why Tokyo had solved the problem of urban transit in a particular way. Then I started collecting maps from other cities. London, Berlin, Paris, Seoul, Singapore, São Paulo. Each one had a different solution to the same problem: how do you move people through a city efficiently and beautifully?

My dad saw the collection growing and said, "Oh, you're interested in city planning?" And I said no, and then he looked confused because he couldn't understand why I would care about something that wasn't leading anywhere. My mom asked if I wanted to learn about architecture, as if that might be a gateway to understanding what I was doing. My little brother just said they were cool and left it at that, which was the most honest response.

The thing is, I couldn't explain it to them because I couldn't explain it to myself. It wasn't about planning or architecture or travel. It was about seeing all these different ways that humans had solved the same problem, and each solution reflected something about the city's values and history and priorities. The Tokyo Metro was elegant and efficiency-focused. The London Underground was historical and sprawling. The Paris Metro was art deco and romantic. The Seoul Metro was modern and aggressively practical.

But I was also looking at them because they were beautiful, and I was lonely, and these maps of distant cities felt like permission to think about something else, something that didn't have anything to do with high school or friendship groups or whether anyone thought I was weird. I could spend an hour studying the Reykjavik Bus System and nobody could tell me I was wasting my time because it was clearly not something I should be wasting time on, which meant it was private, which meant it was safe.

My parents eventually had a conversation where they decided this was either a sign of genius or a sign that I needed to get out more, and they weren't sure which. They tried to be supportive by enrolling me in a summer course about urban development, which I hated because now my hobby had become a Thing I Was Doing and it stopped being mine.

I still have the forty-two maps. I haven't added any new ones in over a year, which probably means the obsession is dying, which is sad because I had hoped it meant something, that there was some version of my future where this mattered. But mostly it just means I got very interested in something and then moved on, which is what people do.

What I wish is that my dad had just asked me why I liked them instead of trying to turn it into evidence that I was destined for something. Sometimes people are just interested in things because those things are interesting, and that's allowed to be enough.

meta.topic: an obsession with subway maps
meta.prompt: Some students have a background, identity, interest, or talent that is so meaningful they believe their application would be incomplete without it. If this sounds like you, then please share your story.

text:
Three years ago, I started collecting rainfall data. I have a rain gauge that I installed in our backyard, and every morning I write down the measurement from the previous day. It was supposed to be a project, but it became something else entirely, which is where the argument with my parents comes in.

The project started in ninth grade for science class. I was supposed to do a weather experiment, and I thought rainfall data over time would be interesting to track. I set up a simple rain gauge - a plastic tube marked with measurements - and started recording. At first, it was just data. Rain fell, I measured it, I wrote it down. The science teacher gave me an A on the project and that should have been the end of it.

But I kept measuring.

I made charts. I tracked monthly patterns, annual patterns, driest days and wettest days. I started comparing my data to the official weather station data and noticed small discrepancies, which led me down a research rabbit hole about how measurement methods affect accuracy. I built a better gauge. I started collecting data from three different locations in our neighborhood to track how rainfall varies geographically. It became this obsessive thing that nobody else in my family understood.

My dad eventually asked me what I was doing with all of this. I tried to explain the patterns I was seeing, the connections between rainfall and temperature and humidity, the way weather systems moved through our area. He listened, and then he said, "But what is the point? Are you trying to become a meteorologist? Are you planning to use this for something?"

And I didn't have a good answer because the point was becoming harder to articulate. The point was that I found it satisfying to know things precisely, to track patterns over time, to understand the minute variations in something as simple as water falling from the sky. The point was also that I was processing my parents' divorce through the lens of meteorological data, which I didn't tell him because that sounded insane.

My mom was more concerned. She said that I spent too much time on this and not enough time on things that would "matter" later, whatever that means. She suggested I find a hobby that was more social, that involved other people, that would look good on college applications. She suggested cheerleading and model UN. She didn't understand that my rain gauge was how I was making sense of my world when everything else had become chaotic and unpredictable.

The argument escalated when my parents wanted to send me to summer camp. Three weeks away from my rain gauge, from my daily measurements, from the one thing that felt stable. I refused. I had a meltdown about it. I said they didn't understand me, that they never respected my interests, that they just wanted me to be someone I wasn't. All of which was probably true, but also, I was being irrational about an inanimate piece of plastic and some numbers.

We compromised. I didn't go to camp. I also agreed to spend less time on the data collection. But the rift was there, the understanding that my parents thought I was wasting my time and I thought they didn't see what I was trying to do.

Here's the thing I don't think I'll ever explain to them: I wasn't just collecting data about weather. I was collecting evidence that the world was measurable and knowable. I was proving to myself that even when everything felt random and chaotic, some things followed patterns. Some things could be tracked and understood.

Three years of data, and now I have a clear picture of the rainfall patterns in my area. I can predict, with reasonable accuracy, whether a given month will be wet or dry. It's not nothing. But I'm also aware that I've spent three years on something that only I care about, that won't matter to anyone else, that doesn't lead anywhere.

Maybe that's okay. Maybe there's value in caring about something just because it matters to you, even if it doesn't matter to anyone else. My parents still don't really get it. But I'm still measuring, and the rain is still falling, and the data is still there.

meta.topic: collecting rainfall data for three years
